title: Really good computer overall
text: I bought this computer twice. The first time, it was only charging to 79%, then it would say "79% (plugged in, not charging)". I contacted ASUS customer support and spent so much time trying to figure out why it wasn't charging to 100%. The whole problem was the stupid MyASUS app. It pops up when you first set up the computer, and it lets you pick a charging mode. I had it on the recommended setting, which only allows the battery to reach 80% (or 79%). I didn't realize this until after I bought the new one and I was setting the new one up and I realized, that was my mistake. I'm still angry that the ASUS customer support didn't realize that that was my whole issue. But it's fine, I figured it out. It doesn't have a touch screen, that's why it says not rated for that. But other than all of my issues, it's a really good computer. I've been using it for school and I'm happy with it, it loads everything quickly.

title: Nice laptop that has some beef to it.
text:
While I know this isn't Amazons fault, USPS took 4 weeks to deliver this package, the outer box was so smashed I could see inside it. But the laptops box seemed intact, I was hesitant to even open it. 4 weeks of being thrown around can't be good. This was sent Priority mail too, but I can't know where this thing went, lol.

However, once opened up, all looked well and proper, and the padding was well protecting. The computer booted right up, quickly too. So far so good with no issues to report.

Now getting used to Windows 11 took a day or two, but I got there eventually and am OK with this OS.

This computer can run in different modes with the video systems, either using the discrete Nvidia 1650 video full time(runs hot), or part time(Hybrid Mode) when gaming, or you can turn it off and just use the AMD Radeon CPU graphics for longer battery life. Very clever.

There are options for fan speed too. And if you leave it plugged in all the time, there is an option for that to save your battery. Some useful tools and versatility. CUP temps while gaming are low too. At light use, the CPU is at 33 C showing good thermal qualities.

And not too full of crapware either. There was the usual anti virus, but I deleted that and I'm good with MS Defender. And if you do not use Microsoft OneDrive (I hate it), make sure you uninstall it before you transfer all your files. You can use up a lot of Gigabytes and not know it.

The 17.3 inch screen is drop dead gorgeous and can be viewed at any angle, it really looks nice. Game play is great too with fast crisp visuals. So far, I have Minecraft running, full video effects on high, and plays like hot butter. The same for Civ 6, full video settings, good visuals, and very fast turn cycles, as fast as I can click the mouse.

Also there are options for upgrades. I can add another hard drive for instance. There are instructions for this online from Lenovo, you can take this thing apart. I've never been squeamish about tearing into a laptop, but this is the first one I've owned that gives you very good detailed how to instructions. Bravo.

There are enough USB ports. One of them is always "On" for say charging a phone. Or, if you forgot your power brick, you can even use a wall wart to get by on. There are also type C USB ports too. And the HDMI port, which I am using right now to view on a monitor. I am using this as a desktop replacement with separate monitor and keyboard.

It has a bit of weight to it, but not too much to carry.

This will serve me well for what I need, hopefully for years. I once owned a nice Sager laptop, which were rebranded Lenovo products. It was always a solid device.

UPDATE: For those wondering about the 32 GB USB memory card, it's the credit card size white thing taped to the box. You have to flip or remove the little part you plug in. Pretty much worthless, but nice sentiment anyway.

I also installed Doom Eternal for a real world test, 75 FPS and flows like hot liquid lead. Fan speed is not obnoxious at all.

title: Great specs and build quality for the price!
text:
I had done plenty of research into gaming laptops before picking this one. Just a little back story, I'm an IT professional and all around computer nerd. After a bad experience with my last gaming laptop I figured gaming laptops weren't practical and thinking about that 8lb monster now I'm quite sure it had a lot to do with size. That was a 17" HP "entertainment notebook"...granted the glorious screen real estate was well appreciated, however I'm glad I chose a 15.6" this time around. Because we're not going to be gaming on these ALL the time! When it's at home and hooked to AC power THEN it can flex it's muscles.

And in truth, you are getting some pretty decent muscle for the price. The 1050 ti GPU is no slouch and during my quick gaming tests proved more than sufficient for most modern games. My Legion Y520 was purchased direct from Lenovo during a sale so I got the i7 7700hq and 1050 ti with 8GB DDR4 and a 128GB m.2 nvme SSD. I added another 8GB of memory and a 500GB 2.5" SSD to beef it up some.

On the go, I appreciate not only the lighter weight and size but - in the case of this laptop - I also really appreciate it not screaming "gaming laptop". The outside aesthetic is sharp and professional with mild edginess. Personally, I much prefer this subtle look. It has a faux Kevlar pattern on the lid and soft touch surface on the keyboard palmrest with a faux brushed metal trim up by the screen hinge. The hinge is flanked by the two Harmon speakers which actually sound pretty good and the design choice looks awesome. The touch pad is bordered in a red accent and the keyboard has a red back light with 3 settings, off low and high. When the keyboard back light is off you can still see the red keyboard accents during daylight.

Of course, there are some complaints. Battery life is going to be minimal to average at best since it's only a 45wh. But realistically that's fine, this just wasn't meant to be an all day road warrior. Also although the sound is pretty good there are laptops that have a subwoofer so if that is a requirement then look at those. And as for the screen while it is an IPS there are definitely better ones. I plan on hooking this up to my 24" Dell IPS Led for the much better brightness and color accuracy so for what it is it suffices and is definitely better than a TN panel.

All things said this is a pretty awesome gaming laptop from Lenovo. There were 2 others I'd been looking into for a while, the Dell Inspiron 15 7000 gaming series and the Acer VX whatever series. The Dell came in an all red option, something I was really digging for a while. But the reviews all decried the poor choice of the screen (which prompted Dell to offer an IPS option now for $50 more). The Acer just looks like a high performance jet engine behemoth, which I also was digging for a while...I just couldn't see me carrying that in public or "unleashing it" when I just wanted to do a quick browse lol!

title: Honest review from a "non-techie"
text:
I've had this laptop about a month now and I am impressed. Full disclosure, I upgraded after almost 9 years from a 13.3" ASUS UX301LA Zenbook Ultrabook with 256GB of storage space to this beauty. Back then I just needed something lightweight to carry to and from college, but obviously my needs have changed. I was always disappointed by the lack of internal storage space (for installing programs) and the lack of ability for tougher tasks like gaming or video editing.

Enter Black Friday sales 2022. Ok, so this was an impulse buy, but I can justify it. The 15.6" QHD display is breathtaking. I don't have a TV (by choice) so I watch anything I'm going to watch on a cellphone or laptop and this Alienware has dramatically improved that experience. Not to mention the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 graphics card which allows me to play games such as the Fallout series, Red Dead Redemption II and Cyberpunk 2077 (more on those later). I went with the Intel Core i9 processor since I don't really know much about AMD and have always used Intel. I also love the 1TB internal SSD drive with the option to expand! I cannot overstate how important this is after my ASUS with limited internal memory. Sure you can use external storage (or even cloud storage) for things like pictures, video, music and other files, but you NEED internal memory to install most programs properly. 1TB is definitely enough for my needs, but if it ever isn't apparently I can add another TB SSD. I'll still use an external for documents and stuff, but glad to know my hard drive won't be full after installing Adobe.

As far as the keyboard goes, I can take or leave the RGB stuff, but it's a nice feature. However, I really love the keyboard. I've read mixed reviews about whether or not it's the Cherry MX Keyboard. I don't know what that is, but I'm about 99.99% certain mine does have the Cherry MX keyboard (even though it's not the AMD version), since it's a whole other level from what I'm used to and has that mechanical feedback feel to it. Better than my previous laptop, better than my work laptop and pretty much anything else I've used.

Other minor observations: sound is good enough, obviously any sound system (including headsets) will be better than built-in speakers. Weight is exactly what I'd expect for a 15.6" laptop, not the lightest thing or the heaviest. 5GHz CPU speed - seems good enough, although when I look at the specs it says 2.50 GHz which really threw me off for a bit until I found out that 5GHz means the Max Turbo Frequency and 2.5GHz is the base. Not sure what all that means, but there you go. 32GB of RAM seems good enough for me. Of course it has a built in webcam (which I haven't used yet), plenty of connectivity options and ports (WiFi, Bluetooth, Ethernet, HDMI, USB, headphone jack). I wish there was a USB port on the left side (2 on the right and one in the rear) so cables wouldn't be in the way of the mouse if used, but so far it hasn't been an issue.

However I do have one, somewhat major issue, power. The power adapter itself is huge, as in the size of a brick! Sure it'll be on the floor out of the way most of the time, but carrying it in a bag is just ridiculous. But size aside, when I game (told you I'd come back to it) even on AC power it drains the battery?!? Not so much to interrupt my game, but it's still concerning to me. Why would the battery drain while connected to AC power? Maybe it's a heating issue? But I even bought a cooling pad and it's still doing it. I haven't really noticed a heat issue (I monitor with Speccy after reading up on the topic and everything seems to be in line with what others say is fine), but some of the graphic intensive games like Cyberpunk 2077 seems to do a number on the battery. When operating normal (not gaming) on just battery I didn't seem to get much more than 2 hrs at the most. So, for me at least, I plan to mostly use this near a power source.

So there you have it, an honest, non-sponsored, review by someone who isn't computer illiterate but not a techie nerd. Would I recommend the Alienware m15 r7? Yes, absolutely!

title: Superb Laptop, poor touchpad
text:
[[VIDEOID:78eee64d0f21eab178a7dbd286a2900a]] I am very happy with this purchase. I was wary of the negative reviews but had none of the problems that the bad reviews mention, though I guess there is always a chance that one can receive a defective product. Looking at amazon reviews every laptop, even macbooks have around 10% defective product rate ... apparently quality control is a thing of the past, now its pure luck.

The system is stable, Windows 10 is not as great as Windows 7 but it isn't as bad as 8 or Vista ... with time (updates) it might actually end up being the next decent Windows OS. The dell auto-update app didn't work for me, I had to go to the dell website, enter my Service Tag, download their system detect and install the recommended driver\bios upgrades. Nvidia drivers upgraded fine through its own application.

The Graphics card is very decent for a laptop. Playing Witcher 3 with HBAO+ shader and Nvidia's recommended settings(most things on Ultra, HairWorks on Low) I get consistent 30+ FPS, including in Novigrad.

The keyboard is satisfactory, keys seem to be full size and typing produces satisfactory auditory response(its not a silent keyboard). The back-light is white and that doesn't look cool. The touchpad is barely acceptable: the clicking keys on the touchpad are flimsy and there is no separation between them, so sometimes left-click engages the right-click and vice versa. Sensitivity and feel is alright, I've seen much worse, but for gaming a mouse is essential.

The SSD is low on space (only 256 GB) but there is an additional port for adding an additional drive, and though small, the SSD is naturally lightning fast (boots in seconds, loads witcher levels in seconds ... both took minutes on my last machine with a HDD).

The screen is crisp, back-lit and has a wide viewing angle. The only problem is that the machine comes with (and suggests) a 1920 x 1080 resolution which is perhaps too high for such a small screen, everything looks unnaturally tiny. Windows 10 has a zooming option that helps a little but its doen't fix everything. Currently I've set chrome to zoom text by 125% and Windows to zoom stuff by 150% and now it feels somewhat reasonable.

text:

The good, the laptop is fast, small, and light. I have not yet put it through the paces with some science data crunching and 3D graphics but so far so good. The only little knock on it is the keyboard keys are a little different from a typical layout due to the speakers but even after only an hour of two of banging away on the keys I am mostly adapted to it with few mistakes.

title: Amazing performance! Plastic but a very durable and fingerprint ...

title: The best laptop in this price segment, guaranteed!
text:
To the point:
You really get a lot of bang for your buck on this laptop. The spec list reads like a laptop wishlist,
- SSD and fast HDD? Check.
- IPS G-sync screen? Check.
- Full keyboard with solid construction? Check.
- Full fat desktop grade pascal GPU? Check, check, check!

Build:
Ultimately the laptop is pretty dang nice, and doesn't betray it's spec list in the slightest. Be aware the the pictured model is the GTX1060 version not the 1070 version, I make this point because the 1070 version is a little heavier, and little thicker. Points off for deceptive marketing, eh? Even still it's only marginally bigger, and is definitely far far thinner than gaming laptops of yesteryear.
The build quality is nice, but only the outer lid is made from aluminum, all other materials present are hard plastic. However, the plastic on the inside is meant to feel like metal and has been texturized to lend to this illusion.
The keyboard is also nice with a good solid feel on the keys and a good amount of travel. They keys themselves are vibrantly colored with the black and red(Though you could swear it's orange) contrast and red backlight. The WASD keys in particular have the sides of the keys colored as well to lend additional contrast to these all important gaming keys.

Performance:
This is what you're really here for though, right? And yes this thing is a beast! The GTX 1070 in this laptop actually has more CUDA cores than it's desktop brother, but a slower overall clock-speed. They say that the 10 series mobile cards should be within 10% of their desktop counterparts but the GTX1070 in particular is closer still, often matching or even in some rare cases where the extra cores are used EXCEEDING it's desktop counterpart. Wow! Just to put that in perspective, this single GPU is faster than TWO 980Ms in SLI or the full fat GTX980 put into the most expensive laptops of the previous generation. We're talking GTX980Ti performance in a MOBILE gpu. Expect 60+FPS in any title, at 1080p/Ultra. (Battlefield 4 at 124FPS, like, wow...)
The CPU is no slouch but be aware that the i7 6700HQ is a solid 20% slower than the desktop variant. It's still an incredibly fast processor, far more than enough for gaming, but this(And only this) part still lags behind it's desktop brother.
SSD speeds are great, right about 500MB/s Read/write, and the HDD is good too at about 120MB/s Read 90ish/write. (7200RPM, whoo!) which is significantly faster than the MSI competitors measily 30MB/s read/write speeds for a laptop of similar price and spec.
The speakers are... Well they're speakers. Nothing to get excited about at all. Use good headphones or external speakers.

Screen:
Colors are nice but not over-vivid. As you'd expect from an IPS panel the viewing angles are superb. The brightness is excellent as well, you "could" use this outside... But you probably shouldn't because...

Battery:
Bad. 3 hours tops doing menial tasks with reduced brightness. Technically you can use this thing without the power adapter plugged in but at an very gimped level and for a very short time. This laptop is simply too powerful for it's own good, yeah?

Conclusion:
Of all of the currently available Pascal laptops I feel like this one delivers the most performance for the best price. For 100-200 less you can have something with far less niceties and a GTX1060 which is quite a step down from the 1070, and for $1000 or MORE you can have a bigger chasis and the SAME GPU. GTX 1080 laptops start at around $3000, ouch! So this is definitely the sweet spot.

Pros:
Performance
Good price for what it is(Still expensive)
Excellent HDD speed

Cons:
Poor battery life
Middling speakers for this price range

title: Lot of power that doesn't reach the monitors...
text:
What is the point of a 3080 in a laptop, if you don't have a discrete displayport or preferably 2!
No MUX switch, means that the 3080 has to send its signal through the AMD iGPU.

Displayport over USB-C only, no MUX switch, means the 3080 sends signal through AMD iGPU, then over a bandwidth limited USB-C port, to an adapter, to your monitor.

I have a 360hz 1080p monitor, that I can only run at 240hz because USB-C cannot handle 360hz @1080p, not enough bandwidth.

The hdmi port, is 2.0, not 2.1. That means that you cannot get more than 120hz on my 1440p monitor through hdmi and it won't do 360hz on my 1080p either.

To top it off, you can only run the HDMI + USB-C to Displayport for these 2 monitors w/ the 1440p @ 100hz and the 1080p @ 240hz WITHOUT the integrated monitor running (laptop cover closed).
Again, probably because everything is running through the damn iGPU.

This is not a cheap low-end laptop. It's over $3k.

This is like having a racing motor in a vehicle that cannot translate all of its horsepower to the tires, but only a portion of it.

BAD DESIGN and very disappointing!

Other than that, this is a beast of laptop, w/ a nice integrated 1440p, 165hz monitor with 100% dci-p3 color gamut.

But then it is cut off at the knees by lack of port selection.
One usb-c only, 3 USB A, no dedicated display port, and HDMI 2.0 instead of 2.1.

Now, if you have just the laptop monitor, nothing else connected, the 3080 also travels through the iGPU it seems!

This means you cannot remove the iGPU power draw overhead and underclock the 3080 for better battery life purposes when not plugged in to the wall, or plugged in via usb-c power.

This means you are limited to the Vega (why AMD, why still Vega on Cezanne 5000 series?) iGPU w/ 3080 turned off on battery power if you want any time on battery that is useful.

The armoury crate software won't let you mess w/ the Manual over/under-clocking mode (used loosely here, since you are just determining max tdp power draw for each) for CPU / GPU power draw on battery... When you need it the most!

You have to rely on 3rd party software and even then, due to the iGPU drawing overhead you can't get the 3080 minimum power draw low enough to compensate for the iGPU power draw overhead and the 3080 simply ceasing to function w/o the power the iGPU is drawing to prolong battery life.

Just too many watts of constant draw total.

A $3k laptop should be able to power its own monitor and 2 additional monitors w/o gimping performance, without adapter cables regardless. It has a more than capable 3080 in it for crying out loud.

Very disappointing!

A mux switch would help, which bypasses the iGPU when using the discrete 3080, but really there should be dedicated display port, if not 2, and an additional usb-c port anyways.

If you are using your usb-c for display port, you no longer have a usb-c port for anything else...Power delivery? nope
data transfer? nope

And w/ only 3 usb-A ports, i have to use one usb-a port attached to a 4-port USB-A hub since any laptop cooling pad worth a damn has 2 usb plugs to power it, leaving just 1 port for keyboard, mouse, headset, etc.

Now, if you have a wireless headset as i do, it also needs a port (in my case, 2 so as to power the extra battery).

This laptop is so close to being really top of the line, but it just falls on its face in the areas that matter!

What good is a 3080 driving 300-400 fps in a game like CS GO, if you can't power a monitor above 240hz?
They have to be on par or or the monitor simply can't display all the frames generated, literally a 100+ frames are simply never shown on screen.

Several versions offer a 300hz, 360hz built-in display on these laptops, but nobody is competitively gaming full time on a 15" screen...so, that makes no sense either.

All the right side has for ports on the laptop is that useless proprietary port thing-a-mabob (keystone) that is useless for most everyone.

It really is maddening that the port selection and lack of dedicated display port take a very powerful laptop and make you use it like a much cheaper laptop that would cost around $1,000 less due to a less powerful gpu only generating enough frames for 240hz @ 1080p.

So close, yet so far.

title: Great gaming laptop, awful battery life
text:
This is an excellent gaming laptop. It is thin, light, the screen is gorgeous, and the chassis looks fantastic. However being thin and light the thermals are always going to be terrible. If you use the discrete GPU this laptop will heat up to around 90 degrees for the CPU and GPU quickly doing even basic tasks such as web browsing, reading emails, or youtube. You will not be sitting with this on your lap at these temps it is painfully hot. This Triton ships with "discrete GPU always on" in the PredatorSense menu. Turn that off and it will only use the discrete GPU when needed (for gaming). This allows this laptop to maintain a much more comfortable 35 - 40 degree temp for everyday tasks and remains very quiet with low fan speeds at these lower temps.

Also be aware because the thermals are so bad when you do use the discrete GPU for gaming the fans spin fast and they are LOUD. Not an issue if you are using headphones otherwise it sounds like you are riding in a small jet. The heat also travels up through the keyboard. Not painfully hot but definitely warm.

The battery lasts around 4 hours with "discrete GPU always on" turned off for everyday tasks. When turned on you will be lucky to get 2 hours.

Overall I really like this laptop but just know going in with any thin and light gaming laptop your thermals are going to suffer which means a lot of heat quickly with loud fans when using the discrete GPU. We also use it with Oculus Quest 2 and the link cable which this laptop is more than powerful enough to handle, and thankfully has the correct USB-C port to connect. Being away from the laptop when using VR and not having to use the keyboard the hot temps are no issue whatsoever. Having the option to turn off the discrete GPU to keep temps down for basic tasks is very welcome and makes this laptop usable when travelling. You do have the option of using better thermal paste and undervolting but this will only bring temps down marginally and the fans are still going to be loud.

title: Happy with this product! ...After some error debugging
text:
Edit: Removed 2 stars because of an issue with the speakers decreasing in volume, and I've tried everything to solve it as a driver issue. So it's probably a hardware issue. On top of the other issues I've had, thought it was best to give it what it is: average.

I have really enjoyed using this laptop over the past two weeks. So far, the battery life when only using browsers is good for a computer with these specs. Haven't timed it yet, but I'd guess 3-4 hours depending on how you're using it. The speakers are fine but can be a little quiet at times and are not the best quality I've ever heard from a gaming laptop.

That being said, there are a few issues with this laptop that you will need to fix if you are intent on buying it. All were things I noticed the first time I opened it and were easy to fix.

1. The fan is annoyingly loud
Straight out of the box, not even opening a browser, the cooling fans were whirring like crazy. The fix to this is to go into your advanced power options, then processor power management, and then to maximum processor rate. From what I understand, anything in the 50-60 range will fix this issue without compromising your performance.

2. The backlit keyboard times out while computer is on if you don't touch it for 2 minutes, causing the lights to go dark (Late Nov. 2018 update in Microsoft Store).
The problem here is with the software that runs the keyboard LEDs, and is usually not a hardware problem. Open ROG Aura Core (the keyboard lighting software). Navigate to Aura settings. Turn keyboard lighting off for Sleep and Shut Down.

3. When plugging in or unplugging the battery cord, the screen momentarily flashes black.
This "bug" occurs because the laptop's battery mode lowers the frame rate refresh, and to accommodate the change, the screen flashes back and then back on. To change this, go into your Intel graphics settings, then to Display, and ensure that the frame rate refresh is the same for both your battery mode and plugged in mode.

On top of that, the computer comes with bloatware (easily uninstallable, save for McAfee which sometimes takes longer, but is typically easy.)

Of the three, the backlight issue was the most annoying to solve, taking me much longer than the others to figure out how to fix. Having fixed all these issues, I'm thrilled to say I'm much happier with this purchase than when I first got it.

TL;DR Don't buy this laptop if you don't feel like troubleshooting some of the stupid problems the manufacturer should have thought through. But if you want a great laptop for a good buy, this is one of the better purchases.

title: Great value and good performance.
text:

One tip, when you connect a second monitor via HTML, you will have to reselect the sound source, it defaulted to the HTML, even if it had no speakers.
Also, after I did all the software updates, I was surprised to see the video source defaulted to the Intel onboard graphics, which will slow the system down. I had to go into the Nvidia settings and select the Nvidia graphics as the default for global settings. I thought that strange and might not have noticed if I hadn't run a benchmark and was surprised at how slow the graphics were until I changed the default.
The BIOS settings are really dumbed down, not much to do there.
The build is good, seems sturdy. It is not a light weight computer, but as a desktop replacement, I did not think it would be. Keyboard is good, and looks sharp with the red backlighting.
Overall, very pleased, so far. I almost marked it down for having to fiddle with the Sound and video settings, and the consumerish BIOS, but it doesn't really detract from what seems to be a fine computer for the price. Highly recommended. It really is amazing the amount of computing power we can carry around in a small package for not much money.

title: As of Oct. 2021 this is hands down the BEST VALUE for $1000
text:
I had been eyeing to upgrade my wife's older Samsung ultrabook that is about 5 years old now. She wanted to get into gaming yet her Samsung only had integrated graphics. She was also looking for something that didn't scream gaming laptop (big, bulky, gamer colors and aesthetics) because she does go into the office a few times a week. All while keeping the price under $1400. I just could not find anything these past 9 months at all. The only things that came close were Razer or MSI or Asus products but at a much higher price point, speaking about their sleek looking creator laptops specifically.

Then Acer released this Swift X with a 3050ti and I bought it so quick.

It literally checks all the boxes and I cannot find a valid reason to spend more on those other laptops. The only thing I will give them is yes those brands do have tighter tolerances, build materials and higher refresh rate screens. That being said, Acer really made this a sleek looking and well built product nonetheless, so you are splitting hairs to spend more for those other options. Acer made the right compromises overall.

Down to the important details, how does it perform? Stellar, period. We have been playing Paladins, New World and Apex Legends with 0 issues and 60+ fps. It can run just fine at Medium to High depending on the game. It flies in day to day tasks that her work demands as well. She lives in Excel and PowerBI.

The camera and microphones are also a nice step up from my HP omen and her Samsung Ultrabook, which was surprising because those both cost more at the time. The keyboard is a bit smaller and she is getting used to it, but 95% of the time she has it on a stand and uses a bluetooth keyboard/mouse. That being said, the keyboard and trackpad built in are good and reliable. Nice key travel and smooth control on the trackpad.

She has not used the device long term on battery power so I cannot comment there, but from other reviewers on YouTube it seems to be well above average.

The screen is vibrant and color accurate with a matte surface (important because her setup has a window behind her which introduced glare on her old glossy screen)

TLDR; At around $1000, this is hands down the best laptop for multipurpose. Its not a gaming powerhouse like my HP omen, but its quieter, sleeker, and can game at 60+ fps very easily on the titles that matter to us. For anyone who needs a laptop to look professional to take for work or school but also wants to game effectively, buy this. You wont be disappointed.

title: Decent laptop, terrible battery life
text:
If you're reading this you may have read independent reviews on another site. Some complain about the weight, build quality, I even found one complaining about how thick it is... I found one review complaining about how it's not comparable to a full power 3070 laptop GPU. While true it's comparable to a 115watt 2070 (looking like this ones 7-9% better by my measures), but it also has a newer better processor than my old 2070 laptop so that's a bonus.

So about laptops, let's be realistic, the rule of thumb in laptop GPUs is that the current generation is nearly equal (+/- a few %) to the generation before it. That's been a pretty accurate saying for the past 10+ years. This GPU is the lower wattage version, if you have a 115watt 2070 save your money it's not going to be a huge difference unless your playing CPU intensive games... Comparing this to my wife's laptop with a full powered 3070 it's lighter, has comparable battery life, and runs a little cooler. It seems to be less FPS at about a 10-20 FPS difference in some games at high to ultra settings, but still maintains 60+ in all tested games. Comparing it to my old 2070 laptop this ones a little better, but not worth the upgrade in the name of performance, for me it was an upgrade in portability.

Yes it gets hot, but mine has yet to approach thermal throttle territory, and yes it has some weight, and yes it's thick compared to almost all nongaming laptops and a little thicker than some other gaming laptops. Admittedly this is my first msi laptop, but the build quality feels good to me in comparison to the Alienware, Lenovo, and Asus laptops I've owned, it's also thinner and lighter than all of the ones I've owned, especially the Alienwares.

One downside is the battery, plan on having this thing on an outlet if you're going to use it for more than an 1 or 2 hours gaming, 3-4 hours just running with word and a browser. This is the biggest drawback I could find, which doesn't bother me much since outlets are easy to come by this day and age. When comparing to other laptops I've owned its dismal, even my 2070 watt laptop got 6 hours when new, 3-4 hours when gaming. I figure this may be a side effect of people wanting to make smaller thinner laptops... Both my wifes 3070 laptop and my 3070 laptop have the same dismal battery life.

Another possible downside is the limited storage. With games like Forza Horizon 5, CoD, GTA, etc you're not going to have a vast library on the m.2 that comes with it. But my external SSD works fine to solve this, and while I haven't taken it apart I read there is either a second m.2 or a 2.5 inch bay - note that's just what I've read, I have not personally confirmed this. All in all the limited storage may affect some, but it's easily remedied using an external drive, thumb drive, and possibly internal expansion (again, I haven't confirmed this yet)

It's a settings game to achieve 144fps, same can be said for getting 240 on a desktop pc, but it's so far been doable at decent graphics in most games I've played on it.

title: Great laptop for the price, only minor issues
text:
I bought this a few weeks ago, and so far I love it. I got it to play games that were a little more technologically demanding than my previous laptop could handle (right now, mostly Dragon's Dogma and Overwatch), and it's been performing admirably. Games run smoothly and at very attractive visual standards, as one should expect from a 960M. Startup is way faster than my (3ish years old) previous laptop, and the screen is a dramatic improvement - I've seen people complain about it, but besides a slight darkening at extreme angles, it's a very good display.

To bolster the memory, I added a Firecuda 2tb hybrid drive in the HDD slot, which was a little nerve wracking but overall painless (make sure you get the cover to sit right when you screw it back on, it's a little too forgiving). I cannibalized an old laptop for hard drive screws, so keep that in mind if you plan on adding memory. It's a great drive, I really recommend it, and I can guarantee that it fits (if you grab one, make sure it's the 2.5" laptop drive, 7mm tall). There are a bunch of guides on how to do it, and how to move relevant files over (and how to make the new drive the "default" drive).

The only real problem is the GPU generates a lot of heat, so when I play games, the fans run pretty high. Keeps the laptop within acceptable temperature ranges though, so it's worth it. Standard use generates zero noise. I guess another problem is the chassis's tendency to accumulate smudges. It's a slick look, and feels good, but if you're a neat freak it might irritate. The touchpad doesn't have detached buttons either, so you mostly get around by tapping the pad, but I've already gotten used to it. Make sure you disable the setting that delays touchpad input for a second or so after touching keys - it's meant to keep your hand from accidentally hitting the pad while you type, but really it just makes the pad feel unresponsive. And while I'm dispensing advice, update all the drivers and the OS ASAP. Basically prepare for an hour of just updating your laptop after it's out of the box. This process is bog standard for laptops, but improved measurably by the fact that restarting this particular device only takes around 14 seconds.

The Obligatory List:

Pros
Great performance for the money (will play basically any game not released in late 2016, at medium to high standards)
Good display
Stylish (YMMV)
Minimal bloatware (I killed Mcafee and installed AVG, personally)
Full keyboard (dunno if anyone cares about this but me)
Easy upgrade (comparatively)
SDD makes for rapid startup

Cons
Audible fans under high load
Surfaces require high maintenance
Not a great touchpad (though far from unusable)

Complaints I read about but have not experienced
Broken touchpad
Low feedback keyboard (it's fine)
Dark screen (it's not)
Bad audio (about as good as you can expect from a laptop, gets pretty loud)
Constant fans
Catastrophic hard/software failure (I did have an issue with an NVIDIA driver update, but it was an easy fix)

Final score: Not perfect, but a seriously good buy and more than capable of fulfilling most user needs with grace.

title: What a difference 5 years makes (UPDATED!)
text:
This replaces my Alienware 17 which was deployed in 2014. How's it stack up? Well....

The BLUF statement: The G7 (and I did receive a G7, not a G5) is a very good "right now" gaming laptop. By that I mean it will play (with two exceptions, see below) pretty much everything out there with high-level video settings. There are some caveats there which I'll get into, but bottom line up front: it may come across as a budget Alienware but the performance is really very good.

Now then.

The G series is replacing the Inspirons in this space. The idea is that if you aren't looking to go whole hog into the Alienware world but would rather have a very easy Stock Spec Is All I Need gaming machine, the G series is there as an option. That Dell owns Alienware does allow for some supply chain efficiencies (indeed, the G7 uses an Alienware 4 cell battery) so there's some good crossover, but make no mistake - if you want the absolute cream of the crop future proofed expandable gaming laptop, the G7 isn't going to be it.

But that's not really the point of the G series. It exists as an easy way to play today's games, and at that it does a very good job. I'll hit various components in turn below and talk about some of the design decisions and compromises Dell made to bring this laptop into being. I'll also have to point out that the 5 years separating my Alienware 17 and this G7 is very noticeable....new games that my Alienware struggles with are a breeze for the G7, all the more interesting since the G7 is, in my opinion, a 2019 mid-range gaming laptop where as 5 years ago that Alienware was upper tier.

Physical design: It looks like a mid 1990's laptop, but that belies the power under the keyboard. When closed it doesn't look like anything special, and certainly doesn't have the attitude that an Alienware has. It would not look out of place in an office. It's about as thin as something like this can be (what with the dual cooling, heatsinks, etc) and the materials are...largely plastic. There's a bit of heft to it but nothing outrageous. In other words, typical Dell laptop look and feel. The tradeoff here is that with case volume being minimal, there are some cooling issues since there's not much free space in the case for air circulation. Cooling tubes help this somewhat, but know that you'll feel the heat after about an hour of gaming.

There's quite a bit made of the port placement on this laptop, with the ad copy saying major ports are placed in the back to stay out of the way. Power plugs into the back, as does a USB 3.1 port, HDMI, security port, etc. BUT there are ports on either side as well, whether Thunderbolt/USB-C or a SD card reader. For controller use there's enough flexibility there to keep mice or other devices out of the way, as well as a (recommended) external keyboard. And why do I recommend that external keyboard?

Because this thing gets warm, hot even. After an hour killing Trinity thugs as Lara Croft, the keyboard was really quite hot, especially in the middle. Fans were working, and working quite loudly I'll add, so it never got to boiling hot but it still was more than noticeable. I got to the point of hooking it to an external monitor with a external keyboard for real marathon sessions. I did notice that the majority of the heat did seem to be coming through the keyboard, so the heatsinks on the side and back do very well in those immediate locations, but I'm not sure they are up to keeping the entire chassis cool.

Processor - ninth gen Core I7. It screams. I'm frankly surprised to see a processor of this caliber in a laptop in this niche. Nuff said.

Screen: On this I've been spoiled with my Alienware 17. The G7 screen is....fine. I mean, given the spec sheet (Nvidia GTX, etc) this is NOT a 4k gaming machine. Because of that, I think Dell may have chintzed a little on the screen and went with a standard 1920x1080 knowing it would never be pushed. I won't say that colors are washed out, but in comparison to the same resolution on my Alienware, neither do they really pop. Blacks aren't as light-sucking as the Alienware either, something that's kind of a big deal in gaming today. Don't get me wrong, it's not BAD...but it's not the best screen I've ever seen on a gaming laptop either. Again, it's becoming clear to me that Dell's focus on this series is to make a laptop that appeals to a wider chunk of gamers than the top .05% who demand top tier screens and don't mind paying for them.

RAM: Not the sexiest part of the computer, but pretty important especially for graphics-intensive gaming where the video memory may be stressed (a potential consideration with the Nvidia GTX...more on which in a minute). 16GB shipped, which because I'm a worry wart seems to me to be on the lower end of the required scale. 2 slots, and I'd say if you're looking forward to Cyberpunk 2077 you may want to put this near the top of the list to upgrade. Don't waste money on LED-blinged RAM either...you won't see it in the laptop, and the physical clearances are a little tight for them anyway. That said, 16GB is a solid amount for a good chunk of games and pretty much every Indie out there. I will be going to 32GB on this machine though. UPDATE: I went with 32GB of Corsair Vengeance (CMSX32GX4M2A2666C18) memory...works perfectly with slightly lower but still comparable latency. It makes streaming on Twitch or doing video capture much more stable. Another point: out of the box 16GB doesn't provide a very comfortable environment for video/photo editing, so the extra memory here is very needed for those tasks.).

Graphics: The G7 has the Nvidia GTX 1660 Ti, which is an interesting choice. This is the first upgrade to the GeForce line that Nvidia has put out for, well, years and uses the new Turing architecture. The card is up to the task of high performance graphics from 97% of the games I've played, including Shadow of the Tomb Raider. What it is NOT is a future-proof graphics card...and specifically, it does NOT handle 4k well if at all, nor does is allow for ray tracing (outside of DirectX via a driver update). Whether ray tracing is going to be a thing or not (I only know of two games that use it...Battlefield V and Metro Exodus) is something the user has to decide and whether to insist on the Nvidia RTX series. Sadly for the Dell G series and unlike the Alienware, the graphics card is soldered in there so any upgrade is going to hinge on your comfort in performing surgery on the laptop. And this is the first part in my opinion that this is a good Right Now gaming laptop...there is NOTHING wrong with the GTX for the current crop of games, but if in a year or two we start seeing developers embrace ray tracing or other highly advanced rendering techniques, the GTX will be out of its depth, and with this laptop an upgrade will not be easy. Video memory is sufficient for high settings on the games I've tried, but more system RAM would help my comfort level. Last point - since you're pretty well kept to a sub 4k resolution ceiling, little surprise you can get most if not all games running well at high settings with this hardware. But to keep hammering the theme, if not having 4k isn't a dealbreaker, this is a good rig.

Keyboard: Weak. Keys are flat and small and while there's a nice generous palmrest, the keypad is a bit too close to the rest of the keyboard which makes general typing somewhat uncomfortable. There's room in the case to spread the keyboard out a bit more, so I'm a bit frustrated. The trackpad is shifted a bit to the left, but in a gaming laptop that's to be expected. Key travel is very short and while I get tactile feedback when the key is pressed (again, expected for a gaming keyboard) it's not what I call a very easy to live with design. It's adequate for general gaming, but for the real deal again I recommend an external purpose-built gaming keyboard. The built-in keyboard does have backlit keys that can be changed with the included Alienware FX application, so you can change the color. My big nit there is you can only change regions of the keyboard (left, center, right) and not individual keys. I like having the WASD keys be a different color than the rest of the keyboard, and I cannot do that with this laptop. I also use an Alienware gaming mouse and the FX application on the G7 will not recognize the mouse to change the colors there.

Sound: Two speakers in the front. They are on the small side and do deliver decent response, but because of their size you aren't going to get much if any bass off of them. They do about as well as they can do given the form factor, but again for Real Deal Gaming I'm more likely to use a headset instead of relying on the on board speakers anyway. Call this a good feature, good speakers, but not something that's going to take the place of a proper sound system.

Battery: It's a gaming laptop. Battery life is not a selling point. With a power-hoarding profile (performance cut down as much as possible, Intel graphics instead of the Nvidia card, etc) I got about 5-6 hours off it it with regular use. Pumping all performance to maximum and using the Nvidia card, I got 90 minutes. Given the dimensions of the case and the use of a 4 cell battery, the constraints keep it from going higher. A six-cell battery is available in this model, but you sacrifice the SATA bay if you want it. My take: I don't use battery much if at all for gaming, and if I'm doing real world work I have a power profile set up to get me my 5-6 hours. I like having the second drive more than a six-cell battery.

Performance: It ships with Windows 10 Home, which is fine BUT in true Dell fashion (and very unlike Alienware) there's a buttload of bloatware on this thing. I took about an hour after initial setup to uninstall all of it. This is even more important because the unit I received shipped with a 512 GB SSD, and with the games I play I can use up that space pretty darned quickly. This unit DOES have the ability to accept a second internal SATA drive, which I used for a 2 TB SSD (installation was quite easy...not as easy as the Alienware, but not a PITA either...). SATA is a little on the slow side for data-intensive gaming, though a SATA SSD seems to minimize the bottleneck. Not the most elegant solution (I'd prefer a PCIe 1 TB SSD as the primary instead of a 512GB, or better yet have 2 M.2 ports!!!!) but this isn't an Alienware where I have a ton of choices for expandability. Another note - if you're going to put a spinny SATA drive in here instead of a SSD, you have a choice of using the M.2 port for Intel Optaine *OR* a SSD drive. Again, this speaks to the low expandability options of the G series in general.

Anyway, with my Tomb Raider game hitting about 70-72 FPS at highest (for the hardware) settings (use the Nvidia experience app to really dial in the video settings....and thank me later) it's easy to overlook a lot of my nits. Play was solid, the system architecture with the Core I7 (six cores) along with the Nvidia card did not create any unusual bottlenecks, and aside from the heat issue I was very happy with the gaming. The screen keeps the bezel to a minimum (though the top bezel is still a bit thick...) which is appreciated.

So overall - it's a good laptop well able to play pretty much anything out there today and do it well. BUT, it's not very expandable. Two memory slots, taking off the bottom to add/change components is a bit of a pain compared to the Alienware, and there's not a lot you can do to add to it anyway. Add/upgrade a SATA drive or the PCIe SSD, increase RAM...and that's really about it. It's at its core an off-the-shelf easy gaming laptop that, aside from removing the bloatware, doesn't require a lot of extra effort to get it running decently. If you like tinkering and working to coax every last bit of performance out of a computer, you will be very frustrated here. If on the other hand you want a good turnkey gaming-focused laptop that doesn't stutter when running graphically- or processor-intensive games, this one fills that niche quite well.

title: A waste of specs and money
text:
When I first read the specs for the 5310 I was really intrigued. It sounded like a whole lot of machine in a very small package. But it doesn't take long to realize that the 5310 crams in a lot of unnecessary hardware and cost for virtually no improved performance.

CPU

The Intel Core i7-11370H. The idea behind this chip was to compete with Ryzen in the laptop/ultra portable gaming sector of the market. But after their previous 6 and 8 core 10 generation series the 11370H is a step back for Intel having only 4 cores, which for 2021 just isn't enough anymore.

The 11370H might shine in single threaded productivity tasks but that's where the pros of the chip end. Paired with a high end GPU (like in the Asus TUF Dash F15 which sports a 3070) the 11370H is passable in modern titles that aren't CPU bound, thought the performance is well behinds competitors. Unfortunately the Inspiron 5310's GPU is far from high end.

GPU

NVIDIA claims the GeForce MX450 slots somewhere in between a 1050 and a 1650. Frankly I don't know enough to be able to compare the three GPUs but my experience with the MX450 is I need to know to come to a conclusion here. For the most part, modern games are unplayable. Anything with higher-end graphics is a no go, you will have to drop your resolution down to 1280x720 to eek above 30-40 fps. At low settings, 1080p the best I could get from Rise of the Tomb Raider was a "steady" 20 fps. On medium settings I was getting ~30 fps on Firewatch. When it comes to gaming on the 5310 I'd say your best best is pixelated/low poly games or legacy system emulation.

PRODUCTIVITY/PERFOMANCE

Even here I wouldn't hold out high expectations for the 5310. Any sort of multi-tasking bogs down the CPU. After two weeks I've yet to have WebEx run successfully for more than two minutes before it hangs and then crashes. Web browsing is smooth, and it's only here I can appreciate the mostly unnecessary headroom offered by the 16gb of ram because I do love my multiple tabs.

Media consumption is another confusing aspect of the 5310. At times the display can be sharp and beautiful, but comparatively speaking even at max brightness it's a little dim. And the native resolution of 2560x1600, while good for some tasks, feels awkward and an odd choice. While it's not exactly rare the 16:10 aspect ratio is a lot less common than 16:9 so expect to frequently see black bars in any gaming or media. And although I appreciate the sharpness of the QHD resolution I wonder why Dell chose to pair this resolution with a CPU geared towards 1080p performance?

CONCLUSION

Design wise this is a sleek little ultra-portable laptop. It's lightweight, minimalist, and a pleasure to work on with the few tasks it handles well. Unfortunately it feels like Dell shoved in a bunch of unnecessary, expensive, and poorly paired hardware to create this mostly unusable, mismatched Frankenstein of a machine. And on top of all that the various Dell bloatware included makes this even more undesirable.

title: Meets and exceeds my already high expectations.
text: Ordered this laptop with high hopes for it as the parts in it looked really good for the price. I must say, you're getting a lot for your money. I'm not the biggest gamer in the world but there is one game I play and that is Borderlands 2. I can run at max settings (Physx on low because that drops frames for even some of the best gaming pc's) at 55-60 fps while not charging. When it's charging it just about always runs 60 fps even when I turn Physx up to medium. It does get a little warm in the top left corner of the laptop about where the speaker is when running Borderlands but it's not too bad. Sometimes I can hear the fan decently loud, but it's a really smooth sound. Borderlands 2 is not an easy game to run at max settings by any means. I'm actually in college right now so I didn't even get this totally for gaming, like I said, only thing in gaming is that I just wanted to run BL2 smoothly. This thing is FAST. Very quick start up, obviously having an SSD. Has an empty slot which I plan to plug the 1tb hdd from my last laptop in to. I personally am not sure why everyone is talking about screen bleed because I don't see any and that was the one thing that scared me when reading the reviews. The screen is BEAUTIFUL and the colors look amazing. The keyboard is pretty decent and I like how quiet it is. I usually type pretty hard, but I don't hear much out of this keyboard other than the spacebar but that's normal because it's such a big key. The backlighting of the keyboard is amazing. It doesn't just stay on, the light actually fades out after about 30 seconds (haven't timed it) and turns back on as soon as you hit a key. For a laptop, the speakers are actually great quality and can get pretty loud for laptop speakers without losing quality. I never really used my pc/laptop speakers before this, I have just used my Bose headphones but I can actually stand the speakers in this. The battery lasts about 6+ hours with moderate use with it leaning more towards performance so I know if you set it to longer battery life you would get more than 7 hours out of it. But heavy gaming drains the battery real quick as in about 3 and a half hours from full down to 10%. The build quality is really nice, I love the way it feels and looks. It doesn't LOOK like a gaming laptop. No one else even knows I bought what Dell considered a gaming laptop, they just think it's a really good laptop (Which it is.). But I didn't buy it to be a gaming laptop, and before I bought it I thought of it as just a great laptop, with great parts, that will run fast. Especially for the money. But now that I've had it for a few days, I know that you could call it a dedicated mid-range gaming laptop. It seems to compete with gaming laptops priced at about 1100-1300 from what I've tested of them (Never really owned them so I can't say anything about long term. I've only tested some out.). I honestly don't have an complaints about this purchase so far. As far as laptops go I've had an Asus and an HP, both of which I had to send in within a month after I got them for having issues that were noticeable within a days. If I run into any issues I'll update but as of now, this thing is a very reasonably, maybe even under-priced, beast that is definitely worth taking a look at and comparing to other options. The other laptop I was looking at was the ASUS K501UX (which is a little cheaper as of right now, but not by much.) because I really did like my last ASUS, but I'm glad I bought this as it is MILES better than my last rig. I chose this one because it was newer, and it is quad-core instead of dual. Also, I don't need an i7 especially with these 6th gen cores, and this is a really good i5 core. Not worth getting an i7. Plus the ASUS looks like my last one and the build quality on that didn't feel nearly as nice as this. Anyways, I think that's enough praise for now. Good luck with your shopping and again, make sure to take this laptop into consideration.

title: Great gaming PC for the price I paid
text:
This laptop is a great device for gaming. I've been using it for about a month now, and most of the games I play I can run on at least high, if not ultra/max/whatever the highest graphical settings are. I sometimes have to tone it down, depending what I play.

Screen quality is good, not really much to say about it. It has good brightness and a good 165hz refresh rate.

The only real issue I had was when I first got it. The speaker on the right was very low and sounded tinny. Like if you've ever had a speaker go out in your car, but the tweeter still worked, it sounded about like that. I was considering returning it, but I decided to open it up to make sure everything was connected properly and found a tiny screw lodged lodged in the speaker. Once I removed it, the speaker worked like normal. I can only assume it fell in there during assembly, and I couldn't find any spots on the inside that appeared to have a missing screw. The sound quality on this machine isn't superb, but for me that's fine. If I need good sound quality, I'll put on a headset. This laptop does have a 2.5mm headphone jack, so if you like wired headphones, that's an option for you. If not, Bluetooth or a headset with a 2.4ghz USB receiver is also an option.

Speaking of disassembly, this was easy enough to open, as well. Just have to remove several screws and carefully use a spudger to remove the back plate. Access to ram and the extra storage bay were about as easy as expected.

It does get warm when gaming, but I think that's expected with gaming laptops these days.

I haven't tested the battery life, but i marked it 3 stars because, from my understanding, its...pretty bad. But I can't imagine that will be an issue for most, unless for some reason you like to game on-the-go and don't have access to an outlet for whatever reason.

All in all, I would recommend this laptop as a good mid-high tier gaming setup, if you prefer to use a laptop. Just keep in mind that the sound is probably the weakest point, so if you prefer to use your speakers instead of a headset, you might want to look elsewhere, but otherwise this is a pretty solid machine, in my personal experience.

title: Sleek, solid chassis, great for 1080p gaming, love the B&O speakers, 144hz, comfy keyboard
text:
I switched over to this HP Victus gaming laptop around two months ago. Based on the build quality (it's sleek and feels great to type on even though no mechanical keyboard), its performance when gaming (mostly MMOs or FPS games), and how it handles multitasking (I run a BlueIris VMS server on it most of the day with about 7 PoE cameras recording through it), I can comfortably recommend it.

The Victus handles Elden Ring on med-high graphics settings averaging 65-80 FPS, Fortnite at over 100FPS on high graphics settings, Halo infinite at 50-58 FPS on high settings, and various other AAA games at 60+ FPS @ 1080p on high graphics settings. If you turn the graphics settings down to low or medium-low you can max out the FPS (144hz for this panel) on older games like Fortnite or Dota 2. I was able to max out World of Warcraft TBC Classic as well on medium and low settings. This laptop has no trouble with large raids in WoW Classic or large battles in Halo Infinite on medium settings.

I don't really notice any bottlenecks when I'm using it besides when I'm gaming and forget to change the recording settings of my PoE cams in BlueIris. You can complete most productivity oriented tasks with this laptop such as data analysis with 20,000+ row excel files, editing videos while completing coursework, and more. This would be a good dev laptop as well even though the specs aren't super overpowered.

The HP Omen button on the keyboard opens up the HP Omen Gaming hub which lets you configure different profiles for optimizing performance while gaming or battery life while using the laptop for normal tasks. I kind of wish it had a dedicated overclock button like other gaming laptops but it's easy enough to toggle the mode to performance and max out the fan using the HP Omen Gaming Hub.

The keyboard feels satisfying to type on. It has a full numpad as well. The chassis feels pretty solid. I like the smooth finish on the top of the laptop. The speakers are actually excellent. I like the tuning and enjoy listening to music from them even though I have my larger bookshelf speakers right behind my laptop and triple monitors. They did a good job with the user experience.

Thankfully this is a semi-repairable laptop as well. You can easily open up the bottom of the chassis and add/remove/upgrade the ram, replace the battery after a few years, or nvme SSD. The ports included are generous and allow for easily outputting to two extra monitors though you will need a usb-c to hdmi converter. It would've been nice if it had thunderbolt as well but it still works well as is and thankfully has an ethernet port.

I've included some benchmarks here as well. For me it's a great gaming laptop, I'd say a 4.5/5, not quite perfect but good enough for my needs. The laptop feels fairly premium which makes me have confidence in its long-term durability even though it has a fair bit of plastic.

title: Best bang for buck in 2016
text:
I'm known among my peers for being able to find the best electronics deals on the market, and after dozens of hours of research, I splurged and bought the Dell Inspiron 7559. My verdict after a couple weeks of use: if you want a laptop that can play all the latest games at medium settings or higher, and you don't wanna spend over $1,000, this is your best option at this point in time. Dell didn't cut corners in this laptop's design - there are no killer flaws or nuisances that detract from the experience, like a keyboard that can't keep up with fast typing, a sub-1080p screen, slow WiFi or a lack of USB 3.0 ports(the 7559 has three USB 3.0 ports, and the one on the right side can charge your devices while the system's in sleep mode). The only flaw I can think of is the relatively high price for a laptop, but it's far cheaper than competing devices with similar hardware; I can't even successfully nitpick about this thing.

The i5 model comes with a 256GB M.2 SSD, and there's a SATA port for a 2.5-inch hard drive. With the SSD as a boot drive, the laptop boots up in less than ten seconds and general computer usage is snappy and responsive. I installed Overwatch on the SSD and the quick load times spoil me. I've yet to try the Dark Souls games on the SSD, but hopefully I'll remember to update this review and report my findings - on a 7200RPM mechanical drive, Dark Souls 3 takes about a minute to load any time you teleport from one area to another or when you initially load the game. From what I've read, the SSD should cut that to closer to 15 seconds.

The i7 model comes with a higher-capacity mechanical drive connected to the SATA port, leaving the M.2 port empty. One point for the i5 model. A week after this laptop arrived, I installed a 2TB Seagate FireCuda hybrid drive for all my future game installs; this is the first laptop I've ever owned with two hard drives in it, and the difference in power usage and weight is absolutely negligible. Kudos to Dell for putting such an awesome feature in a mid-range laptop.

On laptops with a 1080p or higher display, I always play games with the anti-aliasing off. On a 15.6-inch 1080p display, jaggies aren't much of a bother, and I'd rather my system run cooler and the battery last longer than crush a couple jaggies here-and-there.

With its quad-core i5 and GTX 960M, the 7559 can play Overwatch at ultra settings at around 50-54 FPS, and at high it stays at a rock-solid 70. On the character selection screen the game drops closer to 35FPS, but as soon as you hop into the match, the framerate doubles; clearly more of an optimization issue on Blizzard's part than due to hardware. Civilization: Beyond Earth stayed at 60FPS at around medium settings, and I had the same experience with Starcraft 2: Heart of the Swarm. I tried a few other games like The Forest, Black Mesa and Dirt 3 and they all played like a charm. For some reason, though, when I tried to play the new Doom, the game was just as choppy at lowest possible settings, 720p + 50% render scale as it was between medium and high settings. My drivers are updated and the Nvidia control panel said that the game was set to run on the 960M and not the far-weaker Intel integrated GPU, but I'll troubleshoot some more and update my review if I can get it running in a playable form. Doom is the only game I've thrown at this machine that gave me any trouble, and I'm sure I can get it running like a champ on this beast of a laptop.

In the future I'll add benchmark results and what kinda gaming performance you can expect, but beyond Doom acting weird, I've had nothing but a positive experience with the Dell Inspiron 7559. I recommend it whole-heartedly.

Bonus: This was initially delivered the day before Thanksgiving, while I was at work. Unless the package grew wings, someone stole it from my porch. I was so depressed, I stayed home for Thanksgiving and waited by the door in case the delivery was merely a day late. Luckily, I was able to speak to an Amazon customer service rep and they sent a replacement at no charge to me - two-day shipping. Kudos to Amazon for being the best.

title: Very Good Gaming Laptop, This 90w 2070 Super Max-Q is as good as the normal 115w 2070 Super Mobile
text:
A solid and very capable gaming laptop capable of replacing some desktops.

Pros:
- 300hz G-Sync Display, top tier screen, no IPS blur and ghosting. Better than my $410 IPS monitor.
- Excellent CPU, is basically the same as the i7-9750H though
- Excellent GPU with Max-Q design, allowing power allocation for the CPU to GPU or vice versa when needed. Also, the 90w 2070 super Max-Q in this laptop performs as well as the normal 115w 2070 Super Mobile.
- 16GB DDR4 2933Mhz RAM (Decent speed, 16GB is more than enough for most people unless you're 3D rendering)
- Metal body and plastic bezels, superior build quality
- Very good thermals, 3 fans along with 5 heat pipes allow for good cooling. On max fans the cpu hits around the low 80s or high 70s and GPU around the high 60s with heavy load.
- Full Per-key RGB keyboard (There is a bump on the W key if that bothers you)

Cons:
- Relatively expensive
- Average battery life
- Difficult to upgrade due to motherboard being mounted upside down
- 1080p screen
- Loud Fans* (This may be a negative to some people but loud fans are good because they cool your device well which will increase the lifespan of the components).
- Keyboard animation on startup* There is a keyboard effect when you boot-up which can't be disabled regardless of keyboard lighting settings.

Overall this is a very good gaming laptop, I replaced an older version of this one (Acer Predator Triton: i7-9750, RTX 2060 (2019 model) and they've made many improvements. They added a slightly faster cpu, full Per-key RGB lighting to the keyboard, a better screen, and upgraded the RAM speed from 2666Mhz to 2933Mhz.. They also added the RTX 2070 Super Max-Q which is more power efficient and cooler compared to its counterpart. Additionally, the thermals were better because of the Max-Q design on the GPU. This 90w 2070 Super Max-Q also performs as well as the normal 115w 2070 Super Mobile due to the good thermal design on this laptop. Got one of the best benches on UserBenchmark for this graphics card. Very nice laptop, would recommend if you have the budget for it. (Although you should probably wait until the RTX 30 series laptops are released)

title: Acer always come through.
text:
I've used Acer since about 1997 or so, only had about 3 desktops of theirs in that time, which is saying a lot. If there were any problems it wasn't anything major at all. Also bought a laptop from back in 2010 that still works today, the power button just needs replaced, and also a 2008 small Acer Aspire that finally burnt out this year. So yes they do last. My 10 year old Desktop I just gave my parents also works VERY well, even though they don't use it much. My 5 year old HP still runs pretty good (even though I've never been an HP fan) but is getting some age on it. And has Windows 8 on it, so they won't be supporting it much longer. And it has some slight issues. So i figured it was time for an upgrade, and this is the only brand i fully trust.

I know gaming laptops don't have the longest lifespan, but i have a Dell Desktop that is just fine with an older I5 and a good graphics card in it. So i didn't really by this for gaming, even though i may do a small amount on it. It's just a good backup, upgrade with great specs and will do anything i need it to do. The keyboard has very good travel and is great to type on, much like this small Acer Chromebook I have, which is also a little beast. The red keys only light up when touched, instead of on 24/7. Also Acer is one of the few companies that still put a button to turn off the trackpad when you don't feel like using it. Especially when typing reviews. The GTX 1650 can handle any modern game you through at it, although I haven't tested out much, just a few to see how it runs. And the cooling system Acer uses is really nice, showing you the actual fans on the screen, temp, speeds etc. It gets meh, kind of loud but nothing overbearing like a lot of laptops of this size.

The 128gb SSD is also a nice feature and makes windows 10 run a LOT faster. But the real no brainer was the 1TB HDD it also has in it. So there's your real storage. Instead of using an external drive to try and game on, etc. Which isn't a great idea anyway. So overall the build quality is nice, it looks great, is very fast, and I also got it on sale for only $679, at BB, which i hate. But oh well. That's better than close to a grand. The only draw back is the screen, it's not very colorful, but very bright. So the color gamut could be better. Battery life is also mediocre, but i rarely use it on battery, so no biggie. But that's a minor issue. I hope this Acer lasts as long as my others. And since i take good care of my electronics, i don't that being an issue.

title: Don't buy - 5 solid reasons below
text:
The specs for the cost on this computer are okay, but there are just a few nagging problems I had with it that led to me returning it.

1. When you turn the computer on, it plays, at full volume, a cringe-inducing "gamer start up" noise - it will also play this when the computer restarts to update at 3am. Presumably it can be turned off in the bios, but who's idea was this? Who does it appeal to?

2. I can't speak for all units, but my computer constantly struggled with switching to the speakers sound input if the computer was using another audio device as output. Using a monitor, USB headset, or otherwise? I had to restart the computer every time or get errors whenever I tried playing media.

3. Computer has a "turbo" mode, which seems to apply some OCs or something along those lines. It also puts the fans up to 100 percent, which is deafening. In my experience, the turbo button just stopped working like 2 weeks in to using the laptop, which is a shame, because sometimes I would use it during gaming to level out the fan curve, which is audibly jittery as it tries to figure out if it should sit at 80, or 50, or 80, or 50, etc etc etc. The constant throttling is almost more annoying than keeping the fan at 100.

4. This is a problem I had years ago theast time I had a gaming laptop, and this seems no different: a lot of games, AAA, indie, you name it, will not run off of the dedicated GPU by default, and will instead (poorly) run on the integrated Intel GPU. To fix this you need to change the program's defaults from within the NVidia Control Panel.

5. This thing runs HOT. Running a game like Phasmophobia, which isnt exactly "next gen" makes the keyboard so hot that it hurts to use the B key to talk on global comms after a while, because there's clearly a major heat sink underneath it, possibly for the GPU or CPU.

If youre looking at this for a gaming computer, consider running a desktop. If you must go with a laptop, I'd look elsewhere, as questionable design decisions and downright bad ones make the experience here frustrating at best and broken at worst.

title: Great bang for the buck
text:
My Dell Inspiron i7559-763BLK arrived on Tuesday, December 15th. It’s a Christmas present for my son who will be going off to college next year and wanted a PC for school work and light gaming (Hearthstone mostly). The price, hardware, and reviews were what sold me on this laptop.
I’m very PC savvy so I took control of unboxing it and prepping it for use.

After turning on, the first thing that I noticed is that the wifi was connected but continued to show as being “disabled”. “Enabling” did not change the status. Having read the reviews on here, I went to device manager and did an internet search to update the driver. Problem solved. Wi-fi works as it should.

I added some software that I like such as Classic Shell to give the classic windows start menu and CCleaner so I could delete some of the bloatware apps and programs that came pre-installed. I didn’t want to install too many programs right now due to adding a SSD data drive (more on that coming up). Once complete, I turned off and removed the one screw on the bottom of the unit and opened it up.

It’s almost too easy to get inside. I almost wish it had 4 screws at each corner rather than the 1 screw and clips securing the panel. 1 screw for the entire bottom panel seems to be too little. I added 8 GB of RAM that I bought with the laptop that was listed as part of the package that Amazon sold together. It’s the Kingston Technology 8GB 1600MHz DDR3L (PC3-12800) 1.35V Non-ECC CL11 SODIMM Intel Laptop Memory KVR16LS11/8. It’s not identical to the pre-installed stick but that won’t matter. That went easily enough and, upon restart, a BIOS message did come up saying that the amount of installed memory had changed and if I did not install more memory that I needed to reseed the memory stick. Just ignored that and the laptop now shows 16 GB of installed RAM.

I also had a 960 GB SanDisk Ultra II 2.5” 7mm SSD that I installed in the spare drive bay that I will use as a data drive. This isn’t so easy to do manly due to my man hands. The good thing is that there already is a screwed-in bracket waiting for you to use. Just unscrew the 4 extremely tiny screws then remove the bracket, use 4 screws that you must have already to secure the SSD to the bracket, connect the SATA cable then screw the bracket onto the SSD, pop back in and re-install the 4 tiny screws. The issue here, however, is twofold: First, you are not provided with the 4 screws to secure the SSD to the bracket. I’m lucky to have a ton of screws from prior purchases but most people won’t. Secondly, the space for the SSD is sooo tight that one of the 4 screws securing the SSD to the bracket was bumping up against the side panel and not allowing the SSD to seed flush any longer. I had to remove 1 screw and go with just 3 screws holding the SSD to the bracket. This shouldn’t pose any future issues as it’s secure enough. Even just securing 2 of the 4 screws at a diagonal is enough to keep the SSD secure.

Once you turn on the laptop after the SSD install you will not be able to see the SSD listed as a storage device. You must first go into disk management (simply do a search for “disk management” in the search box). There you can click on the storage device and assign a letter to the drive (I chose “D” as my 960 GB SSD data drive but you can assign a different drive letter). Click “OK” and now your extra storage device is ready to go. It was already TRIM enabled by default so no need to manually turn that on.

Installing a typical HDD will be identical to the install of my SDD.

After the SDD install, I installed IOBit Driver Booster 3 and was surprised to see that 17 drivers were outdated. Most of the new drivers had been released in September 2015. I updated those and also used the Dell System Detect to direct me to the most current BIOS update (dated November 2015) and updated the BIOS. I then proceeded to do a Windows Update and install the big November Windows 10 update. That went smoothly.

I installed Diablo 3 and was very surprised at how well it ran on max settings. It looked gorgeous. The sound is “tinny” as you might expect from limited laptop speakers but the graphics are awesome. No stutter. I didn’t check the FPS but it was so smooth.

I also installed ChrisPC Win Experience Index and it computed the following after the RAM upgrade and SSD install (on a scale from 1 to 9.9):
Processor: 7.8
Memory (RAM): 7.8
Graphics (built in): 6.2
Graphics (Nvidia): 9.9
Primary Hard Drive: 8.2

In comparison my desktop gaming PC scored 8.0, 8.0, 8.5, 9.9 and 8.1 in those categories. Specs are i7 4th gen processor, 24 GB RAM, 2 Nvidia 760 GTX GPU’s in SLI, SSD OS primary drive and SSD secondary data drive.

The keyboard is adequate and comparable to other laptops I have used. I use a mouse so no comments that I can give regarding the touchpad.

The construction is my only concern as my son will be mobile with this laptop and hauling it around at school in his backpack. A lot of plastic on this baby. Only time will tell if it will hold up to a beating but I did buy the extended 3 year warranty that Amazon was selling with the laptop through Canopy.

I think that for the price this is a great purchase and, with the upgrades I made, will be future-proof for until it breaks.
