title: Very good for the price, with some compromises...
text:
I bought this laptop with the intention of using it for school and for some light gaming. I wanted something thin, small, light, with good battery life. I didn't expect to pay such a low price for an item matching my requirements. This is a great laptop but it's got things that one should know about before buying.

Speakers: They are bad, not decent, outright bad. There is little sound clarity and they are very quiet. If the sound is important, I recommend looking somewhere else.

Bloatware: Too much, it's difficult to get rid of and it will try to sneak its way back in. At least it stays hidden and doesn't pop up. Be warned, this laptop comes with one of those annoying anti-viruses. It took little effort to get rid of it and it never came back.

Screen: Looks nice, a lot better than a budget laptop. But, this isn't a Surface, Macbook, or XPS. Do not expect an amazing screen. Expect a good screen, it's pretty bright as well.

Battery: This is where she starts to shine. This laptop is rocking some serious specs, yet the battery lasts a good bit. No, we're not talking all day, but 6 hours with a balanced preset and great specifications is a serious contender.

Specifications: **This is the highlight of this computer**. If you don't know much about specs I'll give you an easy summary of this computer. This computer will run smoothly with just about anything you can throw at it, its limits start to show when you start throwing PC games at it. This baby packs a Ryzen 5800U, 16GB of Ram, an RTX 3050ti and a 512ssd. What does this mean? It means this laptop can run Fortnite, Adobe premiere, Vs code, basically, anything that isn't MW Warzone(technically it can run I just wouldn't recommend it) with basically no issues. This laptop also has some options for upgrading, including an extra SSD slot!

Keyboard: Ok, keys feel a little wide but you will get used to them in no time. This laptop has backlit keys, although they can be difficult to see under certain conditions.

Trackpad: Also good, like I said a lot of this laptop is mediocre but it makes up for it in the spec department. When playing games you may want to disable it (if you're using a mouse) as the palm rejection isn't very good.

Charger: If anxiety was a charger this would be it, the charger is very small and looks like I could break it if I pulled it out the wrong way honestly. Not to worry though! You can charge this computer from the USB type C port!

I/O:1 HDMI, 1 Type C port, Charging port, 2 USB 3 ports, and a headphone jack. No SD card slot folks :( .

Build Quality: Mostly metal, with black plastic on the screen bezels. Sturdy, yet the metal feels a bit cheap, I feel that this is because of the texture. Still very good overall. The laptop looks super nice in person, it's no Surface laptop or Macbook but it's a close second or third.

Final thoughts: A fast machine with a lot of "good enough" components and some minor downsides. The good really outweighs the bad. I'm taking a star off for the speakers as they are the only part of the computer that are outright bad. I highly recommend this computer for the college student that doesn't want to end up with a dud computer or an ugly gaming laptop.

title: Okay if you only want it for gaming
text:
So there's one thing you should know before I review this: I have been an Apple user for the past 15 years or so.

I was so excited to receive this HP laptop, as my other laptop has pretty much run completely out of space and I cannot figure out how to free up any more. (Deleting things seems to free up space only temporarily.)

Well I was sorely disappointed to find out this HP laptop comes with Windows and Candy Crush. No Office. No Word. No Excel. And to get Office on the HP is going to cost me quite a bit. I guess this is the norm for Windows based computers, but it made me regret ordering this instantly. (Apple offers their equivalent features for free.)

Now- if you only want it for gaming, I suppose whether it comes with Office installed or not is not an issue. It seems sufficient in areas such as speed, video quality, processing power, and memory. The sound leaves something to be desired and the screen needs constant adjusting because any little movement seems to tilt it out of place. (And I noticed another reviewer mentioned the screen feels flimsy- this is true, though I hadn't noticed until that reviewer pointed it out).

The battery leaves a lot to be desired. I get maybe 8 hours of consistent use out of it before it needs to get charged again. Less if I'm doing more than surfing the web.

I also think the controls are really wonky. Touching the touch pad is equivalent to a click, but only in some circumstances. If I am trying to highlight text for example, I have to actually press the touch pad, and then put another finger down to scroll and highlight. This is really annoying. It is way too easy to just put your finger down on the touch pad and click something, and it is way too difficult to press the touch pad to highlight text and actually get it to work since that is also the equivalent of double clicking.

Lesson learned anyway. I'll go back to gaming on my console, and I'll keep using my old laptop until I can manage to upgrade.

So I realized that I was going to have to start traveling with two laptops, one personal and one for work. And if I'm carrying a personal laptop anyway, why not get in a little gaming while I'm out of town?

This Y520 fits the bill perfectly. It's relatively light for such a large screen, Windows 10 is mostly harmless, and as for gaming... This is the first laptop on which I've been able to crank up the video settings for Witcher 3 to the max without any problems. Display contrast, speed and clarity are excellent. title: Great Laptop Computer!
text:
Lenovo Computer Review

I’m no IT guru, so this is a total non-techy user review. I’ve owned and used this laptop computer September of 2021, and I love it! It was well past time for an upgrade, and I spent a lot of time looking at laptops, trying to decide what fit my needs and wants best. I narrowed it down to a few from Asus, Dell, Acer, and Lenovo. Even though this is marketed as a gaming laptop, it’s important to note that I am not a computer guru, nor am I a gamer. I don’t own a single game, so I can’t review it from that standpoint. I simply wanted a computer for everyday computing and web surfing, managing my music collection, editing photos, and running my telescopes (astronomy is one of my hobbies.)

For my purposes, this computer is fast! It boots up in just a few seconds. The graphics are great! Being able to change the keyboard backlighting color is a great feature for me. Astronomy is a hobby of mine, so my keyboard lighting is red, since I don’t want bright light sources ruining my dark-adapted night vision when I'm using the laptop with my telescopes at night.

No computer is perfect, and I do have a few minor nit-picks with this one, though there are none that I find unacceptable. First, this computer came with ABSOLUTELY NO DOCUMENTATION! No manual, printed or otherwise. Not even a quick-start guide. No CD with a manual or utilities. All you get in the box is the laptop and the power cord/AC adapter. In spite of the lack of documentation, it was pretty easy for me to power it up and start using it. Next, the AC adapter is very bulky, compared to the ones that come with most other laptops. It’s about 6”x 3”x 1”, it’s heavy for its size, and it’s situated in the middle of the power cord. I will say that the power cord is quite long, which is good. The power cord plugs into the back of the unit, rather than on the side. There’s only one USB port on right side of the computer, and there’s a USB-C port and a headphone jack on the left side. I would have preferred two side USB ports, but there are three more on the back of the unit, along with a HDMI port, another USB-C port, and a LAN connection. There’s plenty of connectability, if you don’t mind most of it being on the back of the unit. The speakers sound like typical laptop speakers, and I think it’s silly to expect much more than that. I use headphones, Bluetooth speakers, or I just Bluetooth my music from the laptop to my home stereo system. Last, the battery doesn’t last long as long as I’d like, but that’s to be expected from a computer with the high-end processing and graphics capability this computer has. For every day, non-gaming use, I get about two-and-a-half to three hours of use from the battery before I need to recharge it. If you need portability power, you’d do well to use all of the power saving settings, have an alternate power supply to plug into, or an extra battery, or consider another computer altogether. Again, none of these are things that cause me any real issues, but they might for others. In spite of them all, I do love this machine!

One of the things about this computer that was a big selling point for me is that it was sold directly by Amazon, rather than a third-party vendor on Amazon. I hear a lot of hard luck stories from folks who bought computers from third-party vendors who had a tough time either getting warranty service for computers with problems, or returning them for refunds. And a lot of computers offered by third-party vendors have been modified by those vendors. I read a lot of reviews from customers of a lot of those units, complaining of inferior parts being used for the mods. Luckily for me, I had no desire to return my computer, nor have I had any functionality issues with it. But when I have had to return anything to Amazon, it’s always been a no-hassle experience for me. And to top it off, the Amazon price on this computer was less than that offered directly from Lenovo.

What I like:
Looks great!
It’s fast! Boots up in only a few seconds.
Graphics are top notch.
WIFI and Bluetooth work well
Keyboard backlighting colors are changeable (red is my preference)
10-key pad on keyboard (I use this a lot!)
Sold directly by Amazon (at least it was when I bought mine)

What I don’t like:
NO documentation
The battery could last longer
Most of the connectivity ports are on the back of the computer
Bulky AC adapter
Annoying occasional sales nags from McAfee and Microsoft. Fairly easily removed.

title: Runs warm but read on
text:
This is probably the last laptop I will buy, but not because of this particular laptop. Mostly because the direction manufacturers are heading. Over all this is great laptop, after you spend some more $$$$$ though. The thermals on this thing are horrible, and the Intel 660p needs something.

PROS +
+ has a great screen
+ the 2070 max-Q is a decent all around powerhouse
plays most games on high or ultra without going over 60c @ 60fps+
runs any autodesk software with ease (add extra ram if you are wanting it for this purpose)
+ minimal bloat ware
+ armory crate software is nice but needs others to get full tuning exp
+ For a laptop keyboard this one has a great keyboard, good clicky feel and decent throw

NEUTRAL =
= on board ram latency is meh ( do not buy high end ram*)
if you want extra buy only a 16GB module and Samsung also*
= touch pad could use improvement overall nice but touchy
= USB/ports layout (why in the middle?)
= ASUS customer service isn't horrible, you just have to be really direct and blunt with them
if you have driver issues do not buy their flash drive they offer, all of their drivers are available on their site

CONS -
- SSD isnt that great (unless you add a second in RAID0)
- Runs really warm ( 80c CPU and 75c GPU)
mine needed new thermal paste as what came in it was already dried out
- keyboard does get warm during and heavy task or gaming
even with new paste and cooler it still is warm but not hot like before

Over all this is a great laptop after you spend an additional 300-400 extra. Also if you have thermal issues send it back. Reason being is that when you remove the heat spreader off of the motherboard to re apply Thermal paste it voids the warranty. After correcting the thermal paste issue my temps went from 80c CPU to 60c CPU, the GPU went from 75c to 55c.

The Intel SSD is okay however v. spending an additional 400+ on new SSD for this laptop. I would purchase an additional Intel 660p and configure it in RAID0. Do this right out of the box and it is done through the BIOS not windows. I would recommend doing this if you plan on doing and kind of CAD/CAM/rendering. SIDE NOTE, when and if you do purchase an additional SSD, make sure to get a heat spreader for the SSD, they are cheap.

*If you do plan on using this rig for any kind of editing, obviously I would purchase additional RAM. The motherboard only allows 32GB total, and only has one slot. 16GB is already on board and is Samsung dies, at a CL of 19 and runs at 2666MHz. With that being said I would personally v. spending extra on high end, is to purchase an additional Samsung module. An additional Samsung module @ 16GB should only be an extra 75 bucks here on amazon.

In general I am very happy with this purchase. However thin and light does not equal a cool running machine. Also do not take your laptop apart unless you know what you are doing. This was not meant to be a guide of any sort. Just my personal experience and my opinions on this specific GU502GW.

title: Good specs, but overheats
text:
On paper this sounds like an amazing laptop.
- Core i7 processor
- 16gb RAM
- 512GB SSD
- Nvidia graphics card
- Supposedly better cooling

However real use of the laptop is quite different.
There were a few times where I was just browsing the web and it shut off.
It can get VERY hot so I downloaded a program to see how hot it was getting.

While running a program to see how good the processor is, it was averaging around 80 degrees C and would even get up to 90 degrees semi-regularly.
At one point I felt above the middle of the keyboard toward the screen and if I held my finger there for about 5 seconds it would have burned me, no joke!
Just holding it for a couple seconds I could feel it start to sting from the heat.

That is the main issue with this laptop, it has great components to be powerful but the cooling prevents it as everything will throttle to keep it cool enough.

One good thing is the SSD is replaceable, which of course I did as the default one was averaging 2200mbs read speed and 500mbs write speed.
The read isn't bad but the write speed is super slow.
Installed an m.2 drive that was now getting around 3000 read and 2000 write speeds.
That made a HUGE difference, boot up was much faster, opening files/programs was much faster, even using the trackpad guessers seemed snappier.

My personal opinion is they crammed too many high powered components in a tiny ultrabook chassis.
Maybe after some Windows updates or something it will improve, but for now I wouldn't recommend.
It's not for gamers and it's not for someone who wants something ultra portable and doesn't care about gaming as the fans blare when you're just browsing the web.

title: Unbeatable performance at $649
text:
I've had this Lenovo ideapad gaming 3 Ryzen 5 6600h rtx 3050 version with 8gb ddr5 ram & 256gb ssd for about a month now and so far the performance has been spectacular. There are a couple irritations rather then cons ill get into shortly. I was hesitant not knowing if this setup would run the games I play at the highest resolutions and frame rate this PC offers.
This laptop has been flawless at running call of duty MW 2(2009), COD black Ops and GTA 5 on the highest settings with out any hiccups, choppy video, freezing etc. For me it has been lightning fast and silky smooth. Yes there are higher frame rates out there but the costs are astronomic for what little upgrades you get.
I love the fact I haven't found any bloatware in this PC. Although not recommended by Lenovo it does allow overclocking. It stays cool even with heavy gameplay for hours on end. The fans work great at dispersing heat and are not so loud you get distracted while gaming. When just casually running browsers or streaming the fans never kick on it just stays cool enough to not need them.

I've read users think its not sturdy enough? I think its very sturdy. The keyboard doesn't flex while pushing keys and its quite hefty. The screen doesn't feel wobbly or weak. Its not made of aluminum like an Asus tuf f15 but it does the job well.
Other users say the brightness and colors are dim but that has not been the case for me. Its not 4k but I had to turn the brightness down. The colors are great for me. If you are a professional photo editor or video editor just get an external monitor. You shouldn't be editing professional work on a 15.6" screen anyway haha its a gaming laptop not a photo/video workstation. You'll need more power to render huge files.

The only cons/ irritations-
256gb ssd is just an outdated size for storage. GTA 5 alone is 142gb. Yes it can be upgraded but at least a 512gb should be standard. Crucial says it will support 2tb but I have not personally added that size. I will definitely be upgrading to at least 1tb.

8gb ram has worked flawlessly with the aforementioned games I have installed. But it would have been nice to see a standard 16gb (2×8gb ddr5) cards installed. I will be upgrading to 32gb ddr5 2x16gb cards just because. The price jump for 16gb factory is crazy! Upgrading to 16gb costs like 40 bucks verses a $200 price jump for 16gb pre installed.

So far I have not found any other cons to this system. I love it and am very happy with its performance and price. I don't think you'll find a better laptop at this price for gaming.

Note I do have lightroom installed and it runs flawless. But its just for casual photo editing.

I couldn't be happier. A+ purchase.

title: Essentially a budget Legion, but currently not the best price and with a defect
text:
Major point before I start, I’m only giving this laptop a 4 star assuming that the 80mm m.2 slot issue is unique to my unit, otherwise this device would only be getting a 3 star. I’ll explain the issue below.

Disclaimer, I’m not sponsored by the seller, Lenovo, or Amazon, I’m using this as a review unit. If I had to sum this up quickly, it’s basically if a Legion 5 in design and thermals/performance, but a miniaturized battery and made out of plastic.

Before the review, let me address my main problem, the 80mm m.2 not working properly. This laptop has 2 m.2 slots, a 42mm and an 80mm. The 42mm is prepopulated with the 256GB Kioxia BG5, and both slots should be PCIE gen 4 enabled according to Lenovo’s PSREF. However, when I try to put a PCIE Gen 4 SSD (I tried 2 different models), it would work for the first 3 minutes and then immediately just error out and disconnect w/ a missing driver error. Rebooting makes the device completely disappear from Windows. Surprisingly PCIE Gen 3 SSDs work fine, I’ll attribute this to probably a hardware/BIOS issue and give it to the benefit of the doubt, especially since if it was PCIE Gen 3, the SSD would simply run in Gen 3 mode instead of just erroring out.

The design is very similar to a Legion 5, but made out of plastic, from the location of the hinge to the rear I/O. The plastic is pretty durable feeling, although for a heavy laptop it does feel like a compromise. I’m not a big fan of this “legion-alienware” hybrid, the older Ideapad Gaming 3 looked a lot more “boring”, but by looking boring it looked less “gaming” and “tacky”. The blue accents in the back and on the heatsink fins on this model and given a lot of gaming laptops have moved beyond the gaming aesthetic, I don’t like this.

It does come with a camera shutter, the webcam isn’t the best thing out there but it’s not too bad. The speakers on the other hand, I had an issue where after a while the volume would become distorted. During my review Lenovo released a BIOS with an audio fix that seemed to resolve this issue. The keyboard is like any Legion or Ideapad keyboard, it’s not bad despite the relatively shallow travel. The backlit comes in 2 brightness. The trackpad is plastic, it doesn’t track badly and does have Windows precision drivers, but it’s not the best experience one can get.

Like a Legion, you get the power mode selection that’s typical of some legions, pressing fn+q toggles the different power modes that basically will change some of the power and thermal behavior of the laptop; on battery there’s a power-saving mode and an auto mode, while plugged in there’s 3: quiet, auto, and performance. I don’t think this is in an embedded controller though, it seems to be purely in software (unlike say a Legion Slim 7). If you don’t care about fan noise just keep it in “performance” at all times when plugged in. There’s also the fn+r which switches the display between 60hz for lower power consumption and 120hz; just like the Legion it takes a split second and the screen goes dark, but it’s a very convenient shortcut implemented by Lenovo on their Legion lineup, and that has trickled down to the Ideapad Gaming.

Speaking of the display, it’s not bad. I wouldn’t say it’s super vibrant or anything, but it’s 120hz that you can switch to 60hz for power savings with the aforementioned keyboard shortcut, and it works well enough in games. There is a version of the new Ideapad Gaming 3 that comes with a 16:10 display that’s 144hz I think, but this 120hz is 16:9, which is fine although unexceptional. Oh I forgot, it is freesync, so even though there's no MUX switch you still get the benefit of variable refresh rates.

Bloatware is almost nonexistent, you only need to remove McAfee and I think it’s called the Lenovo Welcome App (which you can remove separately from Vantage).

There is no MUX switch, although the HDMI is wired up to the dGPU. Interestingly the type-C port is wired up to the integrated graphics instead of the dedicated graphics however, so for the external-monitor fps boost you should use the HDMI. There’s options in both the BIOS and in Vantage software to switch the operating modes between Optimus (iGPU+dGPU), iGPU only, or iGPU only on battery + Optimus when plugged in.

The SSD is quite cool, it's a Kioxia BG5, which is Kioxia's latest dram-less OEM SSD that's also PCIE Gen 4. The speeds aren't that exceptional especially at the 256GB model, but it's cool to see OEMs use a PCIE Gen 4 SSD in the 42mm form factor. Almost all PCIE Gen 4 30mm/42mm SSDs aren't available in consumer versions yet, which makes this an interesting test SSD

Disassembly isn’t difficult but it feels tedious. You need to take apart the rear cover (recommended to have some plastic spudgers/guitar picks) before taking apart the bottom panel. Once taken apart you get easy access to both the SSDs, the battery, heatsink, and memory slots. It comes with 1 stick of 8GB DDR5, although I did all of my testing with an additional 8GB sticks I purchased for $65, bringing it up to full dual-channel (technically quad-channel) bandwidth. That’s also another downside, the disassembly isn’t the most straightforward and DDR5 laptop memory is quite expensive compared to DDR4, twice as expensive if not more for a given capacity and speed class.

Battery life isn’t the best but was better than expected for a 45W battery. This is the smaller battery model (you can upgrade it to a 60W battery which I assume would improve things greatly), although with AMD’s legendary 6000-series’s power saving measures on power-saving mode, watching a 1080p Yule Log video from Youtube at quiet mode, 60hz display refresh at half brightness on battery gave about 5 hours and 30 minutes from 100% to 13%. During this, total system power consumption was only 6.5W reported from the battery, which is pretty good for a 15in system, and might be even better in the iGPU only mode.

Thermals are vey good despite the loud fan noise at max speed. Cinebench R23 scored a 10242 after a 10-minute stress-test. The max temperature was around 92.7C, once the CPU temperature goes over 92C, the fans go from a decently high sound into max speed, but at no point did the CPU ever throttle while maintaining a 66W (68W peak) boost. I couldn’t test that many games, although the RTX3050 did struggle a bit with shadows when I cranked them up in GTA 5 (my FPS w/ the benchmark was around 50~70fps albeit this is quite unreasonable settings). The RTX3050 runs at 85W according Nvidia’s Control Panel, so this should score relatively decent for a RTX3050 relative to other laptops, but I was never able to hit this point even in benchmarks (Unigine Superposition maxed out at 60W on GPU and 38W on CPU). Thermals during Unigine Superposition on 1080p Extreme was 72C on CPU, 59C on GPU; 1080p Medium was 66C CPU, 61C GPU. I also ran Payday 2 which typically doesn’t run great with graphics all the way up, but it would stay above at least 70fps worst-case (depending on the heist >100fps is pretty common).

My main concern is the price. If you’re getting something refurb with warranty, an Intel Whitebook (better known as the Eluktronics MAG15 or the XMG Fusion 15, but dark grey) is $700 w/ warranty and gives you a RTX 2070. It’s last gen but you get arguably easier and cheaper upgradeability and more VRAM on a GPU that’s still pretty good. I do believe there’s an Intel version of this laptop that comes with a RTX3060, but at a higher price. Honestly at the current price of $900 you can probably get something with a RTX3060 which would give you a much better gaming experience. Overall, the latest Ideapad Gaming 3 isn’t bad at this configuration, but the price makes it hard to justify given there’s other options out there (sometimes from within Lenovo).

text: I purchased my Razer Blade back in 2016.  I spent the extra money on a higher end model with 1TB SSD and the better processor.  I've enjoyed the laptop over the last 2 years until recently when I noticed a crack in my track pad (image attached).  The track pad is still working but I could not figure out how it cracked. At this point the laptop is out of warranty but in my mind this is a serious defect that Razer should support in some way.  Razer won't sell you a battery. If you purchase this laptop and have any trouble expect to pay over $150 before they address and charge you for your problem. title: Very good gaming and content creation laptop at a fair price.
text:
The Acer Predator Helios 300 is a mid-tier gaming laptop. The metal and plastic construction, makes a bit sturdy and it comes with very good hardware in this price point.

The screen is bright enough, better than the advertised 300 nits. It was able to reach 300 nits at around 75% brightness, and at 100% brightness it went up to 371 nits...not to shabby for a gaming display.
The display is fast at 144Hz @ just 3 ms and the color gamut was quite good 99% sRGB and 78% aRGB and just 83% DCI-P3. It should be able to handle photo and video editing and content creation like champ.
There is a bit of light bleed on top right and top left of the display on the unit I have.

The keyboard has a backlit 4-zone RGB and the it isn't bad, but the keys are a bit mushy to the touch. I just prefer a firmer keyboard keys...maybe I am bias because I use a mechanical keyboard. The Microsoft Precision Touchpad worked without issues and has been very responsive and accurate.

The USB C 3.2 Gen 2 port comes with Thunderbolt 4 and USB Charging and next to those ports HDMI 2.1 with HDCP support and Mini DisplayPort 1.4. There are two USB A 3.2 Gen 1 ports and USB A 3.2 Gen 2 that supports Power-off Charging.
The Thunderbolt port is might fast. I was able to reach 8.5 Gbit/s (1062 MB/s) speed copying files. You could transfer a 4k 25GB film in 20 seconds

The Predator Helios 300 comes with a full Gigabit Ethernet port so you won't lag for lack of reliable Internet connection.
And if you happen to have a Wi-Fi 6 internet, the Killer Wi-Fi 6 is as fast as the Gigabit LAN.

The sound is tiny, since the firing down speakers are tiny. The speaker area is 19mm thick and some laptop as thin as 13mm have been able to fit louder and better sounding speakers...of course they cost a lot more.
A least Acer included Dolby DTS X software that works great with external surround speakers or headphones, and you will need them if you want real sound.

There are 2 DDR4 RAM slots, each one with 8 GB DDR4 3200 MHz RAM for a 16GB DDR4 total, upgradeable to 64GB DDR4.

Acer included 2 NVMe M.2 slots, one occupied by a lighting fast 512GB Samsung PCIe 4x4 NVMe capable of 6900 MB/s read and 5000 MB/s write speeds. Also there is a 2.5" SATA bay available. Acer included the SATA cable and screws in the box. In case you have a 2.5" HDD or SSD lying around and don't want part ways.
During tests the Samsung NVMe went above rated speeds on both read and write performance.

The battery is on the small size for a 15.6" gaming laptop. I would have prefer a larger capacity battery, instead of a 2.5" SATA bay. At least Acer came up front about the battery running time. They stated the 6 hours and how they achieved that results (Battery life was tested using video playback).
So make sure you have the power adapter next to you while gaming, since the battery won't last much unless you dial down screen brightness and disable the dedicated graphics.

The Predator Sense App have several settings to adjust lighting, fan speed and performance settings. There is 'Default', 'Extreme' and 'Turbo' options available. Setting the system to 'Turbo' increases system performance and consequently also increases fan speed exponentially. Of course, is necessary to keep the Intel Core i7 and the NVidia RTX 3060 cool and churning reducing throttling.
The cooling system does a very good job keeping the airflow going and it does even better job at cooling if the laptop is raised a couple of millimeters.

There isn't much to do in the BIOS, beside disabling the intro sound.

Acer does a very good job with the Predator Helios 300 performance and excellent pricing. The laptop is very responsive and it can handle most games above 60 fps on high settings. It has good build quality and the screen is even better than described.
It will be hard to find anything better at this price point and down the road you could upgrade RAM and M.2 SSD to keep up with never ending tech evolution.

The screen felt a bit flimsy, since it has a flexes a bit more than I would have liked. Avoid opening the screen from the sides and try opening right on the center.

title: Good performance, driver nightmare
text:
This thing performed very well whenever it was not Bluescreening or having other malfunctions due to drivers. The temperatures were good, and the overall responsiveness of the system was fine. Game performance was fantastic. I can say you can definitely feel the difference between a dedicated SSD and a hybrid drive, though.

First, the factory default driver configuration of this thing is unstable, which makes installing a correct configuration more difficult. The intel RST driver (for the hybrid drive) version is old, and causes rare system lockups. The intel graphics driver (either the version by default or the one from MSI) also stops responding occasionally under fairly normal usage (game on one monitor, browser in another). Further, the MSI dragon center (default software on the installation) caused a blue screen which lead to me having to factory reset. I looked the dragon center BSoD up, and apparently it is a common issue.

If all it took was simply downloading and installing the drivers from MSI, there would be no problem. After factory resetting and not wanting any more occasional freezes from the HDD, I took the risk and updated the intel RST driver from MSI's page for the laptop. Immediately the computer started getting occasional blue screens on startup and Windows data corruption. By the time I was returning it, the system was in such poor shape from the MSI-provided RST driver that I could no longer access the MSI factory reset, and Windows' own 'Reset this PC' never worked from the start - saying it encountered a problem.

I believe if you happen to uninstall/install the drivers in exactly the correct order and/or do a clean Win 10 installation yourself, this laptop should perform well for the price. MSI used to have a driver installer by disk that would install all the proper drivers in the right order, so you'd have the perfect configuration. This is how the user manual installed on the laptop says to install the drivers. However, the laptop has no dvd drive, and no such driver dvd was provided. Now, you just have to guess the installation order and risk bricking the laptop for many hours and then going through the factory reset again (if it's still accessible). Windows 10 also makes clean driver installs difficult, because if it detects no driver for some things while you're in the middle of doing an uninstall old -> install new procedure, it will immediately try to install a driver of its own choice. I am not new to computers, and have done several setups from scratch without encountering any driver problems of this magnitude.

It's possible I got bad hardware by chance, but all of the issues being directly traceable to drivers suggests the issues were all driver-related. Many other negative reviews are specifically about bluescreens and stability, and its probable some of them they are driver-related as well. Other products in the same price bracket rarely have that many reviews specifically of that type. If MSI can automate or clarify the safe driver installation order and provide external factory restore media by default (such as a recovery disk or USB) which is in a known stable (even if old) configuration, I would be able to recommend this. As is, you have not only the usual gamble of whether the hardware is good, but also whether you happen to uninstall & install the drivers perfectly in an already misconfigured environment.

title: Faulty cooling system that require a copper shim
text:
Besides the 80w 3070 switcheroo that msi pulled on us, my particular laptop had a fault in the cooling system. The copper plate that goes over the cpu die only makes 20% contact on the left side. The right side is completely angled up. In order to alleviate this, I placed a 20mm x 20mm x 1mm copper shim between the cpu die and the copper plate of the cooling system.

Now it makes full contact, but the cooling is still kinda meh. Even with a -65mv undervolt and a cooling pad, I couldn't sustain the full 4.2ghz clock speed during testing, instead it drops to ~3.4ghz. Still, I got a cinebench r23 score of 10955. Not nearly as good as the 11800h in the mp66 version of this laptop. One dude on reddit received a score of 14603 with a 4.4ghz all core overclock, so that's a testament on how powerful the 11800h is.

Some positives: the 80w 3070 (that's the target tgp, 85 is the tgp limit) performs similarly to a desktop 3060 and has a bit of cooling headroom. I personally got an undervolt-overclock of 1530mhz @ .700v. If you're up for it, you could probably flash the vbios with a more powerful 3070 mobile chip. Just make sure to clamp down on the voltage if the tgp of the vbios is 115w+.

Also, the chassis has enough room to put thick heatsinks on the nvme drives.

Overall, I think I'm gonna try the msi mg66 with the 125w 3070 since videos on line show it has better cooling.

title: Great replacement for my gaming desktop PC
text:
Reviewing model PH315-53-72XD. I'm in my 60s and have been PC gaming since the late 1980's owning mostly Dell and Acer desktops through the years. Five years ago I built a desktop gaming PC. This is my first laptop of any kind.

I decided to replace my HUGE gaming desktop rig with a laptop so researched gaming laptops for about four months. I was about to go with a Lenovo Legion when I stumbled onto this Helios 300 on June 24 (2020). I thought the price ($1,199.99) had to be a mistake. Other systems with this video card, storage, and 10th gen i7 processor were running around $1500 minimum. A few more days of research and I started to find positive reviews that actually linked to this exact listing...so I bought it.

For my purposes, this laptop is perfect. I wanted to simply replace my gaming desktop with something I could connect my monitor, keyboard, mouse, and speakers to, then, when necessary, disconnect and take somewhere. So far, a month later, I couldn't be happier.

The other reviews are correct, the battery life is awful. I played Civilization VI (on highest graphic settings) and the battery went from 95% to 9% in about 48 minutes. But for me, that's not an issue as I always play plugged in. The battery does not deplete nearly as quickly if you're just surfing, emailing, etc., but if you're wanting a laptop that you can rarely plug in, this isn't it.

I wanted to purchase an extra power cord so that I could leave my main power cable plugged in under my desk at home, then have a second that I could take with me. That proved to be a challenge as ACER does not sell one (at least at the time of this writing, one month after purchase). Even when chatting with Acer Sales, they were mystified that they were unable to find one. Furthermore, I could not find one for sale anywhere.

A second chat session with Acer a week later turned me on to their accessory supplier, Capital Data. I contacted them and they were able to sell me an extra power kit...for $115 plus shipping. I paid it, as I really wanted the second power cable. But ouch. It took two weeks to arrive, but I now have my "travel cable".

You've no doubt read about the features and specs, etc., so I'll just say this. The desktop PC I built five years ago was still fast and functional. But this laptop is noticeably faster and quieter. Yes, the fans kick in when gaming heavily, but the noise is still not as loud as my desktop was. I love the startup speed, keyboard, screen, etc. When I'm not using my connected monitor, this laptop screen is really crisp and bright. The software tools Acer provides are great. You can customize many aspects of your machine.

The computer world changes fast so research is always a good idea, but for the price and time I purchased this, it was five stars. Have fun!

title: Stopped working within 2 weeks....took 34 days for Lenovo warranty repair service
text:
*** My latest update(s) at the bottom of this initial review.

This is my 2nd Lenovo IdeaPad laptop, the first one was a cheaper regular non-gaming budget laptop that I bought more than three years ago for my brother and it still works great. This laptop is mostly for folks who want a gaming laptop on a budget. If you are a serious gamer, I suggest you look at the Legion line of laptops. This is a very heavy laptop. Build quality is very good. Love the look and feel of the keyboard, it is quiet. It has two USB-A, one ethernet, USB-C, audio out and HDMI ports. I like the ventilation grille design at the back and the sides. The speakers are at the front, not that great but just ok. I love the rear block of the laptop that looks like the Legion, it has the HDMI, power and the ethernet ports instead on the sides. The touchpad is ok, it would have been nice to have the left/right click buttons on top of the touchpad. But I am expecting too much for a budget laptop.

I consider this an entry to mid tier gaming laptop. It has a 1080p 15.6-inch display with a 120Hz refresh rate. The screen brightness is disappointing, I have to increase it to ~70% during the day indoors for decent brightness which is equivalent to 30-40% in my couple years old EliteBook. If you sit next to a bright window, you will end up increasing it to 90 or 100%. The AMD Ryzen 5-6600H processor is powerful, it has 6 cores and 12 threads. This is fewer than the Intel core i5 12500H (12 cores) but the Intel one costs much more. If you can find them at almost the same price, I would go with Intel.

The RTX 3050 is a great budget GPU, and should be good for most games. For some games, you may have to bump down the graphics options. This will get you around 60fps at 1080p at the high settings. If you can stretch your budget a bit, RTX 3060 is a much better GPU, I believe you can get ~40% better performance with around 90fps at 1080p.

One thing that I suggest is to upgrade the RAM to16GB. The laptop is fine with 8GB for normal work and when less demanding software is used. For example, I do a lot of photo and video editing. I use Adobe’s Lightroom (LR) and Photoshop for photo editing which is RAM hungry. I noticed that the memory was 95% used when LR was running. Even then the speed at which it would import / export images was amazing, and did not see much performance degradation except for occasional slow response.

I also recommend increasing the storage, there was only 185GB free space left OOTB and that’s not much as you install other software on the system. I was surprised to see almost 50GB of the storage was used right out of the gate. You can upgrade the memory and storage yourself, there are videos on YouTube on how to do it. There is not much pre-installed bloatware, the Lenovo vantage / welcome pop-up’s have been annoying, I will uninstall them. There are others like the Feedback Hub, MS Teams and couple others that I will uninstall as well.

I am very impressed with the speed at which I can transfer files from a USB 3.2 thumb drive to the local SSD. I copied 31GB worth of files in 1 min and 50 secs, data transfer rate around 280 Mbps.

I can feel the bottom of the laptop warm but it was not hot. Even when the CPU & memory usage is high for extended periods, I have not felt it hot like my top of the line business laptop does. There is good ventilation for the heat dissipation. I don’t hear the sound of the fan running unless I get my ears close to the vents. Since this laptop is heavy, it will sit on my desk most of the time, this is not something I want to carry around quite often.

The battery life is average, it does not last more than 3 hours from light to normal use. So, do not expect to get more than 2 hours of gaming time while on battery power.

So, if you have a fixed budget of $1000 and looking for a gaming laptop, then this is a great buy for the price. This is a good laptop for students who can use it for their school work and use it to play games during their free time. It can be upgraded for memory and storage if needed but this will add to the cost.

If you can stretch your budget by $300, I see the Legion available for $1200 (before tax & after $150 discount) with Ryzen 7-5800H, 16GB RAM, 2TB SSD, RTX 3060 165Hz 1080p. In my opinion, this is a much better deal and a superior spec gaming laptop.

Removing 1 star for the limited RAM & storage and the bulk. IMO, Win 11 gaming laptops such as this should come with minimum 16GB RAM since 4GB min. is OS requirement.

Update 19-Jul-22:
I am changing the rating to 1 star. Today, the laptop / display stopped working, nothing displayed on the screen. Last I worked on it was couple days ago and the last the task I ran on it was to transfer files between two new SSD drives. The laptop was put on sleep mode. This morning, when I open the lid, the keyboard was lit, battery had power but no display. I tried connecting to a monitor using HDMI / USB-C cable, no change. I tried the hard reboot as well, nothing displayed on startup, the fan runs but no display. I let the battery drain completely, that did not help either. I may now have to reach out to Lenovo for support. If that does not work, I will have to open it to try disconnect / reconnect battery pack. This is why I don't get these Windows machines for personal use, they are not reliable. The business line laptops have been good. The last personal laptop that I bought was in 2003. Over the last decade or so, I have been using the Apple Mac's with zero problems.

Update 29-Jul-22:
Laptop was shipped to Lenovo a week ago. Repair service is on-hold since they are waiting on replacement parts. No ETA on when I will receive the laptop back. A week after I shipped the laptop and Lenovo acknowledged its receipt, I received an email with a link to a video showing how to box and ship the laptop. This would had been helpful before I shipped it.

Update 10-Aug-22:
Still no news on when Lenovo will ship the repaired laptop. Last night, received an email saying they will extend the warranty by 60 days. Email says they have seen tremendous demand for PCs and so is the increase in demand for support. Looks like they failed to ramp up the support needs to meet the demand. This laptop stopped working in less than 2 weeks. They could have sent me or given me an option for a replacement laptop instead of extending the warranty. Knowing that it is going to take a while and as a good customer service, they could have shipped a loaner.

Update 22-Aug-22:
It has been more than a month since I shipped the laptop to Lenovo for repair. No idea on when I will receive the laptop back. The last update I received was on 11-Aug saying final testing has begun.

Update 26-Aug-22:
Received the laptop on 25-Aug, 34 days after it was shipped to the Lenovo repair center. Repair summary states they replaced the motherboard, LCD cover and wireless. The hard drive was wiped clean, lost everything I had on it. So, I had to go over the new laptop setup again. I had installed couple of software that required a license key, not sure what grief I have to go over to re-activate them. Happy to have the laptop back. I doubt I will consider buying another Lenovo laptop. I understand not every Lenovo laptop is faulty and things like this can happen but I am not happy that the repair service took this long. Imagine a college going student having this issue and not having a laptop for one-third of the semester or someone on a very limited budget having to purchase another laptop because they need one.
And I forgot to mention, the laptop came back repaired with a loose screw or some metal part which rolls as I move the laptop. I will not be surprised if it causes a short someday.

title: So Far, So Good
text:
As of today, 3/21/2021, I've had this computer now for 4 days.

I bought this computer as an early birthday gift to myself and to replace an old laptop. While I know a few things about computers, I don't claim to know enough to build my own computer. I was a bit scared to get this; gaming laptops have a stereotype of looking "edgy" with sharp corners and LEDs targeted at "hardcore" gamers. I wanted, at the very least, a powerful, competent, portable gaming rig, and I seem to have gotten what I want out of this.

PROS:

1. This computer is no slouch! After a quick Windows setup, I was up and at 'em, downloading my Steam games in hardly any time at all. Within literal seconds, I was playing my favorite games at max settings with no problems.
2. For something primarily made of plastic, it feels really nice and smooth to the touch.
3. After a RAM upgrade (I upgraded the RAM from 8GB to 16GB before first boot), this computer can handle anything I throw at it.
4. The keyboard is really nice. I'm still getting my bearings with it (I'm not used to a laptop with a numpad), but the keys feel nice and springy, they aren't loud while typing, and the illumination is nicer than I thought it'd be. You couldn't mistake it for anything other than a laptop aimed at gaming.
5. Battery life is fine. Not terrible, not great, but serviceable.
6. This bad boy stays nice and cool while gaming! It never got unbearably hot to the touch or loud with its fans. While playing the most intensive PC game I own (Planet Coaster, lol) at max settings, I didn't encounter any dropped frames, hiccups, stutters or lag.
7. The speakers are nice. Good for gaming and watching YouTube videos.
8. The screen is crisp, clear and bright.

CONS:

1. As stated above, this particular model comes with a single stick of 8GB of DDR4 RAM. I'd say don't spring for anything less than 16GB if you're going to be playing graphic heavy games (or games in general, really), but this wasn't an issue that another stick (or two if you're going higher; I believe this laptop supports 32GB at max?) of RAM couldn't fix.
2. Even though the plastic chassis is nice and smooth, it's also a shiny fingerprint magnet, so have a microfiber cloth handy for wipe downs (with the unit turned off, of course).
3. The offset trackpad is a bit of a hinderance for me right now, four days of usage in, but I'm sure I'll get used to it over time.
4. There is no webcam cover.
5. Again, something I'll probably get used to with time: because there is a full numpad to the right of the keyboard, the keyboard is also offset and I tend to misinput and mistype more often. I'll think that I pressed a key when I really hadn't.
6. SO. MUCH. BLOATWARE. Most of it can be uninstalled though, so that's a good thing.

title: Depending on what you are coming from, it can feel like a sidegrade rather than an upgrade
text:
Prior to this purchase, I had the Lenovo Y50-70 UHD for two years. This past summer, however, the motherboard blew out. After I got it back, the screen hinge broke. That meant it was time to look for a new gaming laptop. After much impatience and thought, I decided to get the ASUS. Depending on what you are coming from, however, it can feel like a “sidegrade” rather than an upgrade.

As I continue to use this laptop, I will update my review.

PROS
- Dazzling performance in games and for productivity
- Good value for your money
- Great keyboard (New, 10/11/16)

Although my old Lenovo had a 4K screen, I could not play most games at the resolution. The 860M simply could not keep up, which meant playing at 1080p and on medium or medium-low graphics settings depending on how new the game was. The ASUS, however, has not yet encountered a game that I could not play with maxed out settings. GTA V, XCOM 2, MGS:TPP, and Overwatch play with plenty of processing power to spare and at a steady 60hz. It is quite clear that the GTX 1070 will be futureproof at least through the next generation of games at 1080p.

I also use Lightroom to edit photos and that program runs ten times better on the ASUS than it did on my Lenovo. Clicks register instantly, menus expand or contract on demand, and I can browse my catalog without stuttering. I also use my laptop for occasional STATA or SAS use and it blows through calculations in the blink of an eye – especially as compared to the Surface Pro 4 I carry for work and school.

I must confess that I also looked at the new Alienware 15 that just came out. For a similar configuration, and the extended warranty, it seemed that I was going to pay $2500 or more and I would have had to wait another month or so for the 120hz screen. At the end of the day, though, the ASUS was almost $1000 cheaper and I could not justify spending the extra money for a substantively equivalent system.

I did not include this in my original review, but when I went back to my old laptop to transfer a few files, the difference in keyboard quality was noticeable. I always thought that the Lenovo keyboard was a bit mushy and soft, but it felt especially bad after having used the ASUS for a week. Although not as good as mechanical switches, the keys on this laptop have a satisfying click and firmness that makes typing much more enjoyable than it had been on the Lenovo.

CONS
- Speakers are not that great
- Gets warm

One thing that I feel is disappointing is the speakers. They sound fine – no noticeable distortions other than sounding a smidge tinny – but they do not get especially loud at 100% volume. Next to my Lenovo or even my Nexus 6P, the difference in quality and loudness is stark. The worst part, however, is the placement of the front speakers at the edges of the laptop where at least one hand is likely to cover them while gaming. Doing so degrades the sound quality dramatically, making the use of headphones a necessity for games where sound is important for identifying enemies.

Under load, this laptop gets very warm. While playing Overwatch on “epic” settings, the GPU gets up to 82ºC even with the laptop fans going at full blast (loudly, I might add, further emphasizing the necessity of headphones) and while atop a cooling pad also running at maximum speed. Although the design keeps most of this heat away from the keyboard by blowing it out the rear vents, it does make me somewhat concerned about the longevity of the system – especially as games get more demanding in the future.

CONSIDERATIONS
- Screen is color accurate and bright, but the resolution difference is noticeable
- Extended warranty options (UPDATED BELOW)
- Battery drain while connected to outlet (New, 12/5/16)

Allow me to give credit where it is due. This screen gets VERY bright and its color accuracy is excellent. I do not think anyone will have any issues with this laptop outdoors or when doing Photoshop or other color-sensitive work. However, the 1080p resolution is a noticeable downgrade from my previous 4K monitor. Text does not feel as crisp and images do not quite have the same sharpness. I concede this is not something to describe as a flaw and I doubt anybody will notice if he or she has only ever used 1080p screens, but it does make me wish that I could have an option for 1440p at least.

The laptop comes with an automatic one-year warranty that also covers accidents, which is fantastic. However, their site does not seem to offer an option to extend this unless you live in Europe. I sent an email asking if they offered such services to North American residents, but have not yet heard back. I will update this review when they reply.

Update – 10/11/16

ASUS got back to me and confirmed that they DO NOT offer extended warranties for their laptops, which is quite a shame. They recommended that I purchase such a warranty through Amazon, but the reviews on coverage offered through SquareTrade are alarmingly poor. I guess I will just have to make sure that I take extra good care of my laptop.

UPDATE (12/5/16)

Based on some of the other reviews, I decided to swap the included HDD with an SSD to make my games snappier. Despite never having done any kind of hardware work on a laptop before, the process was simple. All I had to do was take off the rear plate, undo a couple of screws, plug in the new SSD, and I was ready to go. If you want to replace the 1 TB HDD with something faster or larger, you can easily do so without worrying about messing up cables or anything like that.

Having sung the praises of the hardware, I did notice something odd. I recently started playing Watch_Dogs 2 and, after a couple of hours of gaming, I noticed that the battery – which had been at 100% prior – was noticeably drained despite the laptop being connected to an outlet. It had 40% of its power remaining. The same thing happens, albeit much less noticeably, when I play other less demanding games. It seems that the power brick does not provide quite enough juice for the machine, but I am not sure what this means beyond a partially drained battery.

I think I might try pushing this laptop to drain the battery and see what happens. I will update this review when I do. However, the fact that this is happening strikes me as odd and definitely adds to the sense that this is more of a “sidegrade” than an upgrade.

title: In my opinion, a great laptop for the price.
text:
Runs most games I throw at it pretty well. I played Cyberpunk 2077, Resident Evil 2 remake, and Resident Evil Village pretty well. Everyday use is quick also. I always have a million Chrome tabs open and this PC takes it like a champ. No issues there.

The screen is pretty nice as well. Gets more than bright enough for every indoor situation I've thrown at it and it's sharp enough. However, I have yet to take it outside (and I don't plan on it), so I don't know if it gets bright enough to overcome direct sunlight.

The IO array should be alright for most people. It's got two USB type A's (one on each side), an HDMI port, an ethernet port, one USB type C (which apparently you can use to charge the laptop, though I haven't tested it), a headphone jack, and an SD card reader, which is much appreciated.

The speakers are alright to my untrained ears. They're not insanely bassy but they're also not super tinny. They're plenty loud and easy to hear in most situations, but occasionally I do find myself using a Chrome extension to force the volume louder on softer YouTube videos, so keep that in mind.

The only thing I can really complain about is battery life. It's not great. Using power saving mode, I was only able to get a few hours of light work done on Chrome. If you need something portable with a battery that will last you an entire day, this ain't it. At all.

Overall, I don't regret my purchase. It's powerful enough to run most games at at least medium settings, it has a nice screen, a really nice keyboard, a good trackpad, and is enjoyable to use on the day to day. Just keep in mind that the battery life isn't good. If what you're looking for a powerful budget gaming laptop that you plan on keeping connected to a wall and just want the convenience of being able to move it around the house, then this might be the laptop for you.

title: High quality gaming laptop with a couple of quirks
text:
The ROG Zephyrus M is packed full of great features like the BEAUTIFUL IPS display with 240hz refresh rate and response time of 3ms, a 1TB SSD, a 9th generation i7 with 6 physical cores and 12 threads, 16 GB of RAM, a thunderbolt 3 port, a nice RGB keyboard, and some nice ASUS software.

The software allows you to change the settings on your RGB keyboard and make some performance tweaks so that you can control exactly how your laptop runs. This is a nice feature because on max settings the laptops battery life is short and the fan is pretty loud. Like... really loud. This isn't a huge problem for me because I always game with headphones, but if you're somewhere that requires something a little more discreet you can use the ASUS software to set the laptop in "silent mode" and while it's not completely silent while gaming it does drastically reduce the fan speed.

The IPS display is BEAUTIFUL. Note that the display is only 1080p, but for the size of the display I think that's perfectly sufficient. If you must have 4k you can always attach an external display via the built in HDMI port. For a screen this size I doubt 4k would be noticeably better, but if you must have it you'll have to look elsewhere.

The 1TB SSD, 16GB of RAM, and 9th generation i7 all provide a snappy and fast OS experience and is great for virtualization if you do any of that sort of stuff. I'm an IT guy so it's nice to be able to spin up some VMs on my laptop without being too concerned about resources or storage space.

The RTX 2070 Max Q doesn't disappoint. I've been able to max out all the games I play with it just fine. A lot of the games I play are a little dated so I haven't REALLY tested it's limits yet, but for 1080p gaming I doubt there are many games that would push beyond it's limits. If you're looking for 4k gaming you might struggle a little bit, but this is not a priority for me. I recommend you look at benchmarks for the RTX 2070 Max Q because it does have a significantly weaker performance than it's desktop counterpart. For a mobile gpu, though, it does a great job.

My only real complaint with the laptop is the layout of the ports. The Thunderbolt port is located halfway down the right side of the laptop, and the charger port is halfway down on the left side of the laptop. This makes using a docking station kind of awkward because have to run cables to both sides of the laptop, and the thunderbolt cable will actually cross two USB ports on the right side. Ideally the Thunderbolt port and the power port are both located on the same side and are near the back of the laptop. I don't have a super fancy docking station so I cannot provide power to the laptop through that port, but that may be possible I'm not sure.

title: Easily one of the best portable gaming laptops on the market right now.
text: I've had this laptop for about five days and it performs well beyond my expectations. I've had no heating or noise issues which was what I was worried about even while running games thanks to the efficiency of the pascal architecture of the GPU. It's got a solid battery life on casual use for a gaming laptop (4-5 hours web browsing) and a beautiful ips display with very impressive color accuracy with little to no glare and great viewing angles. Thanks to the desktop grade GTX 1070 GPU you can run pretty much any title you want maxed out at 1080p and easily maintain a solid 60 fps (If you have an external monitor with a 120 or 144hz refresh rate you could really push well over 60fps on almost any game). Speakers are actually pretty good but nothing to brag about. I am a really big fan of the keyboard and if you like macbook style keyboards you will most likely like the keyboard on this laptop. All in all I would highly recommend this to anyone who needs a relatively thin and portable laptop that basically has high end desktop level performance when it comes to gaming, video editing, or general productivity.

title: Good general use laptop. Quality at a reasonable price
text:
I am using this for one task only; to keep track of the wines in my wine cellar. I say this because I have read that some find this machine running hot; mine is in a 55F environment, so that’s not an issue for me.

I like the look and feel of this laptop; it’s maybe just a tad on the heavy side for a mini-laptop these days, but it feels sturdy, and I’ve had too many bad experiences with super fragile laptops. This laptop is a nice compromise between heft and portability. Don't get me wrong, it's very light and not too thick, but I'm comparing it to other minis out there. The upside is its greater ability to survive abuse.

I do miss a touch screen; I almost expect that in every laptop I buy now. But, on the other hand, the i7 CPU, the 16 GB of RAM, the Nvidia GeForce, and the 2GB GDDR6 are more than I would expect on a laptop, from a reliable brand, at this price.

Although I have this set for a singular task, I always load it with most of the programs that I use so that if my primary laptop breaks, I have another set up for immediate use. This laptop easily handled any of my typical work programs, most MS Office programs, and web browsers, with no problem at all. They all loaded quickly and ran fast.

I like the fingerprint protection, and it helps speed booting up and opening a program. In addition, the power brick is not too large, it and the laptop will fit easily into any computer bag or backpack.

The backlit keyboard is very easy to type on; the keystroke pressure is very light but has good tactile feedback, and finger fatigue will not be an issue.

One little touch that I really enjoy is the camera shutter, a small built-in slide to cover the lens. And, as the world is moving towards type-C USBs, It’s good to see two of them here as well as a type A. The built-in HDMI port is also great since I usually work with two monitors.

I’ve had many Dell computers, and I think of them as very reliable and, when an issue occurs, I’ve experienced good customer service. That would make me recommend this laptop for home, school, and office use as long as it’s not used for intensive tasks such as gaming or memory-intensive graphic applications.

title: Powerful Gaming Laptop
text:
The 3050ti in this is fantastic.
This is coming from somebody that has a 3070 in his desktop.
This laptop has been able to play anything I throw at it from medium to high settings.
I've been able to get consistent 40 to 60fps in Cyberpunk using DLSS.
Mount and Blade: Bannerlord runs like a dream, especially with DLSS enabled.
The only game I've had annoyances with is Ark: Survival Evolved, but I also have annoyances with Ark on my main desktop with a 3070... Just a poorly-optimized game.

Keep in mind that (by default) you need to have the laptop plugged-in in order to activate the 3050ti.
I initially tried launching a game and experiencing horrible performance, and I was terrified for a few minutes that I'd fallen for some sort of scam, but then I plugged it into an outlet and games started running smooth as butter.
I've heard that this option can be changed in the bios (hit F2 as the laptop is turning on to access the bios), but I only play games while I'm stationary somewhere with access to an outlet anyway. I'd rather save battery-life if I'm using it on-the-go for YouTube and whatnot.

One major annoyance! The Bluetooth transmitter built-in to this system.
Seemingly at random, the quality will drop to AM Radio levels of bad. That would be annoying enough, but when this happens the volume fluctuates from extremely quiet to EXTREMELY LOUD, which has caused me to rip my Bluetooth earbuds out on more than one occasion.
Uninstalling and reinstalling the Bluetooth transmitter in "Device Manager" (along with the driver) and reinstalling it seems to fix the problem. Hopefully it's a permanent solution, but only time will tell.

All in all, great gaming laptop with a great CPU, GPU, and RAM.
This could be used for light/medium, and in some cases even heavy gaming. (Basically any game that's well-optimized should run great and look great, from my experience so far)

Throw another M.2 drive in it!
1tb fills up very fast nowadays for gAmErS.
Super easy process, just pop the bottom off using something skinny and metal (I used a precision flat-head screwdriver), plug it in, close it up, activate the drive in "My Computer", good to go!

Update: It's been over a year of consistent, daily use for gaming / video editing / photo editing / watching YouTube, and it's still going strong. I've been treating it well- only using it on a desk, keeping it in a cushioned sleeve when not in-use, etc.
It's been well worth the money. I'll be back to update this review again when it reaches the end of its life-cycle.

title: Packing a Plastic Punch
text:
This laptop is all about the specs. The CPU seems to turbo at 3.1GHz endlessly, never even getting close to throttling, and the gpu will stay at 1800-1900MHz constantly when plugged in. This PC has 3 major shortcomings:

1) Battery life is horrendous. It's expected of a gaming laptop, but with all the junk the computer comes with it would have been nice if one of those helped you get light use out of this thing. Either the battery life indicator is completely inaccurate or this thing loses nearly a % a minute in light use.

2) The screen is OK, but it feels like the weakest link out of the whole system. Either a faster display or a display with better color accuracy would have been greatly appreciated. It will run pretty much all games at max settings with ease, so while G-Sync is nice it's hardly noticeable with such beefy hardware behind it.

3) Build quality. This laptop does not feel well made in the slightest, as there are messy internals that stick out of the casing on my unit due to poor assembly. The plastic is rather ordinary and provides quite a bit of flex. Both the QC and quality of materials is lacking in this laptop.

The laptop performs extremely well, and if you don't mind a $1700 laptop feeling more like a $500 one I would highly recommend it.

title: The Alienware AW17R3 - A Superb Computer Plus It's Not Just for Gaming!
text:
First, let me state that I am not a 'gamer.'

Then why am I reviewing this [[ASIN:B015P3SO22 Alienware AW17R3-7092SLV 17.3" FHD Laptop (6th Generation Intel Core i7, 16 GB RAM, 256 GB SSD + 1 TB HDD) NVIDIA GeForce GTX980M]]?

It was offered to me by Amazon Vine™ and, as soon as I saw it, I ordered it.

I ordered it because I know that gaming computers are extremely powerful machines and would be suitable for the type of audio and video work that I like to do. I use several programs for these purposes as well as some photography ones. Some of those programs use a lot, sometimes almost all, of a computer's CPU power.

This one does not disappoint. It has just about all the processing power anyone would need. And everything on it runs FAST!

It does run a bit warm (not hot) but so did (and does) every other laptop computer I have ever used with these programs. The very large and heavy power supply runs warm too.

Normally I use the openSUSE (GNU/Linux) operating system but, for the time being, I shall use this computer as it is, with its Microsoft Windows 10 system, for some months just to make certain that there are no problems which might need warranty work.

After I am sure that nothing untoward is going to occur, I shall convert it to openSUSE..

In the meantime, there are several programs I use which are cross-platform. In other words these programs have versions for Windows, Mac, as well as GNU/Linux systems.

So far, I have installed just a couple of them. One, in its Windows version, is about equivalent to its GNU/Linux counterpart; the other is noticeably inferior (or, as we used to say, "Crude but Usable").

Both programs work well and both work much faster than they do on my "old" (2012 - ancient in computer terms!) laptop (which also has an Intel i7 processor [an older version] and 16 GB of RAM). It too runs very fast but its speed pales compared to this new Alienware computer. (I'm sure that when it is converted to openSUSE, it will run even faster. All things being equal on a given computer, GNU/Linux OSes generally run much faster than Windows or Mac OSes.)

I moved all of the data folders (Documents, Music, Pictures, and Videos) to the D-drive (1 TB, 7200 RPM) which, as the computer comes from the factory, are installed on the C-drive (256 GB SSD). (Why isn't this placement done by Alienware?)

I added some Internet Radio Station URLs to the Music folder, downloaded the K-Lite codec package, and played a couple of Internet Radio Stations.

It's certainly not ' ultra high fidelity,' but the sound which emanates from this computer is absolutely the very best I have ever heard from a laptop's built-in speakers. Nothing else that I have ever heard is even close!

The graphics are excellent. Plus there are adjustments to the colors on the keyboard and on the lid and body and they can be very 'cool' if you like that sort of thing.

I had what turned out to be a very minor problem: when I received the computer on May 12, 2016, the AC cord which plugs into the transformer had the wrong connectors. It had round holes while the transformer had blade connectors.

As I learned many years ago, you can't put a square peg into a round hole, so I called Alienware/Dell. Fortunately I had registered the computer (using my older computer) even before I tried to attach the power supply. So when I spoke with a representative, he already had my information at hand.

He asked me to send him pictures so he could show his supervisor the problem.

I did so - and so did he.

He telephoned me within fifteen minutes of receiving those pictures (you can view these pictures below) and, believe it or not, he promised to FedEx Overnight the right cord to me - and he did! It arrived the next day. I couldn't have asked for better service from a computer vendor

I then turned on the computer, went through Microsoft's 'registration' procedure, and started using it.

The keyboard is very well-designed and is a pleasure to use. So is the large trackpad. The 'feel' is just right, at least for me, and I anticipate no fatigue. The display is superb, bright and colorful. (I downloaded and installed a number of Alienware HD backdrops.) And, as I mentioned above, everything for which I use it runs FAST, much faster than any other computer I own or have previously owned.

Is it 'perfect?' Of course not. What computer (or anything else) is?

For me, there are three very minor 'nits' - the computer is very heavy (nothing to be done about that) and it has no internal optical drive (can be remedied with an inexpensive external Blu-ray/DVD/CD reader/writer). In addition, it has only three standard USB 3.0 ports (can be remedied with an inexpensive USB 3.0 hub).

But these are very minor points, at least in my opinion, and two of them are easily 'fixed.' (I already have disc reader/writers and hubs.) And my minor complaints may not even be applicable for you.

I'm sure that you can guess by now that I am very pleased with this laptop! I'm very, very happy that Amazon Vine™ chose to offer it to me as I had been planning to replace my 2012 computer (as always, money being a problem!). I shall (hopefully) make good use of this one's very powerful capabilities. I'm sure that it will be even more capable when it is converted to openSUSE, though this probably would not apply to the majority of people reading this review.

So, in conclusion, let me state that, if you need an advanced powerful laptop computer for a variety of resource-intensive uses and also desire excellent graphics and superb sound quality, I believe that this one is one of the best choices available. (I'm also sure that it would be great for gaming!) And if my experience with Alienware/Dell's service department is any indication, the company stands behind its products, is an easy one with which to deal, and is anxious to please its customers.

Thus I highly recommend this laptop computer.

Thank you for reading this and for considering my opinions.

Lawrence H. Bulk

=====Update: Monday, July 25, 2016

Yesterday I 'wiped' the supplied Microsoft Windows 10 operating system from this computer and replaced it with the openSUSE 'Tumbleweed' (rolling release - a 'permanent' system which 'never' needs to be upgraded) operating system.

As I expected, this computer as well as all its installed programs now operate much faster than previously when it used Windows.

I certainly do not expect many people to do what I did - get rid of Windows and replace it with a GNU/Linux operating system - but if anyone reading this desires to do so, it is quite easy. The openSUSE system will install with UEFI activated; Secure Boot must be deactivated.

Again I thank you for reading this.

Lawrence

title: Acer has come a long way: it builds nice laptops now
text:
Acer Predator Helios 300 & Triton 500

I used to think of the Acer brand as cheap. After using both the Helios 300 and the Triton 500 side by side for several months, I no longer feel that way.

The high points of the Predator experience: solid gaming machines that also do a good job of handling other tasks I frequently engage in: video production, photography processing, and academic and essay writing.

The Helios 300 is the cheaper and thicker of the two machines (see photos). It is also much easier to upgrade, which almost everyone who buys this machine will need to do. Unless you only plan to install a half dozen games and then not do anything else with the machine, the included 512GB storage is inadequate. Luckily, both the 300 and the 500 come with additional M.2 storage slots. It was relatively simple to upgrade the 300, but upgrading the 500 involved removing the motherboard entirely and took quite a bit of time and some specialized tools. You can pay your local computer shop to do this for you. I would recommend budgeting for a 2TB M.2 drive to be your primary partition.

The screens are decent, although to be honest I cannot tell any difference between the 144MHz response time on the 300 and the 300MHz response time on the 500. They look exactly the same to my eyes with one exception - the 300 has zero stuck pixels but my 500 came with one stuck pixel. That is mildly irritating. Acer policy is up to two stuck pixels so be prepared for that possibility.

The 300 is about 30% thicker than the 500. That did not bother me in the slightest. Both keyboards feel identical - they are nice and snappy and I enjoy typing on them.

I do not like the gimmicky RGB on either. A lighted keyboard is nice in a dark room, but I have no use for rainbows and flashing blasts of color so I set both machines to solid blue.

Battery life is adequate, not great.

The 500 has Thunderbolt if that's important to you - it is not present on the 300.

Fan noise did not bother me on either unit but the fans will be audible if you are playing a graphics intensive game or doing video production. This is necessary to keep the units from overheating.

Acer has come a long way since I first used their products many years ago - they have really upped their engineering game. If you need an affordable multi-purpose laptop that does not require taking out a second mortgage the 300 and the 500 are both worth taking a look at. I would shell out a little extra for at least a 1TB hard drive, and if you can afford it, go with a 2TB.
