title: Outstanding value & great temp control
text:
[[VIDEOID:9b8bc93cf53a92f001896b17ed21144c]] Review model: Lenovo Legion 5 15 Gaming Laptop, 15.6" FHD (1920 x 1080) Display, AMD Ryzen 7 5800H Processor, 16GB DDR4 RAM, 512GB NVMe SSD, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050Ti, Windows 10H, 82JW0012US, Phantom Blue

TL;DR: I’ve recently tried out three gaming computers on three tiers: a high-end Alienware m15 R4(10th gen i7 with an RTX 3080), a more entry-level Acer Nitro 5 (10th gen i5 with an RTX 3050) and this mid-range Lenovo Legion 5. Out of the 3, the Lenovo Legion (Ryzen 7 with an RTX 3050ti) is actually my favorite. It comes out on top as the best value, with very impressive overall performance and excellent features with few trade-offs.

Form & Build:
This computer looks fantastic. The subtle navy blue color differentiates the Legion from a lot of other “gaming” computers. The matte finishes hide fingerprints without looking cheap. The monitor hinge is inset from the rear of the computer by a couple of inches making the whole machine feel a lot more stable when the monitor is open--it never feels wobbly or top-heavy. The computer is beefy without being so heavy that you can’t have this thing on your lap (on a good lapdesk, natch).

Keyboard & touchpad:
If you’ve ever used a Lenovo Thinkpad for work, the keyboard on the Legion will feel very familiar. The main keyboard keys are well-sized and very comfortable to type on. They have good travel with just enough clickiness. Very quiet. I do like that there’s a full number pad. The number pad keys seem like they are slightly smaller than the alpha keys, which makes for a little bit of a lopsided look, but you get used to it very quickly. If you don’t often use the number pad, you barely notice. The touchpad is comfortable and responsive, but could be larger. You’ll likely be using a regular mouse for games, anyway. The RGB backlighting on this laptop is beautiful. There is a selection of different zones and color schemes (it’s not expansive, but the light pastel-y scheme was my favorite), so you can probably find a style and brightness that you like.

Display:
The screen looks great and even when I wanted something bigger, I had no problem hooking it up to my monitor via HDMI. The bottom bezel is large, lifting the screen a bit and giving you a better viewing angle. The matte finish of the screen succeeds at reducing glare.

Graphics:
Really impressive given the relatively low-end 3050Ti. The combination of the 3050Ti and the Ryzen 7 CPU seems to be a sweet spot for laptop gaming. Honestly, under every-day play conditions it was hard to tell the difference between my Alienware with a 3080 and the Legion. Based on my play tests with World of Warcraft: Shadowlands and Code Vein, the biggest tradeoff with the Legion (Ryzen/3050Ti) and Alienware (i7/3080) is in ray tracing and anti-aliasing. When ray tracing and anti-aliasing were turned off, the Legion frame rates were almost as good as the Alienware, but I did have the occasional screen-tearing issue, and light bouncing off shiny objects (ray tracing) was not nearly as cool. I also did turn down some distance detail to reduce the rare stutter.

In return for a surprisingly meager reduction in visual quality, the Legion gave me outstanding temperature performance. I was totally impressed by the Ryzen 7 in terms of temperature control. I was able to have the Legion out on my lap desk questing while watching TV on the couch. I have never been able to do that with the Alienware. After playing for hours, the keyboard on the Legion never heated up noticeably and the bottom of the computer remained cool to the touch. The Legion effectively ventilates heat through the rear and sides using fans. With my feet up, I could definitely feel that hot air output on my legs, but that heat was consistently moving away from the laptop. The power brick, however, DOES heat up quite a lot. Make sure it’s located somewhere away from metal and loose papers and can get good airflow.

title: Powerful, Sleek and Elegant
text:
Pros:

1) Extremely powerful. Nvidia 1650 graphics card and 8GB of RAM make for fast processing. Was able to simultaneously download 2 50GB games while watching Netflix. Was then able to play those games at 45-60FPS on high settings with no lag (Overwatch and Battlefield V).

2) Elegant. Design is discreet and simple; good for the professional adult who loves to game. No need to embarrass yourself by lugging around a machine that throws up green and red lights with its brand and logo plastered on the chassis. This is a laptop you wouldn’t mind taking into the meeting room.

3) Privacy Shutter. A simple design add-in, but an appreciated one nonetheless. It is a physical piece of plastic that slides shut over your webcam, so no gimmicks there.

4) Connectivity. Offers an ethernet port, HDMI port, 2 USB ports, headphone jack, and USB-C. More than enough for my needs. If you need more, you can easily get adapters.

5) Matte screen. By this I mean that the screen is not glossy or prone to glares like OLED or LCD screens are. It’s much softer on the eyes, and your screen won’t be blocked out by the sun or if you are next to a light source.

Cons:

1) Storage. This only offers 500gb, which is very small compared to the standard of 1TB that most laptops offer now. However, this is easily fixed with an external hard drive that can be bought from $20-$45.

2) Matte Screen. I realize that I listed this in my pros; that is because due to its anti-glare properties, the colors have suffered a bit when compared to OLED or LCD screens. However, the amount of color diminishment is very low; I’d say this would matter much only if you are a serious content creator. Otherwise, it makes no difference to the average PC user.

3) Mousepad sensitivity. It is low compared to other laptops, such as the Microsoft Surface Pro or the MacBook Series, so that may throw some users off. This is easily fixed by downloading a free program called Windows Precision Tracker. Otherwise, a wireless mouse is just fine.

Conclusion:

Overall, this is a very attractive laptop that certainly delivers on its power and speed. It is perfectly balanced between being a work and gaming laptop. Lenovo has really poured their efforts into this laptop, and I am a lifelong Lenovo customer after experiencing this machine.

title: Best laptop for your money, if memory ain't an issue...
text:
Basically, the best budget computer. Yeah, including Desktops.

You're telling me I can buy a gaming computer that outperforms AND replaces Xbox, can be used on the go, and only costs 800$?? That's amazing. Gaming laptops have never been more affordable, and powerful, all at once. Half the price of your standard gaming laptops, without the assembly of a gaming desktop.

Enough gushing, though. It's not perfect. At this price, you can play generally any of the standard games with only minor problems. I played Halo Infinite and Modern Warfare well, loading faster than my Xbox buddies, but some menu navigation issues here and there were difficult to ignore. These games themselves run very well, but really push your computer's GPU, which means don't expect to play high end games for long without charging. That is to be expected.

The material that makes this computer aren't the best, but good for the money. It's not the most delicate computer, but maybe don't go crazy and throw it or spill anything on it. It's a bit heavy if you plan to vibe out in bed or on the couch. Definitely don't game with this thing on your lap. Keyboard is so-so. Maybe don't eat over this computer unless you are okay with crumbs in the keyboard. Speakers are fantastic in my opinion. You can connect some Bluetooth speakers or earphones easily if you think otherwise.

The AN515 model, the cheaper 800$ish you're likely looking at, you'll gonna lacking in RAM and SSD memory. It's not the end of the world...who am I kidding? 250gb SSD? That's way to small! Maybe consider the models with more RAM and Storage. They can run between 1000-1200$, but if you can afford it, or upgrade the RAM and storage yourself, it makes a world of difference. The most you'll need is an external HDD, which is maybe 80$ for 1tb. Still cheaper than most laptops and desktops.

The Nitro 5 is definitely the best computer for a budget or if you're starting out and want a computer you can play right out the box. This can replace your Xbox, or a spare Xbox when you have friends over. This plays the majority of PC games at good resolution and framerate. As a casual laptop for websurfing, videos, programming, Photoshop, you're in good hands, and can be easily upgraded if RAM or memory is an issue. Think of it as a portable desktop, or even a portable Xbox. You won't be disappointed, especially at this price. Great for newcomers.

title: A solid player in the gaming laptop market
text:
My First Windows Laptop purchased with my own money...ever. (I've owned 5x MacBooks)

Looking at the prospect of being on the road for work for an extended period of time with my work provided MacBook had me filled with concern about 'what the hell will I do every night'. There is only so much surfing the web you can do before you go insane.

So I thought about 'what would it be like to get a personal gaming capable laptop' and started down that rathole. This led me to a Dell computer, but I thought I would be leaving monday and it was friday afternoon and I needed to find something that would actually ship and not cost a fortune, so I started spelunking amazon.

I went with the i7 GTX 1060, 16GB, 1TB HDD version and added another 16GB Chip, a Samsung Pro 950 SSD (512GB), and a 2TB Seagate drive. How you people get by on SSD only I'lll never know. One thing I wish windows would get their crap together on is to implement something like the Fusion drive on Mac's here where I could have 2.5TB of space and it handles keeping the files i need on the SSD, but no.

I initially looked at the 15", but decided it'd be really nice to have a slightly larger screen. Getting old sucks. While the screen is larger, it's only 1080P. After using retina display for quite some time that's a bit of a let down but it's not terrible. The screen is rather solid and supports this NVIDIA G-SYNC thing that while playing some initial test games I can say works rather well.

If I sit this laptop on top of a closed MacBook 15" it only slightly wider and longer, I mean you have to look closely to see the overlap. The case is put together nicely, the lid is metal on the top, but plastic underneath. The trackpad is usable. My biggest challenge is translating the keyboard. There are two things that are still bugging me after a weekend. The first is the fn-ctrl-alt-windows key layout compared to the mac. the fn/ctrl are swapped. so I'm hitting fn-V a lot trying to cut/paste passwords and codes as I get things setup.

The other is this 'gaming optimization' button. It's to the right of the delete key. I've hit that damn button so many times typing when I'm going for the delete key and it insta launches a full screen program which is annoying. The program is great it's a tuning program but having it next to a highly used key in a touch typist gets old, it takes a while to learn not to hit it.

The keyboard itself is nice. I do not have any complaints about it at this time. It feels about as nice to me as a mac wireless keyboard, but with the added benefit of a full number keypad. I've yet to use that extensively, but it's nice that it is there. I picked up a cheap but decent mouse to use for FPS, but am waiting to install too many more games until the 2TB drive comes in and I can move data around. In case my clone doesn't work I don't want to be re-installing 50 games after that drive gets here in a few days.

Performance wise my only comparison is to my Alienware X51 R2 with an ATI Radeon R9 290 in it. So the games I've tried all look prettier on the new one because the 1060 is a couple years older. the R9 gets FPS warnings in Battlefield 1, the new laptop does not.

So let's talk heat. This has a high end CPU and high end GPU in it. it's gonna get warm. Now I'm old and you younglings might not know this but laptops used to be this hot with just regular laptop boring old guy work like Lotus Notes and Microsoft Powerpoint on Windows 98. Except now it gets hot when you're running around fragging people in BF1 in full glory. So for me, it's not that warm. I've had no overheat issues but I was playing with it sitting on a wooden TV tray on the couch. I've had a laptop shut down due to heat laying a bed surfing the web back in the day so to me it's working as designed here. yeah it's warm on the bottom, but the keyboard/top isn't even noticeably warm so far. I'll keep poking at it but for now I think the thermal concerns are overblown. It may be the 15" is worse as there's more room in the 17".

Battery Life. I laugh at the complaints, back in my day if you got an hour you were happy ;) My first test of playing Civ 6 it lasted about 2.5 hours before I got nervous. This was their default power management where I just installed Steam, installed Civ 6, and started playing & pulled the power cord. So whatever the default is in their settings is what I used. I only used the trackpad while I was playing and had no peripherals attached. The sounds were coming out of the speaker until i got tired of it and muted it while watching TV / Playing.

All in all if you're looking for a portable gaming capable machine i think this is a good option. The added benefit to me was I was able to order it, pay a tiny bit extra and get it overnight, and other than having to wait for windows 10 to update itself a few times which took a few hours after that I was off to the races.

I haven't had to use support or anything. They do have a forum you can check and it's a bit confusing on it at the moment as I think these are brand new models and there is a lot of information (and mis-information) about the 752 model on the forum. This caused some confusion when I went to get an NVME SSD. Apparently the previous model sometimes supported m.2 and sometimes could support NVMe when a bios thing was flipped. Asus could update their spec sheet to say more than 'SSD' as it took me a while to figure out the 752 <> 702 that this was. I only figured it out after finding some reviews, the Asus website wasn't any help so a ding for that.

title: The Legion Lite
text:
This laptop sits in an interesting space...it's not built to the max like the Legion series, but it's not a netbook either. Call it the Legion Lite. I shy away from calling it a “budget” gaming laptop, for reasons I’ll explain below.

Since this is a Lite product, some compromises had to have been made here (more on which in a minute), but what really interests me is the overall foundation...can this thing be made more than what it is out of the box? I'm happy to say it can, and indeed there are two things you'll want to do almost immediately.

But let's start with the CPU - it's a 12th Generation Core i5 12500H. Does that mean anything to the casual gamer? No reason it should, so I’ll just say that in terms of performance it’s a pretty solid choice. It’s not the fastest CPU in Intel’s stable, and if I’m being honest I think it’s a bit power hungry, but it does work well for most scenarios. To help with performance, the laptop has some pretty effective thermal management. Cooling ports abound, taking care of both the CPU and GPU, and looking rather kick-butt while doing it. Fan speed is noticeable at high performance profiles, but nothing outrageous. There are also cooling pipes inside the chassis.

And now we come to the first thing you’ll want to do with this rig. Memory is your typical DDR4 SODIMMs with two slots available. It ships with 8GB which is pretty spare for a gaming rig. 16GB is in my opinion the entry point to get access to most titles. It’s fairly simple to add memory – opening up the chassis is a little tricky (undo the two screws in the back in addition to the screws on the bottom cover….) but it’s smooth sailing otherwise. The system architecture handles up to 64GB, though frankly with the rest of the hardware that’s pretty overkill. I put in 32GB of gaming oriented RAM which, although probably a bit overkill too, did result in somewhat snappier performance.

Storage is in the form of two PCIe M.2 slots, one of which is already taken up by the shipped 512GB SSD. That is job 2...upgrade the storage. 512GB is adequate, even appropriate, for a boot drive with a backup image on it and maybe a few titles, but it's a bit limited for any kind of serious gaming rig. So get yourself a 1TB SSD and install it in the second M.2 slot. Or 2TB if you want. Go nuts. Note that the slots are differing sizes, with the shipped SSD taking up the smaller slot. The slots are Gen 4 if you want the fastest speed, but again…mind the rest of the hardware and decide if your use case justifies 7000mbs speeds (in the case of the latest Sabrent SSD Rocket drive….).

Graphics are either on-board AMD Radeon or a discrete NVIDIA GeForce RTX3050...yes, the RTX offers ray tracing, and yes it's fantastic. This card can handle high settings even on AAA games at 1080p as well as offer flexibility in settings vs resolution on an external monitor. Most gaming laptops shoot for a TDP setting of 80W on the gaming card, which this laptop meets at 85W. I will say that unlike the previous generation IdeaPad Gaming, this one meets that setting consistently (long story, but in a nutshell power delivery to the previous generation system was a bit wonky, with battery losing power even when plugged in and everything set to Super High Ludicrous Turbo mode. This one ships with a much beefier power supply, and it’s very helpful…..).

The display is...well, remember the compromises I mentioned? This is the main one. The screen isn't a disaster, but it's brightness leaves something to be desired. Resolution in this model is FHD (1920x1080), another compromise. Then again, the screen offers a 120hz refresh rate, so it's capable of surreally-liquid movement. As this refresh rate is still a relatively new phenomenon in gaming laptops, I'm inclined to overlook the brightness factor as a serious deficiency, but would still have appreciated something capable of lighting up the joint a bit better. I mean, it’s appropriate for a casual gaming laptop, and if a brighter screen is desired there’s always the ability to join it up with an external monitor.

Sound is decent (thanks, Nahimic!) though to my ears the speaker placement isn't ideal. It's a laptop though, which isn't an ideal platform for immersive sound. Since I game with a set of cans on my head anyway, the sound is a non-issue.

Ports are rather adequate, with 2 USB-A (one on either side), HDMI, Ethernet, audio-out, and a USB-C Thunderbolt that is capable of charge in and out, which also does double duty as a DisplayPort 1.4. The USB-C is not the laptop's charging port (it has a separate proprietary port for that) which may have bothered me in a non-gaming laptop. In this form though, doesn't bug me at all since I use the USB-C for other purposes.

Keyboard is backlit (yay) with only one color (boo) with key travel and such really quite good, I think. In a Lite product, it’s honestly a better keyboard than I would expect. But then, I only really care about WASD and the mouse...

So enough about specs. Does the bloody thing work? Well....yes, yes it does, but after memory and storage upgrades it works EVEN BETTER. For example, it doesn't have any problem at all with Lego Star Wars Skywalker Saga, not even the corny jokes. Given that the screen is FHD and the level of the supporting hardware, running things at high settings wasn't a problem at all. Honestly, this hardware could likely drive an even higher resolution display.

System settings are handled via the Lenovo utilities where cooling profiles and system checks can be made. Pretty standard, really. Windows 11 comes on this machine, and mercifully Lenovo didn't lard this thing up with bloatware. System updates took about an hour to get things caught up.

So what do I think? I think it's really tempting to call this a "budget" gaming laptop, because as I said earlier this is sitting in an interesting space. However, to do so kind of skips over the expandability of the machine. It’s easy to add more RAM and storage at a later date, in a configuration that Lenovo may not offer from the factory. The CPU and GPU are not the absolute fastest, but then in this space they aren’t supposed to be…they are designed to be wholly adequate for 80% more-or-less casual gaming, not professional eSports.

There's definite value here, and in terms of raw computing performance this system can really hold it's own. The screen is my biggest criticism, but even at that it is more subjective than anything else. Quite frankly, at the price/performance ratio where this sits...this is a serious contender for those looking for very good gaming performance and very excellent adulting. I like this laptop quite a bit.

The throttling is actually a good feature as high end graphics require a lot of power consumption but I would have liked to have gotten a notification to let me know this was the cause of the drop in frame rate (and a feature rather than a bug).

The only downside of this laptop is that the USB-C port is a USB 3.2 port and does NOT support Thunderbolt. It also doesn’t have a DisplayPort (only HDMI). This means if you plan to use this device for VR, the Occulus Rift 2 is incompatible even though the graphics card is well within spec. HOWEVER, the original Rift (which uses HDMI) will work as will the Occulus Quest. So if you’re wondering if this is VR Ready, it is but keep in mind that there’s an asterisk here depending on the headset. In a way, it’s actually ironic that the older Rift model works and the newer model does not.

title: Almost perfect
text:
UPDATE: I've been using this laptop for a while now. I've raised my review from four stars to five. It's true, the touchpad is quirky, but I use the computer with a Bluetooth mouse. The reason I've upgraded my review is that even compared to my MacBook Pro, the HP envy stands out. We've recently moved and I spent the last three weeks using this laptop instead of my normal desktop computer. The more I work with it, the happier I am. I've read reviews to complain about the Wi-Fi connectivity. I had absolutely no difficulty. For a while, I was using the personal hotspot on my iPhone. The laptop flawlessly connected and stay connected for days. Speed is incredible! I've been using Photoshop and variance absolutely no delays even when doing complex editing. I admit that I don't use the touchscreen much. I'm just not used to that idea. But when I do, it's accurate and fun.

This laptop seems to be HP's attempt at directly competing with the 13 inch MacBook Pro. It certainly looks like one. It's very light; under 3 pounds. It has a powerful four-core Intel processor (Please note that the description of this product says it has a dual core processor. That's not correct mine has a four core.).

The screen is great. It has adequate brightness to use in daylight. The colors are vivid and accurate. The touchscreen is every bit as good as any I have ever tried. I have to admit that I usually forget the touchscreen is present; I'm so used to doing everything on a keyboard. However, when I realize I can use my finger, the results are great.

This laptop has 16 GB of memory. That's more than enough to run Photoshop and edit large images. I've also run Premier Pro with no problems at all. The combination of the powerful processor and fast, plentiful memory makes this machine perfect for a power user like me. This laptop could easily replace my desktop computer in terms of processing, memory and disk size. My unit has 512 GB of SSD. Considering that most of my data lives in the cloud, I'm never going to run out of disk space.

The touchpad is the one weak spot in this nearly-perfect laptop. I find it not nearly as responsive as my Mac's. It's very fussy about where you press it to get a left click or a right-click. The Mac works with just a tap with one finger for left click and two for a right-click. That doesn't happen with the HP. I use a Microsoft mobile mouse to compensate.

That brings me to one really great feature of Windows 10. If you go to the Control Panel and then the mouse screen, you'll find that there is an option to disconnect the touchpad when the mouse is present. This is an amazingly important feature. In the past, I've disabled the touchscreen to prevent accidental mouse activity while typing. Then, on occasion I had a problem at startup and needed to use the touchscreen. Of course it didn't work. Now, if I connect my mouse (Bluetooth), the touchpad is disabled. If I want to do something quickly in the car, and there is no mouse, the touchpad works.

The keyboard is generously sized and the keys have a nice solid feel. I have one little quibble: in bright light I find it difficult to read the white markings on the silver keys. In a normally lit room the keys are backlit and very easy to read. I've used HP laptops in the past. I think the keyboard in this laptop is a real step forward for them.

Priced similarly to the MacBook Pro, I expected a great deal from this laptop. From the perspective of processing power and useful features, this HP competes favorably. If anything, the screen is better. Colors are accurately rendered, brightness is more than adequate, and the touch functionality is a great bonus.

Battery life is excellent. I don't have the standard test suite to verify the manufacturers claim of about eight hours of working on a charge. I can say that I had absolutely no problem getting through the day without needing to recharge. Of course, battery life is dependent on how you are using the laptop. For example, when I worked with it in my car I had to crank up screen brightness which of course, eats up battery. Even so, I never ran out of power.

Wi-Fi operation is flawless. The built-in camera and microphone provide excellent quality for videoconferencing and other AV needs. I like that there is a physical switch to turn off the internal camera. That certainly improved my comfort using the device in my hotel room.

If HP could fix their quirky touchpad, this could be a true MacBook killer. Even with the less-than-perfect touchpad, it's a joy working with this computer.

title: Best performance for the price
text: I spent a long time doing a lot of research on different gaming laptops and which ones offered the best performance for their respective prices. This laptop had been in a lot of the reviews I read and watched, but never quite took the number one spot for an array of (arbitrary and bias things) in my opinion, like coming in second to a razor laptop because it looks less "childish" or that "while they were impressed with its performance" the other (always more expensive) laptop slightly edged out the Nitro 5 by a negligible margin, and therefore is better. In all the articles and reviews and videos I found testing out this laptop, one thing stood out to me; every single review (except one guy who recommended a laptop that's about $500 more lol) all said how impressed they were, considering what it costs. I finally bought the laptop, and man am I glad I did. If you're wondering which model to go for, I'd personally recommend the i5 model because in a couple of the testing videos I watched, the i5 model would be pitted against its i7 counterpart and in almost all the testing would only perform ever so slightly above the i5 models in some tests, and in most was equivalent or ended up thermal throttling and losing by a significant amount. Basically, it doesn't make sense to spend the price difference for the "better" processor thats only sometimes better and only slightly so when it is. Another thing I found with this laptop is, is that the battery life is actually quite impressive for the hardware and size of the laptop. Some reveiws on "professional" PC sites claimed horrific battery life of only 3 1/2 hrs with 4hrs at absolute best. I dont know if they didn't properly update/install drivers or maybe they just had the laptop during a bug in the driver software, but when I set mine into power save mode and disable features I'm not using like Bluetooth and the GPU (yes you can do that) I was seeing an average of about 6 hours while browsing the web, checking email, and even some youtube watching. I also found the speakers that were supposedly "a big let down and basically useless" according to another "professional" PC reveiwer to be totally fine. They definitely aren't gonna blow you away or make a MacBook Pro feel insignificant, but considering the price of the laptop, and all the performance it delivers in so many other fields, they are as good and maybe even slightly better than I was expecting. As for every other aspect of this laptop, m.2 nvme Intel optane as the standard included storage with another m.2 nvme slot available AND an available 2.5" ssd bay with the hardware needed included, AND a second available ram slot so that you can upgrade without having to spend an arm and a leg on a big single ram stick, and can take advantage of dual channel is f***ing awesome for a laptop, let alone one at this price! At the end of the day, if you're like me and looking at basically every "gaming" laptop ever made to try and find the best one for the price, I have to say go for this one. Every other comparable laptop performance wise, is NOT comparable price wise, and visa versa.

title: Easy RAM upgrade needed to maximize potential
text:
This is the laptop to get if you want to game on a moderately sized portable laptop and don’t mind opening up the laptop to upgrade it.
The laptop has nice mid range specs for gaming overall: Full backlit keyboard with numpad, silky smooth 144hz matte screen, and an RTX 3050 Graphics GPU that will crank out those frames without excessive compromise to detail, and is even capable of light VR. The 8 thread Intel i5 10300H CPU uses older 14nm lithography than the current gen 10nm stuff so efficiency and heat will suffer slightly, but it is nevertheless perfectly adequate as most games are not CPU intensive anyway.
For a $1000 laptop, the memory is equipped more like a web browsing thin-and-light laptop than the moderately-thick-and-moderately-portable gaming laptop it is. The 256gb SSD performs well for load times but will fill up rapidly if you aren’t careful – considering some modern titles take up 100gb or more. 8GB RAM is adequate for many games, but has potential being a major bottleneck as the system itself consumes 3gb of your 8gb just idling.
If you don’t want to be limited to a small amount of browser tabs in your powerful gaming laptop, then you will need to upgrade the RAM. An additional 8GB 3200mhz PC4-25600 DDR4 SODIMM RAM will run you about $30-$50 at current prices. Thankfully, the laptop can be easily opened by opening up the bottom panel, with nothing more than a typical x shape Phillips screwdriver and a prying tool. There are no “warranty void” stickers sealing the interior and you won’t damage anything as long as you are gentle. There are 2 RAM slots, the 8gb of preinstalled RAM is thankfully a single stick that only takes one slot and I was able to insert and use a 3rd party ram stick of equal speed and capacity, no problem.
As mentioned, 256gb is a very limited amount of disk space that may not work for everyone, but you cannot simply slide in an extra SSD. There is space for a 2.5” slot but that slot is not equipped with a SATA connector, so if you want to upgrade the storage you will either have to rely on an external dongle (the USB 3 ports are capable of at least 1 GB/s speed), or clone the system from the factory SSD onto a larger SSD. There also may or may not be a pin on the motherboard that you can buy a SATA connector for but I don’t know enough about motherboards to say for sure.
There is also no SD or micro SD card slot at all. I find it very interesting that Acer is omitting the SD card slot in multiple product lines ranging from small ultrabooks to their big 17” gaming laptop, to this laptop as well. Given the small disk space, an integrated card reader would have provided an easy way to upgrade storage.
The coaxial barrel charge port is interesting: it is centered on the rear between the exhaust ports, rather than on the side. Power consumption when idling with the screen on is about 35W. Power consumption in a stress test pushing cpu, gpu and screen brightness to the max with no peripherals connected is measured at 154W. When stress tested in this state, displayed GPU temperature hovers at 62C in a well ventilated 76F environment.
The exhaust shoots out the back and to the side as well, so if you use this sitting next to someone you may annoy your neighbor with hot laptop exhaust.
+ This does include a battery management option to limit to 80%, and I recommend you turn this on as keeping the battery charged at 100% is bad for longevity. The option can be accessed in the “Acer care center” in the “checkup” section.
+ 57.48 watt hours is the size of the relatively small battery pack. The battery does not contain any special technology to supply 150W of power, it is only capable of 60W output so when unplugged you get an hour of use with significantly reduced performance. Interestingly Acer uses the same battery pack for the larger and more powerful 17” 3050Ti model of the Nitro 5, so if you intend on gaming on battery power, there isn’t much benefit to getting the 17” model in terms of performance since the RTX 3050 GPU itself is able to gobble more than 60W (the TGP power use can be as high as 80W) and the battery will be the main bottleneck anyway.
+ The laptop is able to supply at least 15W to at least 1 USB port. Nothing too fancy but a decent amount of power for more hungry usb peripherals.
+ By default the backlight turns off after 30 seconds but this behavior can be disabled in Acer Nitro. Red is a good eye friendly color for keyboard backlights, providing illumination without distraction
+I did achieve 950mbps on wired gigabit internet
- The laptop has a type C port but does not charge itself by type C at all, the main purpose of the type C port is for information transfer. Usually laptops with C ports allow charging from type c which is cool because type C charging is much more convenient than AC charging, plus there is the potential of using a power bank. The (much more expensive) Dell XPS17 charges by type C from its 130W charger, yet this Nitro 5 with similar power consumption refuses to draw any power from the wall type C charger at all. To be clear, laptops don’t need the charger to supply the full power, if the external power is weak then they will simply enter a deficit and slowly drain down the battery.
- Volume and brightness buttons are in a weird place: fn+arrow keys rather than on the function key row.
+Silky smooth 144hz screen for competitive gaming and other high framerate content. You get a normal amount of bezels and no touchscreen which is fine by me. 1080p is plenty for enjoying gaming and movies, a bit low for productivity. The matte screen isn’t too bright but does a good job making the screen usable in bright light, the difference between max brightness and minimum brightness is around 3Watts of power.

title: Great For Gaming Without Going Broke
text: I needed a new laptop for gaming, streaming, etc. I went with HP because my old  HP laptop is 6 years old and still works fairly well and that impressed me that I was getting something new that would last awhile. But, as always happens, it had become frustratingly technically out-of-date for running some games and was also very slow due to low free memory. This new model is tons more powerful and triple the memory. I have yet to find a game I was unable to play on it and watching videos/streams is mostly without flaw. Battery life is not great, I would imagine because of the amount of energy it needs to be as cool as it is. This was not a deal-breaker for me because I really wasn't getting it for portable use anyway, so mine is always plugged in. 2 relatively minor issues I've had should be noted: The keyboard is backlit but this model turns off the backlighting after about 10 seconds of you not typing. As far as I'm concerned that defeats the purpose of the feature in that it doesn't remain constantly lit in the dark. There are no BIOS or other setting options to change this so it's a little annoying. Secondly, there seems to be a slight problem with the volume when watching movies off of streaming sites like Amazon Prime Video and NetFlix. At MAXIMUM speaker volume and MAXIMUM stream volume, the sound is acceptable but you can't get it any higher than an average output. It does NOT, however, have this problem when playing games, so I dunno what's up with that. I contacted HP about it, but they've never gotten back to me on it. I've found it to be a pretty minor annoyance though as if needs be I can still use my old laptop if I need to watch something at a  louder volume. All in all, I'm pretty happy with this model, though I'll update this review if anything new, good or bad, comes up with it. I decided to wait 3 months of using it before offering my opinion, and there you have it. ;)

title: A gaming laptop true to it's nature
text:
So I've been toying around with this since I got it today. I've been running benchmarks, playing a few games, and I can't express how impressed I was.

I wasn't expecting too much to be honest. I just wanted a nice little laptop that could run games at medium or high settings at 30fps. What I got was a laptop that could run games at high and even MAX settings varying anywhere between 35-60FPS depending on the game.

The first game I tried was Tomb Raider (2013)
Running the benchmark with 100% maxed out graphic settings (minus the hair effects), at 1080p, the laptop managed 30-50 FPS in the benchmarks most "stressful" areas. It didn't drop below 30FPS the whole time, in fact, 30 was the recorded minimum.

Next was Far Cry 3. A gorgeous game, with a lot going on. Starting in Amanaki Village, I noticed it was slightly above 40FPS, at 1080p, with max graphic settings, in DX11 mode. Outside the village, it maintained 50-70FPS easily.

I tried a couple other games as well, all maintaining fully playable framerates at max graphical settings. Needless to say, this laptop packs some serious power.

As for its other features, it all performs above expectations. The fully lit keyboard looks beautiful in the dark, with many different colors and different settings to mess around with, giving some great spectacle.

The sound also blew me away. It didn't sound like it was coming from a laptop. Not nearly high quality, desktop speakers, but with the built in subwoofer, the MSI GT70 Dominator certainly can get loud and produce some great quality sound on it's own.

Build quality feels alright. It's not going to withstand a lot of abuse, but a bit of slight carelessness doesn't feel like it would really cause any damage or issues. The nice looking brushed aluminum on the top looks sharp, and the rubber feet both give some clearance and grip to the underside of the laptop for cooling and stability.

It's a bit heavy, but for a 17 inch laptop with the power it packs, it's a fair compromise.

I'm not keen on flashy company logos on the outside of my laptop, but the MSI logo, even though it lights up a little, really isn't too showy, and doesn't seem to distract from the overall design too much.

The matte screen, while it does a decent job at resisting glare, isn't the best. There's a bit of noticeable texturing on the screen itself because of it's matte nature, which can distract slightly from what's on screen. Other than that however, games do look very clear, but not nearly as vibrant as some people would like. Some toying around with the settings should clear it up.

Overall, this is what I would consider a desktop replacement. It has above average graphic capabilities, great design, and just amazing in general. I'll be very happy and satisfied occasionally gaming on this while on a trip or just at a friends house. It's a nice alternative than lugging around my massive desktop case, even if it means I won't have the power of a GTX 780ti.

title: MSI GT70 Dominator does just that!
text:
I bought this system 3 months ago. I held off on reviewing it until I had used it for a while.

I had specific wants when I was looking for a new laptop. It had to be a TRUE Gaming Laptop and not a Craigslist "gaming laptop". I wanted:
* An i5 processor or above - check (i7 @ 2.7GHz)
* 4GB RAM or above - check (8GB RAM installed)
* A full size backlit keyboard with numeric keypad - check (SteelSeries with customizable colors across the spectrum. 4 color profiles you can save and change on the fly!)
* A large HDD - check (1 TB 7200RPM HDD partitioned to C: and D:)
* Dedicated graphics card - check (nVidia GTX870M with 3GB RAM / there is also an onboard Intel HD 4600)
* Large screen - check (17" LCD @ 1920x1080 resolution)
* Minimum 3 USB ports with at least 1 USB 3.0 - check (5 USB ports and 3 of them are 3.0)
* Windows 7 64-bit - NO (Came with Windows 8.1. More on that later though)
* Good battery life - check (EDIT 10/21/2015 - I constantly run 2 instances of Everquest and I do it on battery often to keep the battery fresh. It runs at least 3 hours running both instances and using the WiFi before I get the 10% charge notice. Not bad at all.)

My last laptop - a Toshiba Satellite A665-S6094 - was purchased 4 years ago and while it still works great it was time to upgrade if I wanted to play games on one. So when I had the opportunity I looked around for the best deal. I REALLY wanted an Alienware but after comparing the brands and the specs I found that I could have the same PC for a lot less. I am not interested in paying an extra thousand dollars for a name plate.

GOOD STUFF:

My biggest surprise was Windows 8.1. I hated Windows 8 when it came out so I really wanted Windows 7 on my system. Nothing sold currently had 7 on it so I had to go with 8.1. This is the main reason I waited three months before reviewing the laptop. I wanted to see how bad Windows 8 would ruin my experience. I can honestly say I am happy with the OS. The improvements they made to 8.1 make it completely usable and since I can boot to a "desktop" like Windows 7 and still have the tile screen available I don't have anything bad to say about it. It hasn't locked up once and everything I installed has run just as I'd expect.
*** EDIT 9/13/15 - I have completed the upgrade to Windows 10 and this laptop still outperforms anything I have ever used. Upgrade was easy and has changed nothing operationally. All installed games and programs still work 100%.

I have been extremely happy with this system for gaming as well. I have run everything on high or ultra settings with no problems. The system gets very warm at times but never overheats. I have run with no hiccups:
- Starcraft II
- World of Warcraft
- Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare
- Civilization
- Wolfenstein: New Order
- XCom Enemy Unknown
- Elder Scrolls Skyrim
- Tomb Raider

You can also specify which programs use which graphics card. I assume this is to max your battery life. For example you do not need Microsoft Excel to use the GTX870 gaming card. You can set which programs use which graphics card in the nVidia Control Panel. This is a very nice feature. I have my choice of the GTX870 or the onboard Intel HD 4600.

It comes with a DVD writer which I rarely use. It works fine though. I've installed with it and tested a few movies in it. I didn't want to spring for a Blu-Ray player since I don't buy DVDs or Blu-Ray discs anymore but I believe that is an option or available upgrade. (On my last laptop I bought an enclosure that slid into the DVD drive slot and added a 2nd HDD. I may do that again. Here's the item name on Amazon - SANOXY® SATA 2nd HDD caddy for 12.7mm Universal CD/DVD-ROM)

The WiFi has been great. I get the same speed tests from the WiFi as I do from a wired ethernet cable. I have used the Dominator to stream to my Apple TV and I haven't experienced any lag or slowdown. I've used it in multiple locations and it connects every time.

The USB placement on my old laptop has been a huge source of friction for me for the last 4 years. The Toshiba only had two ports - on the RIGHT side and right at the spot where you would naturally use a mouse. I am overjoyed that three of the USB ports are on the LEFT side of the Dominator (and all 3.0). I can plug in my USB controller, USB external drive and wireless mouse dongle and not constantly hit them with my hand while using the mouse. There are two more on the right on this unit too(both 2.0) but I have yet to use them beyond testing they worked.

The touch pad is very responsive. It recognizes multi-touch gestures and if you swipe right to left from the edge it brings up Windows side menu. There's a convenient button right above it that turns it on or off as well. I use that button more than the touch pad itself though because I use a wireless mouse. My only nitpick about the touch pad is that the system should remember I turned it off and leave it off when I reboot.
*** EDIT 6/4/15 - Found the setting in the Synaptic options that shuts the pad off when an external mouse is connected. One less nitpick.

The quick access panel has a few nice options. The Movie button loads PowerDVD for playback. There's a button you can use to override the fan and make it run at 100% speed and maximizes airflow. I've never had to use it but it is nice to know it is there. The button that looks like a brightness control cycles through the 4 preset keyboard illuminations you define in the SteelSeries engine program. There's an Airplane Mode button which turns off all the wireless functions. The next square button changes displays. The last one - the G - opens the Dragon Gaming Center which gives you a snapshot of what your Dominator is doing at the moment and allows you to change some settings on the fly.

NOT SO GOOD STUFF:

The built in speakers are good. They sound OK up to maybe 75% volume but after that they distort a bit - especially under heavy bass load. I first noticed it when I loaded World of Warcraft. The theme music is bass-heavy. And, unfortunately, once you have heard it you cannot un-hear it. There is a program loaded called Sound Blaster Cinema that can change the way the audio is played but I haven't found a good setting that makes this go away. Thankfully I don't blast the speakers much unless we're watching a video or movie on the laptop.

The laptop is heavy. Granted it is a gaming rig so I expected it to be heavy but for a 17" laptop it seems a little heavier than it needs to be. Considering all the features and cooling installed though it's easily gotten used to.

There's no touch screen. I didn't want one personally but keep it in mind if you're looking at laptops. Windows 8 was made for swiping and hand gestures so a touchscreen would have been good for most people. (I'm glad it doesn't have it. Fingerprints on my screen would drive me nuts.)

BAD STUFF:

I can't honestly say I have run into a BAD thing so far.

OVERALL:
4 1/2 stars. I knocked a half star off for the speakers. I'd call my experience with it 95% great and 5% tolerable. I love my laptop and with the lower thousand dollar price tag I am ecstatic with the performance I get! Alienware is overrated! In my opinion of course... :)

*** EDIT 10/21/2015 - It's been 9 months now since I bought this laptop and it still runs perfectly. I use it daily and most times for hours at a time. I have had no issues. The lid is still tight and stays at any angle I put it in. Keyboard backlighting is still bright and keys works perfectly. Not once have I overheated or had a shut down. LCD is great and sharp. The multicard slot works fine. I've had a few occasions to use it for file transfers.

*** EDIT 2/21/2017 - I just wanted to check in one last time and state, again, that this laptop has been fabulous. I have owned it for two years now (original purchase date 2/10/2015) and have had ZERO problems with it. I use it daily and have not had to do anything to it other than boot it up and Windows updates. It has never overheated, it plays everything I throw at it, the HDD still runs like new, the keyboard is as responsive and as bright as ever, the display is still crisp and the wifi has not diminished in any way. If this laptop died tomorrow I would immediately buy this exact same model again but I don't have to worry about that happening at all. Massive A+ rating from me. :)

title: A fantastic gaming laptop!

title: A Lot of the Negative Reviews are Misinformed
text:
I bought this bad boy directly from Acer refurbished, so that's why this review isn't verified as purchased. I just want to clear up a misconception people seem to be having here.

Misconception - "The gaming is poor."

This is simply not true. For what this device offers (a wattage-neutered 3050 Ti), gaming performance is outstanding. Update your drivers and make sure your games are set to use the dedicated graphics, and not the iGPU (Vega 8) inside the 5800u. You might be surprised how many people have no idea they're not even taking advantage of the 3050 Ti when attempting to game. Surprise surprise -- user error.

Furthermore, you can actually increase the power limit and overclock the 3050 Ti by a fair margin, though of course this will vary on a card by card basis. I myself have gained a 5-10% performance increase (varies depending on application/game) with a quick and dirty overclock. Oh, and don't forget about DLSS. If your game supports it, abuse it and thank me later. Use the tools at your disposal.

1/5/23 Edit: If you have the know how, it's possible to flash the vbios of this 3050 Ti to that of a Dell or MSI model. With the MSI bios, although temps are vastly higher due to more voltage, I'm seeing a 25% (you read that correctly) boost in performance over the stock vbios. Wacky stuff. Be sure to do your research first, though!

Beyond that, I see a lot of complaints about the screen being 60Hz. You're paying a premium for a 14" thin and light laptop that can still "get up and go" in terms of gaming, but without the gaudy "gamer" aesthetic (does everything REALLY need to look like a jet?). Are there games out there that could make use of a 120Hz+ panel? Of course, but would you pay an extra $300 for the privilege of hitting those frames in 1 or 2 games? What about users that won't be playing those very specific titles? Is that price justified to them?

Let's be serious, if you're a "competitive gamer" in need of "all dem FPS" you either aren't buying this laptop, or would connect to an external monitor and use a real mouse and keyboard (nobody games "competitively" on a laptop keyboard, change my mind). Why complain about something you had every chance to research? The internet is a very informative place. Perhaps you should start using it before making purchases.

title: It's a tragedy what Alienware has become.
text:
I bought a 17" laptop from Dell. I got every single hardware upgrade and I even got the extended warranty. After 7 months, the screen started going bad and I had to get service. A bit later, the system wasn't working quite right and I needed some more service done (I've got 20+ years experience in the IT field) and that went south, with the screen going completely out less than a month later. They required me to send the laptop in for service. I use my laptop for work, so I replaced the laptop with another and have let my wife use this laptop since then.

Three months after that previous service, she hadn't used it for several weeks and when she went to verify the battery level before going on a trip, it wouldn't boot up. I called Dell and honestly wanted a credit for what I spent on this, but they insisted and sent someone out to replace the motherboard. Well, he replaced the motherboard and when he was done, the motherboard had a password on that they couldn't reset (they sent a bad motherboard).

I've had this thing serviced four times in 14 months. They want me to have it serviced a fifth time. I simply wanted them to give me something else, as when something goes bad five times, it's clearly a lemon. They won't do anything but give me the exact same thing again. I've let them know that I need them to talk to my lawyer, who is pursuing a refund through the court system now.

In the last six to seven years I've bought twelve laptops, between work, my wife and my kids. I have had exactly one that needed service. In the twenty plus years of owning laptop computers, I've only had six instances where I needed service - five were on this Alienware laptop. I will likely buy twelve to twenty more laptops in the next six years.

I can tell you that nothing I buy for the rest of my life will be Dell or a Dell owned brand like Alienware. At the place I work, they just replaced thousands of laptops with Dells. I've never seen a failure rate so high and a company so completely in denial about their issues. They blamed issues on everything from the Windows load to the users, even though the issues were consistent and repeating at very high frequency. It's unconscionable the way they behaved.

I bought Alienware to get the best of the best. I got a pile of junk. Save yourself, avoid Alienware and anything else by Dell.

title: What a Beast!
text:
[[VIDEOID:b59c3fcefb85db221b9541409c0e9f2a]] Dell G7 7790 is the model I am reviewing.
Dell has been well known for Alienware products for quite some time though this isn’t formally an Alienware product this is more or less and Alienware computer. It has the Alienware software preinstalled and that is where you are able to customize things like the color of the backlit keyboard.

So let’s look at specs:
i7-9750H. 9th generation i7 is a great touch
RAM 16GB DDR4. I would have expected more at this price point but that is an easy upgrade if you want it. This is a dual bay with two 2x8GB 2666MHz sticks from the manufacturer. It is upgradable to 2x16 or 32GB total. I will end up upgrading this because I love having as much RAM as possible. Chipset is Intel HM370
Storage is a 512 GB SSD which is fantastic I will only use SSD because the speed for reading and writing is insanely noticeable compared to standard hard drives. This is a decent size drive though if your storing games this may be a little on the small side.
Now for the dedicated graphics. I am glad this comes with Nvidia as I prefer it over AMD. This model comes with the GeForce GTX 1660 Ti. Beautiful graphics off the bat. I haven’t customized or overclocked anything at this point.

This is also the 17” screen model and if your going for a gaming laptop let’s face it, you want the big boy. I was a bit surprised to see that it’s not a touch screen. Not a big deal as I don’t use that feature much. The mouse pad is extremely responsive and takes a little getting used to as I keep right clicking by mistake. The keyboard is outstanding. Backlight with full color range and completely customizable. You can have just the WASD keys a certain color independently if you like. The Alienware control panel is user friendly and easy. I will say out of the box your benchmarks will seem low and disappointing. It takes some system updates and tweaking to really optimize this computer but for anyone getting a gaming laptop you shouldn’t have any issues figuring out what to do.
The physical body is heavy and a bit bulky but that’s to be expected with a gaming laptop that has a dedicated graphics card. I would have expected a little thinner as it uses an SSD but it’s not too bad. The ports on this computer are well placed and throughout. The power and Ethernet plugs located on the back is clever. There is also a lighting port, three usb 3.0, an HDMI, a card reader and also seems like a display port.

All around the computer is a beast. Battery power does not last long especially if your using all the features. It looks like you get about 2-3 hours of full usage with the keyboard at full brightness as well. That’s honestly not terrible for how much you have running inside this computer. Price is a little on the high side but your not by much. With the specs this computer has your going to be pretty close to this range in cost. Just a fantastic piece of technology here.

title: Great Balanced Machine with Gaming Ability
text:
I was pretty excited to receive this IdeaPad Gaming 13 laptop.

The idea of a fast computer, which was also capable of gaming was very appealing to me. I do want to note that the computer required being connected to power the first time I turned it on. Even though the battery was over 50 percent, it would not turn on until connected to power.

The build of the machine is plastic, so you should be careful with it. Nevertheless, it looks good. In particular, I like the decision to include a small number pad to the right of the keypad. There are two USB A ports, one USB C port, headphone jack, HDMI, and ethernet.

The Ryzen 5 5600H is a very quick processor that will take care of your general computing needs with lightning speed. The 1650 graphics gives you the ability to do some graphic intensive tasks like video editing, but also play some games! I installed steam and downloaded the 2013 Tomb Raider and Witcher 3. I could play the 2013 Tomb Raider at well over 60fps. Witcher 3 I could dial back the settings and get around 60fps, or put it to high settings and get 30fps locked. This isn't earth shattering gaming, but it's capable especially if you're willing to tweak the game's settings and get configuration you prefer either for frames or resolution.

Also, be sure to click the battery icon in the taskbar and moved to max performance, before you start gaming.

The battery is somewhat disappointing, but considering the computer is already pretty large and has some decent weight being a gaming computer with plenty of venting, I can live with it. In general, if you're going to game, you want to be plugged into power. If you're web browsing or listening to some music, you can get well over three hours without problem. However, if you're gaming on max performance, you will get under a hour of battery life.

On the specs lists, the compromise on this machine besides an entry level gaming GPU, is the 256GB storage and 8GB of RAM. The 8GB ram can be upgraded pretty easily. There is a second slot if you take off the bottom of the computer. I'm going to bump mine to 16GB total soon. However, for many tasks, the 8GB is fine. There is also some adapters included that if you don't mind working with electronics, you can add a 2.5 inch SSD inside the machine to get more storage. I plan to do that eventually too. Again, unless installing large games like Witcher, if you're doing regular computing tasks, the 256GB storage will be ok for you.

Overall, I am super impressed with this laptop. It presents a very good value. You can open this up and out of the box have a quick machine that can also play some games. The most serious gamer might not want it, but if you want to play games casually on a machine that can do your other tasks, this could be the one for you. Being a bit of a gaming machine, you get the benefit of a fast CPU and GPU no matter what takes you are doing, which is nice! The one reason you might not choose the notebook is if you never game nor do serious video editing, you might could pick a machine that was smaller/lighter since cooling isn't as important they make some really slick machines when they don't have to be able to handle gaming. Overall, very much recommended!

title: Support finally gave me a fix! If you’re having an issue with this PC, this might be the answer!
text:
I’ve updated my original, scathing review. I hope to help EVERYONE with this issue. Apparently the optane drivers do not play well with windows updates and it causes corruption issues if they aren’t updated correctly. If you haven’t updated optane by going to the intel website to do so (would have happened before your computer turned into a slow, useless slug), that’s the first problem. So if it hasn’t happened to you yet, do that! Otherwise, that’s almost certainly the thing that’s causing a corruption issue. I was helped by a wonderful, INCREDIBLY helpful support person today. If your computer is locking up before Windows gets a chance to boot, you can at least attempt this. I’m not at all experienced in BIOS and all those things, but I managed this, so feel free to give it a shot

(Pre step 1 disclaimer. I had all my Windows updates installed at the point where I entered step 1. I've had a feeling the entire time that this issue had to do with windows updates - and it does - to the extent that the two sets of drivers just don't function unless BOTH windows and Optane drivers are updated. SO, YMMV. If your Windows version is older and not updated, proceed with caution. You can probably update Windows, after disabling the Optane drive, but it will take somewhat longer to do, I'm pretty sure (at least it will boot at all instead of the black screen I've gotten), or you can do a fresh reinstall with a newer version of it and then immediately go and update the Optane drivers and that might work too. I'm not at all a tech guru, but the following scenario is what worked for me and after a seriously long struggle with this laptop).

Step 1: upon powering up the PC enter BIOS by pressing the delete key upon startup (around the time the MSI logo appears)

Step 2: Once in BIOS, tab over to the “advanced” tab, go down to the Optane/intel rapid storage tech tab. Select your normal hard drive (mine was 931 GB, if that helps), then press disable. I think the next one asks if you’re sure you want to do this. Say yes. Then the next option is to keep the user settings (answer yes). Then, move down and confirm the disable “disable intel rapid storage”, down at the bottom of the options. This will potentially take multiple hours (it says “a couple of hours” there and it can be more per my experience). If you did it right, BIOS will appear to be frozen. It isn’t. Now you wait.

Step 3: After it’s done (screen will change a little bit) - hit F10 and restart. YOUR PC WILL RUN SLOWER THAN USUAL HERE, (BUT, UPSIDE, IT SHOULD BE RUNNING).

Step 4: Now, go to Intel’s optane website and download the optane drivers and software. You want to get the "Rapid Storage Technology Tool". I did this via the search menu on Windows, you can do it however you choose. Whatever you do, DON’T use MSI website’s version of a driver - it’s outdated and there are more tools available via the actual Intel website. I now have a tool that should keep my PC’s optane drivers updated as they’re released. I got every Optane tool and driver I could get from the site. I would recommend doing that. You can go ahead and restart when it asks you to for the updates.

Step 5: Under the Intel Rapid Storage Technology tool that you hopefully downloaded in step 4, you have basically one option, and that is: enable the optane drive. DO THAT. It seems to be a quick thing, but then the next sub-step proves it isn't. Immediately restart your PC, once again, after all the updates are installed and the drive is reenabled. Now comes anotherwait. I had a blue windows update type of screen for probably an hour or two at this point.

Once this is done and you're restarted, Voila. Your PC should be actually functional again.
(After this step, I restarted a couple more times, just to verify it was back to a fully functional status. It was, but feel free to do this if you so choose. I'd probably do at least one more restart once you have everything working and booted, just to make sure it's working and running fast for you too, but I'm a little old, and that's just how I roll.)

This entire process took me upwards of 6 hours. However, with any luck it shouldn’t have an issue again, and I didn’t have to delete my data this time to make it work. I suggest you settle in and have a LOT of patience.

After probably 20 windows reinstalls in 6 months, this is the one fix that has seemingly resolved the issue without a reinstall. My PC restarts fast, it runs fast and it works without blowing all my data away. So grateful to the person who helped me through it. (Hey MSI, would love to give this guy props becaus he cared enough to fix it and deserves HUGE credit for that).

It’s all about the Optane drivers! I wish MSI included the update software with the laptop, but hopefully this can help others in this situation.

title: Please consider what your getting yourself into if you purchase an Asus gaming laptop
text:
Mark my words. You need to really consider what you are using this laptop for. This laptop has a serious overheating problem. Basically what happens is if you are playing a game without the laptop being plugged in, you cannot get the same performance as you would if you plugged the device in. For example, with the laptop plugged playing Blade and Soul it's possible to get 60fps. But if you un plug and use the battery, you will run around 31fps. Blade and Soul isn't too heavy so this is pretty bad. So you plug it in and your good right? Wrong...

When you plug this Laptop in, it immediately begins to make a lot of noise and start to overheat while playing games. Then the laptop starts what I believe is called THERMAL THROTTLING. Basically the laptop starts to lag and stutter. It's a consistent lag spike. every 3-4 seconds. So basically this laptop only works when it's plugged in, but doesn't work when it's plugged in.

This Laptop is not designed for heavy gaming. It can't handle Grand Theft Auto Online for more than 30 minutes on battery, not to mention only on lower graphics to make the game playable. So I would recommend, if you are thinking this laptop will be some type of gaming monster, you are mistaken. I watched a lot of reviews of people saying this laptop is amazing and that the overheating isn't that bad, but it is. Please. Whatever you do......Do not purchase this laptop for the purpose of HEAVY gaming.

title: Really solid ultra light
text:
I've only had the laptop for a day, so keep that in mind. I got the graphics model on sale for $500 off MSRP. The main thing the big reviewers complain about is how you pay a premium for the name, well, this sale completely negated that. I literally could not find a better 13" laptop for the price. XPS13 cost several hundred more, Matebook was identical, Thinkpad X1 Carbon was $500 more. Crazy, right?

After purchase I researched a little more in depth and read up on many rampant issues that gave me pause. Loose USB C's (needed to charge the laptop), discharging while playing games, running hot, weird throttling issues, various quality issues with displays, coil whine, etc. I'm quite thankful to say mine has none of those issues (at least so far).

It did initially run a little hot, like around 85C max. Fans were cranking up high as well. So I used ThrottleStop to undervolt (-95mv for CPU/CPU cache, -50mv for iGPU). Everything is absolutely stable and I haven't seen higher than 62C max, and the fans haven't ramped up at all. Idle is upper 30's. Really quite decent for something so small. Definitely plan on undervolting.

The USB C's plug in very solidly, I purchased some little rubber plugs for them to keep lint and such out. I have not encountered discharging while gaming, technically the CPU and dedicated GPU can max out over the 65W maximum of the charger. I read somewhere that while it can charge from either USB C, the right one is better, so that is what I've done while doing anything intensive.

My complaints are very few and minor. One, the power button is where the del key normally is. I haven't accidentally hit it yet, but I can definitely see it happening. I would have preferred a dedicated button somewhere. Another oddity with the keyboard - typists will dislike the smaller right shift key, but I never use it and actually prefer the larger arrow keys, so not a problem at all for me.

I had a 1TB Samsung 970 Evo waiting for the Blade Stealth to arrive. Getting to bottom off is easy, 10 T5 torx screws. No issues swapping it out. The ram is non-upgradable, but that seems to be the new trend. Putting the cover back on, two of the screw heads went in, but stripped out. Awaiting a big variety pack of screws to replace them. I usually repaste everything, but given the really decent thermals I've been seeing undervolted, I'm going to wait and see. Looked super easy to pop the heatsink off.

I haven't encountered any weird throttling issues yet, I hit 3.8GHz on battery on all four cores and 4.1GHz while plugged in. Latest firmware with Windows 10 1903. So yeah, nothing abnormal to report there.

I know Razer markets this as a gaming laptop, but lets face it, it really isn't. AAA titles are eons out of its league. However, if you are like me and enjoy games like Minecraft, Stardew Valley, even some 5+ year old AAA titles (like Skyrim!), and maybe even have a nice desktop you can stream from when you are home but don't want to be tied down to a desk... this little guy will play those just fine. Just realize what you can and cannot expect from this laptop.

At 2.8lbs, this laptop disappears in my backpack. I'm really looking forward to having this for travel, instead of hauling my 17", 10lb behemoth of a gaming laptop around. The chassis is so rigid too, I couldn't get it to flex anywhere.

I honestly can't speak too much about battery life right now as I've been working it fairly hard getting it all set up and trying out games. I'm estimated to get around 8 hours while doing things like web browsing (like writing up this review!) or using Pycharm. Razer claims 11 hours for the graphics edition, so taking the usual manufacturer's inflation with a grain of salt, I'd say 8 hours is on par. Playing Minecraft with a Bluetooth controller dropped it down to 2.75 hours, so keep that in mind. But again, I just haven't had it long enough to say how true my observations on battery life are.

I'm very pleased with this little laptop, my fears have been dispelled and I just have some extremely minor annoyances with the keyboard. Its worth noting that unless you specifically want a 13" thin and light, you are much better off getting a 15" laptop. A 15" should be around the same price, yet will actually have a decent GPU, better thermals, etc at this price point. Some only weigh around 4lbs too, so it really isn't a huge tradeoff. The Lenovo Thinkpad X1 Carbon and MacBook are superior to this, but they also cost a LOT more than I purchased this for.

Update:
I've had it for about two weeks now. I further tinkered with undervolting and settled with -104.5mV for CPU Core and Cache, the iGPU is at -105.5mV. Running absolutely cool and stable for me. Idles around 35C, peaks around 68C. My 25C ambient temperature isn't helping.

The battery is quite decent. I can get about six hours of gaming on full clock speed, using the MX100 (light stuff: Minecraft Bedrock). Around 8 of web browsing, videos, streaming, etc. If I disable turbo, increase speed shift to 255, and keep the brightness below 50%, I can get a solid 10 hours of movie and game streaming. 12 of web browsing on Edge. Easily over 12 hours of simple programming with a PDF up as well. So yeah, so far I'm pretty happy with the battery life!

title: Entry-to-mid level gaming laptop that can pass as a respectable business machine
text:
A lot of gaming laptops are very flashy, with RGB lights or other gimmicks. This looks like a chunky but non-nonsense laptop but is also a decent entry-to-mid-level gaming machine.

Gaming on a laptop is always a tradeoff. There's always a balance that must be struck between power, price, and the ability to shed waste heat, and being in a portable factor only complicates things.

The tradeoffs here aren't major, but there are some.

The graphics card is good, but not high-end. You will be able to play every current game I can think of, but you can't max all the settings. That's expected on any gaming laptop.

Price-wise, this machine isn't at all bad for what you get. As soon as you start to add gaming components to a laptop the price shoots up dramatically, but HP has kept costs down by avoiding the gimmicks other manufacturers throw in their machines. (Compare to a Dell Alienware, for example.)

Instead, they give you things you can actually use. A nice, oversized trackpad. A backlit keyboard that has a decent feel and a numeric keypad, and a screen with good (but not amazing) brightness.

There are a few oversights, in my opinion. There's only a single USB-C port, and the A ports are limited in speed compared to the modern 3.1 standards. This is a failure to think about the future that I would have thought wouldn't have been an expensive upgrade to include. At the very least, a USB-C port on each side would have been nice. Also, a fingerprint reader would have been great.

The SSD is undersized for a gaming machine. 512GB is fine for a business-class machine, but a handful of triple-A games will use up most of that space too easily. And there's apparently no second slot, so you have to go to the trouble of replacing the base drive if you want to upgrade. A second slot would have been a no-brainer on a gaming laptop.

Those issues aren't enough to detract that the machine is a good deal for the price. The build feels solid (though heavy), and even when the fans are running at full speed they're not distracting.

The sound quality is good. It's not audiophile-grade but it's loud and clear. The screen is quite bright for a laptop. The high refresh rate is the draw for gamers. Viewing angles are okay.

Battery life - well, you're not going to actually do much gaming on this machine when disconnected from power. Honestly, I haven't run a test, but if you're actually using anything that pushes the GPU up, you're going to drain the battery extremely quickly. When you're not gaming, battery life isn't great either. I haven't run the battery all the way dead, but after only 1 hour of very light usage (and near max screen brightness), I was already around 50%, so my guess is 2 hours tops, and even less with any serious usage.

This laptop is fairly heavy, and the power brick is big and bulky too. (It has to be since it's rated for 200 watts.) You can't charge off of USB-C. (I tried with two different 100-watt PD power supplies, and the battery was still discharging while the machine was idle.) So this laptop isn't even close to an all-day machine without bringing the charger, but that's expected in a large-screen gaming laptop.

The caveats in this device apply to most gaming laptops.

The shortlist of the biggest pros and cons:

Pro:
No flashy gimmicks.
Solid, (but not stellar) gaming performance.
Decent price for a gaming laptop.
Solid build.
Fans operate at a reasonable noise level.

Cons:
Ports are lacking.
SSD is a bit small for a gaming-focused machine, without the option of adding a second SSD.
Heavy and you will need the bulky power adapter if you actually travel with this (which is a common fault in all gaming laptops.)
