title: This Acer Predator laptop had weird design and hardly upgradeable!
text: This Acer Predator laptop is more expensive than other Acer brand lower level gaming laptops, but it's hardly upgradable. It has weird design in the bottom case with very sticky parts on the hinge and side. Even with proper toolkit, it's difficult to open the entire bottom case for RAM and SSD expansion. Most importantly, the laptop comes with Windows 10 Home 20H2 version OS. After initial set up of the laptop, it requires to do mandatory updates to keep up with the current system. After a few seconds of wait, the laptop tries to restart and said Windows updates are running. Then the nightmare loop happens again and again. The restart process has repeated over 50 times, but the laptop has not finished Windows updates for more than 10 hours. Just returned the laptop with original box and accessories to Amazon within 24 hours receiving it. Do not bother to contact the manufacturer for technical support, since they will tell you to do the same. The only way to resolve the issue is to open the bottom case and take out the SSD to wipe out the defective Windows 10 Home OS 20H2 version (it's not compatible with latest 11th gen intel processor), and then reinstall Windows 10 Home 21H1 or Windows 11 on the laptop. You cannot do that on your own, since the laptop's bottom case is very difficult to open.

title: Good CAD & video editing laptop
text:

Especially if you're doing video work or downloading games. The 16 inch version of this laptop does have the ability to have 2 SSD's installed at the same time.

title: cpu not as advertised
text: Only first impressions after a few days. Most importantly, the processor is listed incorrectly. It is actually 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-1165G7 @ 2.80GHz . I am not a power  user, more work oriented day to day spreadsheets, accounting software, word processing, web surfing. this is a replacement for a 4 year old Lenovo yoga intel i5 @2.50, 8GB which served me well but has become too slow. title: For the price, a solid laptop
text:
For the price, this is a solid laptop to be used for basic gaming. However, I would say that this laptop is not really great at anything it does. The SSD is too small for a lot of games to be installed, but it does have an extra SSD and HDD slot, so you can easily upgrade (which I did after about a month). The RAM is also lacking, but another easy upgrade to make. Another negative is the build quality. The laptop feels cheap and plasticy (which I don't think is a word), but for the price that you pay it can be expected. The battery life for basic tasks, like writing, internet research, and light movie watching is pretty terrible. At most I get 3-4 hours. But for gaming, you wouldn't use it off the charger anyways so its a mute point if you plan on using the laptop for its stated purpose.

Now for some positives. The display itself is really nice. Games look great as well as movies and it has a really nice refresh rate. I actually enjoy the typing experience of the keyboard.

For games, this laptop plays Farming Simulator perfectly on maxed settings. Call of Duty Modern Warfare 2 can be played at slightly less than max settings as long as you are using it off the laptop screen. If you are using an external monitor, depending on the size of the monitor you might run into a little bit of trouble. I have a 49" monitor and when I tried plugging the laptop into it wasn't able to maintain the same quality and performance.

Overall, I would say that if you are looking for a cheap gaming laptop to do some light gaming on the road then this is a good laptop for that. If you want a gaming laptop and one you can do work on the coach with, this isn't it. If you want hardcore gaming, this also isn't. For the price though, I would say that its a solid laptop just don't expect to do everything you want at max settings.

title: I returned it and went with something different

title: Amazing laptop - HATE the keyboard
text:

title: Gamers, heads-up.  Wi-Fi 6 is here.
text:
You know Acer is speaking to you when you open the box, lift the heavy power brick, and see (because it's bigger) that they are using a standard computer power cable instead of the usual brick cable (a plus, because you can misplace the cable!), but then you see a small package of screws. Why? So you can upgrade the SSD (this model shipped with 512GB) if you want.

That speaks to me. We're not just gamers, we're tweakers and perfectionists. OK, I exaggerate.

PRO
- Cool, efficient boot process. Lights, camera (well, display) & (keyboard) action.
- Boot keyboard illumination signals might be useful given a legend
- Illuminated keys
- Wi-Fi 6 (a serious improvement -- see Consumer Reports story on benefits for WiFi 6 routers)
- Even the network ports are named "Killer." Now we're talkin' (courtesy of the Intel Killer DoubleShot Pro)
- Wired ethernet port
- Adequate USB-A and USB-C ports
- You'll notice the 144Hz refresh rate
- Expandable - 1 x 2.5" Hard Drive Bay unused
- Memory slots not hard-wired
- NVIDIA GeForce 30

CON
- FHD only
- No touchscreen
- Not USB-C style PSU (interchangeable with other laptops, hubs, docks)
- No Thunderbolt
- Norton bundle (I guess this holds down the cost?)
- You'll want 32GB

NOTE
I have to change my PC hygiene a little, since this computer supports concurrent Wi-Fi and wired connections. (I usually disable one in order to simplify things for the drivers, or at least the part of the stack that has to sort this out.) I was skeptical, but it did seem to work, at least on a modest load. Nice.

SUMMARY
You get a lot for the bucks here, considering the Nvidia component. Of the missing features, the tradeoff that bothers me most is the touchscreen, since we're so often switching between smartphone and laptop.

title: Good Price Point . . . But read on if gaming is secondary for you
text:
Other reviewers have pointed out the performance features of this unit, which are quite good at this price point.

Adding to those observations:
• Full wired ethernet port
• Displayport
• Touchpad (not a fan, but everyone uses them)
• 16GB RAM is pretty minimal, but it's owner-upgradeable (Woohoo!)
• Backlit keyboard
• Serious CUDA cred (that's what makes this a "gamer laptop"
• Lots of USB ports (some laptops are cutting back on these in favor of external hubs)

SCREEN DISCUSSION
But in this era of the cell phone, on which the touch screen interface is ubiquitous and habitual, not having a touch screen laptop feels like a handicap. I'm sure it costs more, but touch screens appear on Chromebooks at even lower price points than this unit.

The display limitations don't end there. The FHD resolution for the screen is fine, but it's now an aging standard except for the gamer laptop niche. Even if you don't use that resolution for gaming (it creates multiple performance overhead for editing, saving, broadcasting), it's great to load up the screen with multiple apps that you don't have to constantly minimize and maximize.

By now you have probably pierced the veil and seen that I'm only an occasional gamer.

FHD is a gamer standard resolution in order to achieve frame rate objectives. There may be other design limitations imposed by touchscreens that I'm not aware of.

THUNDERBOLT
You don't get this emerging interface.

GPU DISCUSSION
For gamer purposes, you will want to read a comparison of the Nvidia GPU used here -- RTX 3050 Ti vs the recently released 3060. In one analysis I read, which compared 15 games, when aggressive settings were used the 3050 had issues. It either maxed out on VRAM (4GB is supplied here) or was as much as 50% or more slower

Because the GPU is not surprisingly a beast, you'll be carrying to rather beefy 95W PDU. But you're a gamer, right?

CONCLUSION
I like the price, but I'd probably opt for a Lenovo model with
• Windows Pro (swap space and image overhead chews up a 512GB SSD)
• 1TB SSD
• Touch screen
• I might hold out for the 3060 with more VRAM
• A can of beer to cry into as I live with FHD to get my FPS fix

title: An Excellent Computer for People who Prefer GNU/Linux Operating Systems
text:
This review is primarily for people who prefer GNU/Linux computer operating systems and are familiar with the process of installing such a system on a computer which comes with Microsoft Windows pre-installed.

I received this < Acer Swift X SFX14-41G-R1S6 Creator Laptop | 14" Full HD 100% sRGB | AMD Ryzen 7 5800U | NVIDIA RTX 3050Ti Laptop GPU | 16GB LPDDR4X | 512GB NVMe SSD | Wi-Fi 6 | Backlit Keyboard | Windows 10 Home > [ https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B093TK1PXF/ref=ppx_od_dt_b_asin_title_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1 ] from Amazon Vine this past Thursday, July 22, 2021.

I immediately went into the UEFI/BIOS, made the few obvious changes necessary (primarily clearing the TPM, deactivating Secure Boot, and activating the F12 key to select the boot order), and then booted from a USB drive which contains the EndeavourOS operating system. (This system is an ArchLinux-based system and is primarily for those people who are familiar with using GNU/Linux operating systems.) However, this computer will work perfectly with ANY GNU/Linux operating system.

I selected the option to install the NVIDIA drivers and the process began. During the installation I chose to completely remove Windows from this computer; dual-booting with Windows is of course possible if that is what you want (you can have both Windows and Linux installed on the same machine) but I myself do not use Windows or any of its programs.

Once the installation was complete, I rebooted the computer and then updated the system. Updating was of course necessary as the latest EndeavourOS installation ISO is a couple of months old and there have been many changes (a new installation ISO should be introduced in the next month or so).

The entire process described above took just about a half hour.

At that point EVERYTHING worked perfectly, including the Fn keys.

I installed quite a few programs which I have on my other computers (all of which use EnOS). There are a few Terminal commands which allow one to create a list of every program one has installed on an ArchLinux-ased computer and take those programs and install them AUTOMATICALLY onto another ArchLinux-based computer (which EndeavourOS of course is).

I have 674 individual programs which I installed onto this computer plus one program which I always install separately.

This process took about another half hour (due to the large number of programs that I use) but, when finished, everything again worked absolutely perfectly.

Of course now it is necessary to configure all of those programs to my liking. This will take most of the afternoon. But once done, I will have a computer which looks, feels, and works exactly as all of my other ones work - except that this Acer Swift X SFX14-41G-R1S6 Creator Laptop will be much faster.

The quality of construction of this computer as well as the materials used in it are absolutely first-class. The keyboard is superb as is its "feel."

I am very happy with the screen brightness and the NVIDIA graphics (I am not a "gamer" and I do not play any "games" on my computers). Videos look superb.

The sound quality is adequate. When I play music via a computer I either use Bluetooth or a USB DAC. (When playing music via a DAC, the only limitation is the quality of your stereo system.) Therefore the sound quality from the internal speakers on any computer are of little importance to me.

This computer is FAST. I have never had an AMD processor in any of my older computers and I have to say that I am impressed with this AMD Ryzen 7 5800U along with the 16 GB of RAM.

The light weight is also impressive as is the battery life; so far I have used the computer on battery for over four hours and there is still plenty of 'juice" left.

If you use Linux, you know that there are a myriad of programs available to you (and if you use an Arch Linux-based system such as EndeavourOS, of course you know that the sky's the limit!).

EVERY program I have installed on this computer thus far works perfectly, just as all of them do on my older computers.

My wife and I plan to take this computer along with us when we travel (if that day ever comes!). We also have two other "travel" computers which are relatively lightweight though not nearly as lightweight as is this one, nor are they as "fast" as is this one. However I shall probably use this computer far more often than I would if this were solely a "travel" computer; it is that good!

I do have a couple of (VERY) minor "wishes" - I wish there were some way to add RAM; I would prefer 32 GB and, while the 512GB NVMe SSD is okay, I would have preferred a 1 TB SSD. But you can see that these "complaints" are really minor.

All in all I am completely pleased with this really excellent computer and if you prefer Linux to Windows, as do I, it is my opinion that you just can't go wrong with this one. At Amazon's current price of $1069.99 I feel that this computer is an excellent value.

VERY, VERY HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!

Thank you for reading this.

Lawrence H. Bulk

title: Perfect For Gaming On The Go!
text:
This is my first gaming laptop and I was not disappointed. For a bit over $800, it's value is pretty great. I wanted something budget friendly as I have a gaming desktop already and just wanted to play games when out and about.

Pros-
- Keyboard and trackpad. Key strokes feel great and my hands feel comfortable after typing sessions and the red backlit keys look amazing! Some people have complained about the shape of the trackpad, but I haven't had any issues with it.

- Build Quality and design. Even though it's mostly plastic, it's pretty durable. The screen has a lot of flex, but the base is pretty solid. Really like the design of the laptop overall. The cooling with this laptop is pretty good. CPU and GPU never throttled even after a few hours of gaming. Weight isn't bad and was lighter than I expected.

- Storage. Even though it only comes with a 256GB SSD, it is very quick. Boot time is less than 10 seconds. There is a place for a 2.5" drive for more space. It isn't as easy as some gaming laptops, but easier than most normal laptops. There is no mounting for the second drive, but if you're installing an SSD like I did, it shouldn't cause any issues. Put a 512GB SSD in for game storage.

- CPU and GPU. The combination of the 4-core/4-thread 7th Gen i5 and the 1050 Ti is great for a budget conscious buyer as laptops with the 1050 Ti tend to run a bit more expensive. The CPU never bottle necked the GPU, but did come close a few times. Games like GTAV, Rainbow 6: Siege, Wildlands, Witcher 3, and PUBG all run at medium to high-ish with 40-60FPS, which is perfectly acceptable to me. If you want more frames, drop setting lower and it should be good.

Cons-
-The screen. With any budget device, some corners have to be cut to help with the price. The screen isn't very bright. This isn't a big deal to me as while indoors, it looks fine. Also, even though I found the display colorful enough, do not use this for photo editing or anything where color accuracy is important.

- Battery. With just web browsing, I was at 50% batter after an hour and a half. I don't want to even try gaming on the battery. But I'm normally always plugged in, so it's not really an issue for me.

- Ports. Not sure why companies are still putting USB 2.0 ports on laptops, but I can only guess it has to do with cost. No second display out, just an HDMI. USB-C connector is just USB 3.1. No display out, no Power Delivery. All of this to me isn't a big deal, but it might be for others.

In Conclusion-
Over all a great budget laptop that offers more than others in it's price range. I have actually been strictly gaming on this laptop instead of my desktop to really put this laptop through the ringer and I've been pleasantly surprised by it. Granted I have to have the graphics on lower settings than the desktop and the CPU isn't nearly as good for video rendering, but for the price, it does a spectacular job and I could not be more pleased with my purchase.

title: Light as a feather, huge screen, insane value
text:
This is an amazing value. The screen is huge - like a gaming laptop - but it's insanely light. This time around, I wanted the lightest laptop I could afford that had the keyboard feature I needed (see below). As many have mentioned, it feels like an empty case. It's lighter than my friend's Macbook Air, and feels kind of miraculous. Here are some thoughts.

Screen. The screen is vivid and bright. Truly lovely colors. As others have mentioned, it's shiny, so you can get some glare. I've noticed it only a few times while watching videos, and changing the angle a bit solved the problem. Not a big deal. I haven't noticed glare while doing anything else. It's a touchscreen, which I don't care about. I might eventually end up using the touch screen feature. Nice to know it's a possibility. The size is what it's all about. I use a laptop only when I have to because I'm much more productive and comfortable with a large screen. This one takes away 90% of the pain. It's not 27", but it's a huge productivity/comfort upgrade from my old one.

Trackpad. I hate trackpads, but I don't hate this one. I have a mouse attached, but sometimes I find myself using the trackpad without thinking. It's smooth, comfortable, and some smart programmer got the speed, acceleration, and whatever else goes into the "feel" just right. Unexpected plus.

Speed. All I can say is I never experience delays. I don't do any video editing or gaming. Anything faster than this would be wasted on me. Watch out though, it was slow when I first used it because it has a lot of housekeeping to do. I freaked out a bit when complicated web pages took three or four seconds to load, but you don't need to worry. It had to download updates, initialize things for their first use, etc. The next day it was fine. As I said, at this point everything is so quick and smooth that I wouldn't even be able to tell if it were faster.

Keyboard. First the good (and very important to me). There are dedicated arrow keys as well as page-up, page-down, home, and end keys. I'm a writer, and I always use these keys to navigate documents and select text (holding shift), so that's non-negotiable for me. I lucked out big time that this fantastic value laptop has that feature. Other than that, the keyboard isn't great, but I didn't expect miracles from something this light and thin. It's adequate. It's why I took off one star. Not that the keyboard is bad in any way, I just think five stars should be for something that gets everything right. I used to buy Lenovos because they have very good keyboards. But I couldn't afford a Lenovo this light with such a big screen. Now that I've used the Acer, I see I made the right decision. A small annoyance was that you have to hold down Fn for the function keys. The default action is adjusting brightness, volume, and other laptop stuff. That's probably best for most people, but I use alt-F4 to close windows all the time, F2 to rename files, F5 to reload web pages, and occasionally F11 to make the browser window bigger, so this was not good for me. Luckily, you can easily flip things so that the function key is the default and brightness, etc. requires the Fn key. You just change an option in the BIOS. Google for instructions.

Fingerprint reader. Forget about it. It's finicky. It will eventually recognize your finger, but it can take many tries. It's not worth using. It would have been cool if it worked, but a fingerprint reader wasn't on my need list or even my want list.

Appearance. As others have noted, it's dull and boring. Fine. I don't care. One thing that bothers me is that the bottom has bubbles around the cut outs, like warts. It looks terrible. I was going to send it back, but the hassles of packing it up and exchanging it weren't worth it. It's on the bottom and I'll never see it. It still bothers me a little, and is part of the reason for losing a star.

Cr*pware. It comes loaded with cr*pware. If that's part of what makes it so well-priced, then I'm all for it. It didn't take long to clear it all away with the free, open-source BCUninstaller Bulk Cr*p Uninstaller. Not an issue.

Bottom line: Great purchase. I've highlighted the drawbacks, but that's only because I thought it would be helpful to a prospective buyer. Overall, I love this laptop. When I started researching the purchase, I never imagined I could afford something this light with such a large screen. It looks and performs like something double the price. It's a crazy good deal. Many thanks to the good people at Acer for pulling off this engineering feat.

title: Solid, Standard 500gb HD Machine; You may need to update the Wireless Driver
text: I got this machine for my dad to use as a compact desktop by using it in tent mode with an accessory bluetooth keyboard & mouse (his preference--he doesn't like trackpads).  It isn't blazingly fast, but we knew that; it isn't your old office Win 7 machine, either.  It is decent.  My needs for this machine are modest, and this has a good 720p style screen.  Note that some of these machines have a problem that could seem like a deal-breaker: the wifi module has an out-of-date driver, and wifi can either not connect or make only crazy, intermittent connections.  Note that I have never in my life had success with Microsoft's own "search for a new driver" function.  The driver in question could date from 1997 and Microsoft's search engine will shrug and say, "that's the newest driver going, man."  In this case, do your own research.  Look up the name of the wifi module and go to softpedia for a new driver.  The wifi module on the Asus 15.6 I got (a refurb--I predict this was why it was refurb) was useless until I did that.  (I used an accessory wifi dongle until I got that fixed). Ignore lots of forum chatter online that this is a dark, unsolvable problem.  Wifi module name.  Softpedia.  New driver.  It is a solid machine otherwise.  Also, the refurb needed to have the Microsoft product code physically keyed in to validate Windows.  (This was the first time I had encountered that since the 1990s).  The seller had helpfully written *the wrong &*&#@! code* on a card in the box.  For reference: the correct product code for a Windows laptop is likely on a Microsoft sticker on the bottom of the machine.

title: I Don't Know
text:
I feel conflicted about the 3-star rating. I think that the product can be reviewed as a 4.5-Star or 5-Star performer if it wasn't for the issues that I suffered.

Summary: I received a first product that came with a "blue screen of death" issue. It started up and it went to the blue screen error crash, after rebooting itself for 6-7 cycles, I shut it down and contacted Alienware. After I spoke to Alienware support.... They have CONFIRMED a software issue. NVIDIA sent Dell/Alienware a memo/notice about the new video drivers for the card.

They said that the old drivers should work fine. since the computer wouldn't land on the desktop for me to address this, I decided to not endure the issue of a new $1600 computer that should work out of the box. Amazon promptly replaced the item and took the return without a hassle. Always great.

The second computer worked fine, I didn't install drivers or anything. It booted up without any hassles or difficulties. The performance and graphics are fantastic. I played World of Tanks and Final Fantasy 14 without issues. FF14 runs at 70+ FPS at the highest settings. Boots up very fast and it runs programs very quickly. The sound is great for a laptop, It even has a port underneath for some deep sounds.. It's not a boom box, but it's pretty rich for what it is.

After 24 days, it was dead. The light on the power adapter was on, but as soon as it got plugged into the laptop, the light went out and the laptop wont power up or recharge. Who knows what's wrong with it.

I contacted Amazon about the issue, they were helpful immediately and issued a return order and refund.

I titled this review "I Don't Know" because part of me knows for a fact that this can't possibly be the norm and it must be an isolated incident(s)

Here's where I stand. A laptop computer priced at this level should work without any issues, software or hardware. I am very understanding and it is a likely case of getting a couple of damaged/defective units. It is interesting to know that Dell would probably spot the issue and repair it. BUT, Would you REALLY want a mended computer that you JUST purchased for $1600?

In my opinion, the performance of the device should be a reflection of the price paid for the product. We should not have to tweak the hell out of the computer to get it to work.

title: AMAZING LAPTOP, NOW THAT I HAVE THE BUGS WORKED OUT.
text:
Received my Alienware 17 R3 a few days ago.
Build quality is great, it feels very sturdy.
Keyboard and touch-pad are some of the best I've ever used on a laptop.
Screen is gorgeous, and the video card is running all my game at high or ultra settings, just like I had hoped.
It doesn't run overly hot, even while gaming.
Battery is decent for a rig this powerful, of this size. I get about 4 hours out of it before I have to plug it in, while gaming (almost all I do).
I suspect it would last longer if I wasn't gaming so much.
In short, this laptop is everything you expect a high quality, top of the line (or close to it), rig to be.
EXCEPT...
I had LOADS of IRQ, BIOS and Driver issues out of the box.
Crashes, blue screens, conflicts...
I spent a day updating and troubleshooting various problems, updating practically ALL my drivers, the BIOS...
I wont go into all of it here, because there was a lot, and these sort of issues will be different with each computer, so a lengthy explanation wouldn't be useful, with one exception.
I had the exact same problem as tons of other people with the Killer Wireless dropping signal constantly.
Seriously, do a search, it's a VERY common problem with this laptop.
After spending some time researching the issue (which will generate a lot of possible solutions), and trying several "fixes" to no avail. I downloaded the newest Killer Network Manager from their website, then uninstalled both the existing suite AND the existing killer wireless drivers. Then I installed the newest version of the Killer Network Manager (which includes drivers). This fixed the issue. I have gone several days now with no Wireless issues. NOTE: be sure to DL the newest version BEFORE you uninstall everything or you won't be able to get online to DL it!

Long story short, after spending a couple days updating, uninstalling and reinstalling, and a 2 hours on the phone with Alienware to fix a few issues that updating drivers wouldn't fix, I now have an amazing laptop that runs perfect, and is everything I had hoped it would be.
Having to do all that work was a pain in the ass for sure, but it shouldn't be a deal breaker. None of the problems were defective hardware, etc.

As someone who is fairly tech-savvy, and someone who spent months researching before pulling the trigger on this purchase, I still feel that this laptop represents the best value at this price-point.

The battery with mixed use of gaming, streaming, browsing, lasted on average, 5.5-6 hours in balanced mode. About what I expected going in, so I was fine with that.The power button has a light that indicates which of the 3 power modes you are in.
The webcam is not great, but there is a physical switch to disable it, which I definitely appreciate.
The speakers aren't tinny, but don't get very loud at all, so plan to use wired or a bluetooth speaker if watching movies, or headphones of course.
Speaking of Bluetooth, this laptop has version 5.2, which many new accessories are currently released with.
One thing that I was surprised by is that the laptop, even while playing control, did not run hot at all. The fans never got that obnoxious wurring sound, and the laptop stayed reasonably cool to the touch, regardless of what I used it for.
Generally, this laptop is very quiet, something i couldn't say about previous Lenovos i've owned. i could tweek things with those as needed, but didn't need to with this model.
over all, this is great hardware and a great machine for a fair price.
Great value for money, for a laptop that does so much, and does it well.

title: Computer 4stars -- HP service ZERO (UPDATED)
text:
The shortest possible version is that brand new out of the box, we hit a snag that should have been a piece of cake to fix, but it required a call in to HP's customer "service" because neither my husband nor I are particularly technically savvy. It shouldn't have been a big deal (password not recognized, needed to reset something and couldn't quite figure out the right steps to take). HP customer "service" hung up on us twice, transferred us to a department that was closed, and then insulted us for being old. (Sadly, quite literally so). Next they wanted us to cough up $15 a month for the "warranty" on a brand new, still-under-warranty computer. This old lady told them where they could go with that suggestion.

Tomorrow, we'll take it in to our local Microsoft store where they are very nice to us old foggies.

So (again, short version) the bottom line for me is that as far as we can tell, the computer is a decent value for the money and meets our needs in terms of specs (I play the Sims 4, hubbs plays Fallout and Minecraft and sometimes we watch movies on the laptop) -- but if you need service, HP isn't exactly the friendliest company to deal with. Thank goodness for the nice "kids" down at Microsoft!

UPDATE: the nice "kids" at Microsoft told me it looked like a bad....something internal. Basically, "it's dead, Jim". Amazon quickly, easily, and without a fuss replaced it. (I understand HP couldn't have possibly known that over the phone, the point is that they gave absolutely no support; they didn't even give me an option to mail it to them to look it).

So, now that I've had a couple of weeks to play with it, I can give a more accurate review. I stand by my initial 4 stars for the laptop itself.

Pros:

It lives up to my expectations. The Sims 4 (with all expansion packs and a LOT of mods/cc) runs perfectly. We haven't sat down to watch a movie or anything, but I can't imagine it would be anything less than stellar given how gorgeously and flawlessly it renders the Sims graphics.

No-glare screen! That is such an awesome thing.

Cons:

Not thrilled with the (admittedly heavy-duty) plastic body. Maybe it's just as good as the metal body on my Spectre (and my old Asus), but I always feel nervous around plastic. That said, it was within our budget, so only so much room to complain.

I am sure it was somewhere clearly on the product page, but I hadn't realized it wasn't a touch-screen. That's hardly a deal-breaker, but it's hard to fathom an $800 laptop that **isn't** a touch screen. Like I said, not a deal-breaker, I just have to remember to not try and do stuff by touching the screen!

The so-so

The sound isn't great, but it isn't dismal. The Sims sound fine. YouTube videos sound fine. I know I'd have to shell out a lot more for the graphics we need for gaming PLUS a good sound card. If I have to choose, I'll choose graphics anytime.

Overall, I am very pleased with the laptop, HP just needs to **seriously** step up their game in terms of customer service. Amazon's Prime Day deal coupled with an interest-free payment plan were huge factors in my choice this time around. Next time, I may go somewhere else.

text:

I do use a cooling pad) I now primarily use this computer for gaming, i have it setting on the cooling pad under my VIZIO tv, super easy to hookup with an HDMI, i ended up getting a Logitech wireless track ball mouse that was plug and play. I prefer to use a controller. Hooking up my DS4 controller was supper easy via Bluetooth and i use JoytoKey to map the controller for some older games like the Witcher 1. And i can also use my Sony playstation gold wireless headphones, all i had to do was plug in the receiver into the USB port and it connected!

I am very very happy with my purchase and would highly recommend getting this!

I may do the SSD upgrade many people talk about? Filled by using to 16 mb of ram, even though that could be overkill

Lastly don't let the low rating reviews scar you, I read almost all the reviews and research this computer extensively YouTube is actually a really good source.

Hope this review helps you out

This is the update for installation of the SSD

Hopefully this write up will help somebody else with the problems I ran into on my installation. When I put the SSD in the computer all those steps really easy there's actually some good YouTube videos. But when I turned on the computer right clicked on the start menu and went to "disk management" and it was not listed..

So then I had to go into the "bios" here is a easy explanation at this link [...]

Once in there it still wasn't displayed so you have to go over to the boot tab and changed the type to "Legacy" and then the one under it to "Legacy First". Then go back to the info screen and it's there!? After that go back and turn off Legacy (like it was before) but save changes and boot it up... Boom ssd is available! Weird.

Next Boot into Windows, go to "Disk Management", create & format (GPT) the M.2,

This is where I ran into more issues... was Data Migration Software, which will do all the work for you, even making the M.2 the boot drive.

What DIDNT WORK! The free program from Samsung didn't work it migrated but the computer would boot from the new SSD and I had a repeating blue screen where I had to go back into "bios" and switch start up to the older "HHD"

WHAT WORKED!! I purchased to $20 "paragon software" [...]. Make sure you read the instructions and the trouble shooting guide. Once installed I thought it froze because it displayed 0% for a few hours but after about 4 hours it worked. And did an amazing job! It actually named the new SSD as the "C" drive (so then no "steam" migration or anything was needed!) and renamed the HHD as the "E" drive.

I hope this helps anyone who finds it! It took me hours of searching all over the web.

title: Amazing 15" laptop with lots of power!
text:
Ok, so we are going on a trip and I needed a laptop to continue be able to do my website/graphic design, video editing and other managed services that I provide through my company, Ocala Website Designs LLC. After much research (two weeks) it came down to two options: the ASUS ROG Zephyrus G14/G15 and the RAZER BLADE 15.

Due to price, I was strongly leaning towards the ASUS as it was several hundreds of dollars cheaper. I have had an ASUS ZENBOOK before and it was a great laptop for many years, and these G14s and G15s are coming with the amazing power of the RYZEN 7 4800 processor which has been topping a lot of the charts for video encoding.

I was about to hit the buy button on the ASUS, but was having a difficult time making sure I was getting the proper loadout that I wanted due to the many many different variations listed on Amazon. The confusion made me decide to re-review all the YouTube videos about each and re-visit all buying options again.

That's when I realized that I could also buy the Razer on Amazon through the official Razer company store front (not third party companies) and there were a couple different loadouts than what was available on their company sites and at a lower price point with better parts. There I found the Razer Blade 15 2020 model with a full RTX 2060 NVidia card and 500GB SSD and an extra open M.2 slot for upgrading, which was the model that was getting a ton of praises by the reviewers on YouTube, for a little less than $1500, which put the razer squarely back on my radar and I spent another couple of days again comparing the Razer to the ASUS models.

I finally decided to go all in on the Razer. I have a Razer Ornata Chroma keyboard, The Razer Mamba Tournament-Edition mouse, Firefly LED mouse pad and Orb Weaver keypad, Razer Thresher Headphones and another pair of Razer Kraken headphones already, and they all are fantastic products although my Threshers are starting to fall apart at the headphone seams I just noticed. I didn't realize I had collected so much Razer hardware through the years.

I could live with the i7 6-core processor which gives me Thunderbolt connections, I'm not heavy into mobile video editing and would mainly do that type of work on my main computer with the ASUS ROG RAMPAGE V EDITION 10 motherboard with 96GB of RAM and larger monitors. However, I can certainly output video on this Razer with the i7 with little effort if I needed to. It's a great processor.

The laptop is high-quality for sure, right down to the aluminum frame and braided power cord. Some were knocking the proprietary power connector but I really like it, it's secure, thick and doesn't feel like its going to slide out. One guy didn't like that it blocked the USB ports but apparently didn't realize that it can be plugged in both ways, which is cool, see photos.

I am finding it a little difficult to get used to typing on the keyboard, but I'll have that down in a few days of using it. The keys are solid and doesn't take much effort to press them. I work mainly on the Razer Ornata Chroma Keyboard on my main computer so the keys are much much different, which is to be expected on a laptop.

The laptop comes with a great graphics card: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060. That's important for Cinema 4D rendering.

Battery life for regular work seems to be great so far. I don't do a ton of gaming, but I would probably have it plugged in anyways for gaming, I like a bright screen and don't want to risk losing my game progress because I wasn't paying attention to the battery lol.

One of the ONLY things I dislike about it right off the bat is that with all the LED stuff they offer in their products, you would think that the track pad would have a thin light ring or bezel so you can see the outer edge better. As you can see in the photos, you can't see the trackpad hardly at all, even in a lit room. In lit areas, the shadows from your hands do a good job hiding the edges of the track pad so I have a hard time telling where i'm at on it. The good thing is that it's a huge trackpad, which is awesome, but I feel like I get lost on it until I lift my hands up to see exactly where i'm at on it to make sure i'm clicking the right click. It's not a big deal, and i'm sure I will get used to it soon enough.

You can't go wrong with this Razer Blade. I have no trouble recommending this as a great laptop. Great job Razer!

title: Acer has come a long way: it builds nice laptops now
text:
Acer Predator Helios 300 & Triton 500

I used to think of the Acer brand as cheap. After using both the Helios 300 and the Triton 500 side by side for several months, I no longer feel that way.

The high points of the Predator experience: solid gaming machines that also do a good job of handling other tasks I frequently engage in: video production, photography processing, and academic and essay writing.

The Helios 300 is the cheaper and thicker of the two machines (see photos). It is also much easier to upgrade, which almost everyone who buys this machine will need to do. Unless you only plan to install a half dozen games and then not do anything else with the machine, the included 512GB storage is inadequate. Luckily, both the 300 and the 500 come with additional M.2 storage slots. It was relatively simple to upgrade the 300, but upgrading the 500 involved removing the motherboard entirely and took quite a bit of time and some specialized tools. You can pay your local computer shop to do this for you. I would recommend budgeting for a 2TB M.2 drive to be your primary partition.

The screens are decent, although to be honest I cannot tell any difference between the 144MHz response time on the 300 and the 300MHz response time on the 500. They look exactly the same to my eyes with one exception - the 300 has zero stuck pixels but my 500 came with one stuck pixel. That is mildly irritating. Acer policy is up to two stuck pixels so be prepared for that possibility.

The 300 is about 30% thicker than the 500. That did not bother me in the slightest. Both keyboards feel identical - they are nice and snappy and I enjoy typing on them.

I do not like the gimmicky RGB on either. A lighted keyboard is nice in a dark room, but I have no use for rainbows and flashing blasts of color so I set both machines to solid blue.

Battery life is adequate, not great.

The 500 has Thunderbolt if that's important to you - it is not present on the 300.

Fan noise did not bother me on either unit but the fans will be audible if you are playing a graphics intensive game or doing video production. This is necessary to keep the units from overheating.

Acer has come a long way since I first used their products many years ago - they have really upped their engineering game. If you need an affordable multi-purpose laptop that does not require taking out a second mortgage the 300 and the 500 are both worth taking a look at. I would shell out a little extra for at least a 1TB hard drive, and if you can afford it, go with a 2TB.

title: Great CPU, clear display, but weak GPU considering the other components
text:
The build quality of this Acer Swift is excellent and on pair with every other high-end laptop I have owned. The screen is clear and crisp with no dead pixels.

The AMD Ryzen 7 5800U is an outstanding CPU with amazing performance and low power consumption which performs far better than any other laptop CPU I have used. Having 16GB of ram and a nice 512 GH M.2 SSD makes this a low power monster of a workstation with one major drawback which is the inclusion of the RTX 3050Ti. Why Acer decided to pair a top-of-the-line CPU with a low-end GPU makes me wag my head considering this missed opportunity. While as a workstation, this laptop will perform great and easily performs all the task I did in Photoshop, Acrobat 2020, Sketchbook, and DaVinci Resolve, loading up my Steam games was a totally different experience. The CPU is more than capable of playing any modern game, but the 3050Ti struggles with only 4GB of ram. The result is Shadow of the Tomb Raider, The Division 2, and Kingdom Come: Deliverance had to be set at low settings, so the games are playable. Games like EverQuest and WoW worked great, but these are older games.

This is a mixed bag for me because on one end the performance is excellent for workstation tasks, and on the other end gaming is weak with a questionable selection for a GPU. Based on my testing of this laptop, I cannot recommend it if you are looking for a gaming laptop, but I can recommend it if you are just wanting a workstation.

Sadly, this could have been a great all-around laptop if a better GPU had been included. The build quality is excellent, the system runs cool, the fans are almost silent, and the keyboard is very well built. Overall, this is a good laptop. It is marketed as a creator laptop, so gamers are not the intended market.

title: Awesome laptop that runs like a dream
text:
I did a lot of research before buying this laptop and for the cost (right now a new one is about 1350$) your not going to find much better. I had an ASUS ROG before buying this that I had been using for 6 years (ROG's are great laptops as well by the way), but I decided to pull the trigger on the Alienware mainly because of the Gforce 970m it had under the hood. First off its a great looking laptop, with one of the best screens I have ever used on a laptop. The resolution is great and the keyboard layout is nice and works well for gaming. It does heat up a bit where the underside fans are so if its sitting on your lap its going to get a bit warm, but that's nothing you can't solve with a cooling pad, or just putting it on something harder. The video card is awesome and I am having no problems running things on ultra settings (battlefleet gothic, vermintide, just to name a few). I bought the entry level R17 with 8gig of ram and a 1tb 7200 hd, which was fine. However right out of the box I installed 16 gig of ram (the laptop has 2 expansion bays so you can put in 2x4gig or 2x8, 2x16 gig for a max of 32gig) and put in a samsug 850 evo 250 gb m.2 in one of the expansion slots for much cheaper than it is to order those things from Dell. I also did a fresh windows install over to that ssd and now this thing flies. The one frustrating thing is finding a screw to hold the ssd down (you need an m2xl3, or in other words a screw that has a 2mm thread that is 3mm long). I went over to best buy and asked the geek squad guys for one and they let me look through their loose laptop screws and just take a few for free. Do yourself a favor though and pull out one of the screws that holds the back panel on to use as a guide (they are also the right size to hold that ssd down). After those few upgrades this thing is a total monster and I am looking forward to using this laptop for years to come. I would recommend that you update the bios from dell though, and update the network card drivers to avoid some of the other problems people have had with this laptop. I did not have any problems with mine, but I updated them still just in case. Both of which can be found on dell's website for download. If you do a clean install of windows onto your new ssd make sure to update the video drivers as well for the Gforce970m (or 980m if you get the better model) from Nvidia. I will update this review in a few months to report back on how this baby is running, but I expect no problems.
(Updated 5/27/16)
I am still very very happy with this laptop almost 2 months later. I have had no problems with it and it makes me happy every time I hit the power button and within 4 seconds its up and running. One thing that I did not mention before is that the lights on it can be changed to any color you want, or you can have each area (there are about 9) different colors if you want. title: 4K Ultraportable Plus Casual Gaming
text:
After a bumpy start with the first laptop having to be returned due to a hardware-based screen flickering issue (for which both Razer and Amazon were very supportive and helpful), I received this laptop, which was to replace a 2014 Razer Blade 14. I purchased the 4K model with the 512GB SSD.

The laptop is for me the ideal combination of SIZE and POWER. It doesn't hesitate to do whatever task I ask of it, including playing the latest Doom game (through Steam). I know better than to expect it to play "hardcore" games, but I knew that going in. I have used it for MS Office 365 programs and Visio. I also use it for UXWeb design (building HTML application prototypes). So there aren't any complaints about the performance factor. It gets the job done, though occasionally, there is the slightest lag between requesting a task and the system providing a visual indicator that the task has begun.

The USB-C CHARGING cable is slightly annoying in that it causing the power cord to stick out the side of the laptop and occasionally catch on stuff. To get around this I purchased a Thunderbolt compatible Right-angle USB-C 90 degree adapter.

The CHROMA keyboard back-lighting is good and configurable, though it acts on the entire keyboard with whatever customized profile you create. You CAN create your own color pattern. Note that whatever you customize is only in operation while you are logged in; once you lock the laptop, it resorts to the default ROYGBiV color cycling.

The KEYBOARD feel is nice and the key spacing is comfortable. That said, understand that I was already acclimated to typing on smaller keyboards, having used ones considerably smaller than this one. The keyboard is not silent, but I like the sound it makes. If you plan on typing next to a sleeping partner, however, keep in mind that they'll be able to hear you typing. That said, the keyboard has a couple of minor quirks to be aware of, but that I have been able to adapt to:
(1) The placement of the right shift key is half-sized, with what would otherwise be the left half of the shift key replaced by a full-sized UP arrow. That takes some getting used to if you're a touch typist like me.
(2) Usually the characters on keys have the upper case symbols above the lower case on the keys. For example on the number 2 key, the at symbol ("@") would be shown ABOVE the "2". For some reason, Razer reversed that on this keyboard. That'll confuse anyone who is NOT a touch typist.
(3) The Power key is NOT separated from the rest of the keyboard, instead appearing at the right end of the row of function keys. That said, it is at least intelligent requiring more than a momentary press to be recognized. I've missed the DEL (delete) key a couple times and hit the power key without the system taking any action.

The TRACK-PAD is the best I've ever used and does a great job with palm recognition (properly ignoring my palm when I get lazy and allow my wrist to momentarily touch the pad. The pad is HUGE, easily consuming a full third of the laptop width. The track-pad is very sensitive to the touch, occasionally detecting my touch just BEFORE I touch the track-pad. It successfully avoids my pet peeve of previous pads making my swipe twice to move from one side of the screen to the other - this despite the 4K resolution. I have not had to adjust the settings in any way (other than to reverse the scrolling direction) and have not have any issues with the "buttons" embedded in the bottom corners of the track-pad.

The DISPLAY is..well...AMAZING. Flawless color reproduction for my purposes that came perfectly calibrated out of the box.

Ports are obviously limited to 2 USB-C ports, only the right one of which is a 4-lane Thunderbolt port and 2 USB-A 3.0 ports. This is fairly common on ultra-portable laptops, though, and I got around that by buying a USB-C hub (with pass-through power to charge the laptop) and purchased a Bluetooth mouse (that doesn't require a dongle/transmitter).

One funny/odd note: The box that the laptop came in had large "HDMI" lettering on the side of the box. Odd, because the laptop does NOT have an HDMI port (causing me to have to buy a USB-C to HDMI adapter capable of 60fps at 4K). Razer should have been more careful with the labeling on the box.

I am very pleased with my purchase and would continue purchasing Razer products in the future.

title: Amazing value for the money with caveats
text:
In terms of dollars to performance, I haven't found a workstation that matches this. That being said, there were a couple of issues that I ran into, but that I was able to fix. I'm not sure if the average user would be capable/willing to go to the lengths to dial in this workstation like I did. But now that I've addressed the issues I found, I'm really very happy with this workstation.

Packaging and Finish 5/5:
The unit came in a very well fitting air bag that protected the unit on all sides. Overall fit and finish of my unit looked great. Scuffs were very minor. Keyboard and trackpad feel new and there were 0 dead pixels on my display. All of the USB ports function. For a refurb unit, I was very impressed.
I ended up opening the internals to do some work that I'll get into later and again, I was very impressed. The internals are very, very clean with 0 stripped out screws.

Performance (4)5/5:
Like I said in the intro, this workstation is basically unmatched in terms of dollars to specs. Great CPU speed, dedicated graphics, and good amount of RAM. When I first received the unit, boot speeds weren't stellar, but I'm spoiled by SSD's. I already knew I would be picky about this so I had ordered an SSD with this and promptly swapped hard drives (I'm partial to Samsungs). Boot and load times came down to seconds.

Issue 1: Excessive Fan Spin
After installing an SSD, I promptly installed and started working with Fusion 360. When I would get to computationally heavy calculations, the fans would start spinning up very quickly. I downloaded a CPU/GPU Temp utility and found that they were getting close to 100 deg C. So naturally I thought that the thermal paste could use a refresher. This is where I take a star off because I don't think the average user would be very happy with a fan screaming at them constantly or perhaps running into the occasional CPU temp shutdown.
That being said, if you're comfortable doing this sort of this, Dells are relatively easy to work on. There are great teardown videos you can find and no quirky long-screw-in-short-hole traps like you'll find in Apples. If you've done laptop teardowns before, you shouldn't have much trouble re-thermal pasting the CPU and GPU.
Once I refreshed the thermal pastes, max temps on the same calculations dropped by 20 degrees.

As of 2/23/2020 5/5:
After a new SSD and fresh thermal paste, I have to say, I'm very happy. To have a really great performing workstation for much less than half of what I would have to pay for a new workstation feels great. It's boxy and on the heavier side, but I don't care about that. I'm looking for a workhorse, not a Macbook Air. If you're looking for a great value and aren't afraid of peeking under the hood to address some minor issues, this workstation is for you.

title: Outstanding desktop replacement; Competent gamer

This button-down dark gray HP laptop will spend the majority of its time doing algorithm driven stock index futures trading. For that task, it really has the Right Stuff; wired gigabit ethernet port, world beater office task performance, a bright, crisp 1K display, and the ability to drive a 4K external monitor to its full potential. Sometimes I'll bring this machine with me and the fact that its appearance has about a zero "Star Wars coefficient" is totally a plus. I like the keyboard, its nice white backlighting, and overall style and build of this machine.

I can think of many ways this laptop could be better. It could have a magnesium aluminum alloy or even a carbon fiber case. It could have a 14-hour battery life. It could have a state-of-the-art graphics card. It could have multiple TB of NVMe storage. It could have a 4K OLED screen that displays colors that can only be detected by the James Webb Space Telescope. And none of that would add anything to the value of this very capable laptop for the missions I have for it.

At $699 on an Amazon flash sale, it represents an incredible value. When I had the back cover off to install a 32 GB RAM upgrade, I was very happy with the overall build quality plus the fact that this model came with the larger 72WH battery. And the back cover is held down by 7 Phillips screws of equal length. Some designer at HP should receive an international award in industrial design for just accomplishing that. title: Nice, upgradable computer. Mediocre for gaming.
text:
This machine comes with a capable mid-range AMD Ryzen 5 processor and a low end graphics card. The screen is non-touch 1080p FHD which is good, 4K is too high a resolution for a screen of this size. The key to the screen is its 120Mhz refresh rate. It will not be your bottleneck when gaming. At 250 NITs it is not very bright.

The laptop comes with 8GB if ram in a single SODIMM. By adding 8GB to the other free slot you double the ram to 16gb and enable dual-channel memory for a speed boost. However, 16GB is not the maximum despite the answer by Lenovo in the answer section. I put in two 32GB SODIMMs and have 64GB of ram in my unit (the actual limit).

In side it comes with a 256GB boot NVME. It is mid-range in speed. You add either another NVME or a 2.5 inch SSD. A kit is included with the laptop to add the SSD. I opted to add a 2 TB Inland NVME and left in the 256GB boot NVME. The boot NVME is the small size NVME, not full length so you have to find one like that to replace it, they are uncommon.

The speakers are barely good enough to watch youtuber videos. I suggest you connect to a good Bluetooth speaker.

In summary, I upgraded the memory to 64GB and the storage by adding a 2 TB NVME. This makes it a very cable workhorse computer to tackle most productive work loads while still enabling light gaming.

title: Runs uncomfortably hot, GPU died after 1 week, Acer not honoring warranty
text:
Tl;dr Acer Predator Triton 500 (PT516-52S-73YD) has quality control issues. Heat dissipation from the GPU goes through the w,a,s,d keys on the keyboard making for VERY uncomfortable gaming unless you use an external keyboard. GPU started glitching after a week of use. Acer warranty support technicians couldn’t fix it after 3 attempts and 6 weeks of back-and-forth with their repair center. The technicians damaged the laptop during the repairs. Acer Corporate Support tried to replace it with an inferior machine (Acer Nitro 5 with lower specs), which I refused, and Acer has so far refused to issue a refund.

Full story:

My Acer Predator Triton 500 (PT516-52S-73YD) worked well for about a week. The keyboard, especially under the w,a,s,d keys, would become uncomfortably hot while playing games. It seemed all the heat from the GPU was dissipating through some of the most popular keys used in gaming keyboard configurations. This seems a questionable design choice for a gaming laptop.

After about a week, games started to distort, especially in games that utilized fading, video playback, or parallax effects. Horizontal lines and visual artifacts began appearing during game rendering. It even affected games with less demanding requirements (e.g. Terraria) and demanding but less visually intense games (e.g. XCOM: Enemy Unknown). The problem became progressively worse over time, and eventually became so bad that games were unplayable.

I sent the laptop back to Acer for repair. They sent it back unfixed (they just updated the drivers and re-installed the OS, which I had already tried myself). Immediately sent it back, telling them it was likely a problem with the GPU and explaining exact instructions on how to reproduce the issue. They sent it back unfixed (they replaced the mainboard this time). Immediately sent it back a third time, this time including a video showing exactly how to reproduce the issue. They sent it back unfixed (they replaced the mainboard again and the LCD display, damaging my laptop lid in the process). This whole process took 6 weeks.

I called support, they said all I could do is send it back again. They said there was no way to escalate the issue or otherwise complain. I just had to put up with their process.

I ended up calling the Acer corporate number. I was eventually connected with a “Corporate Customer Support” rep. That rep tried to offer me a new laptop, a Nitro 5, and tried to pass it off as an upgrade because it had a 2TB hard drive and more memory. Sure, a bigger hard-drive, but the memory was DDR 4 vs DDR5 and the Nitro 5 they offered had a significantly smaller display resolution and slower refresh rate compared to the Acer Predator Triton 500 I originally purchased. Plus, the Nitro 5 has a cheaper construction quality (more plastic on the chassis; heavier components; thicker, less portable body; etc). I declined their offer and asked for them to commit to sending me an exact replacement for the model I purchased (Predator Triton 500). All I wanted was a commitment that they’d do this, but said they could not make this commitment in a timely fashion, so I requested a full refund.

As of the time of this writing, it’s been a week since I requested the refund, and, despite multiple calls to corporate customer support, they have so far refused to commit to issuing a refund. I’ve filled out the forms they requested and have provided the proof of purchase they requested. To be clear, I understand it takes a while for an actual refund to be issued. All I’m looking for is a commitment that they WILL issue a refund, which they still refuse to give. The rep I’m working with says that it’s in “the finance department's hands”, and that I have to wait for them to make a decision on whether or not my machine qualifies for a refund, which the rep says could take “weeks”. When I asked if I could escalate the issue, the rep said no.

I have given Acer 7 weeks now to make this right and to stand behind the quality of their products. They’ve so far refused to do so. In the meantime, they are holding the money I spent on this laptop hostage while I’m left with a broken gaming laptop that does not play games.

title: Fell in love with the 300hz IPS panel, blown away by the snappy performance and lightweight chassis
text:
Initial Impressions:

The first thing I noticed when unboxing the Acer Triton 500 was just how lightweight it is compared to other gaming laptops or even some ultrabooks for that matter. Compared to my Dell XPS 13 9370 it actually feels lighter or at the very least less dense which is impressive. In fact the power adapter included with it feels like it weighs almost half the weight of the laptop itself.

After plugging the Triton 500 in and powering it on I found myself nearly drooling when navigating the Windows 10 home screen with the 300hz panel (which defaulted to 300hz out of the box). I know that according to many the difference between 144hz and higher refresh rates isn't too noticeable but for me it was extremely noticeable. This laptop is incredibly responsive making it challenging to stop using the primary panel and instead a secondary external monitor. In a sense it ruined my 144hz and 120hz monitors even though it has a lower PPI, the screen on this laptop is just that beautiful and responsive.

As for the keyboard it feels tactile enough for my taste even though I'm used to blue and black switch mechanical keyboards. The keys have a bit of a click and spring to them and the rgb lighting is a nice inclusion though I have mine disabled. The touchpad isn't macbook pro large but it's adequate for my tastes. The speakers are decent on the Triton 500 but didn't really knock my socks off. I prefer to use headphones anyway though and the inclusion of a headset port is a nice feature though I've been using bluetooth 5.0 headphones primarily. The webcam is good enough for most business meetings or zoom meetings though low light performance is subpar.

Though the Triton 500 does come with some of the Acer bloatware it's not really a nuisance and in fact helped me find the driver update page quicker. Thankfully I didn't have any issues out of the box so I haven't updated any of the drivers yet but I probably will for security updates fairly soon.

Ease of Repair and Upgradability:

For upgradability the wifi card seems to be mini pcie so you can always change that out in a few years and there are 2 m.2 slots though you have to remove the motherboard from the chassis to access it (as well as the ram). This is a bit of a nuisance but understandable due to the heatsinks and fans they had to include on the bottom to optimize performance. It was fairly easy to access the battery though (just remove the bottom panel) so for battery replacements in the future it shouldn't really be too much of a hassle.

Gaming Performance:

For VR I had no issues hitting 90hz on Arizona Sunshine, the Walking Dead: Saints and Sinners, Pavlov VR, Superhot VR and Rec Room using a Samsung Odyssey VR HMD over the HDMI port. One thing to note though is that the bottom of the laptop does start getting pretty hot after 30 minutes of game time so it's a good idea to have it plugged in and enable the turbo fan boost key to bring down the temps.

Normal Browsing/Work Usage:

For everyday tasks and normal browsing usage I found that I was enjoying using this Triton 500 more than my desktop and ultrabook mainly due to the performance of the i7-10750H combined with the 16gb DDR4 ram and the 2070 Max Q. Running some scripts in Jupyter Notebook felt effortless and although I'm not working with massive datasets I could tell that it handles my normal tasks with ease. 40+ chrome tabs and no stuttering or lag when changing tabs.

The only minor criticism I have is the lack of a mechanical keyboard and a slightly larger touchpad but in its current state it still satisfies most if not all of my needs. The Acer Triton 500 is such a pleasure to use and blows past most performance metrics. Whether you're an avid gamer, game dev, or a programmer looking for faster compile times this laptop will likely exceed your expectations. I've since replaced my Ryzen desktop with this laptop.

Will update this review if I have any issues with the hardware in the future.

TL;DR:
Excellent portable gaming performance for VR, FPS, RTS, or any other gaming genre really, NVMe drive is lightning fast, wifi 6 card confirmed working with an 802.11ax capable router (stable and fast speeds), i7-10750H provides fantastic single core performance and good to fair multi core performance while not draining battery too fast, 2070 max Q easily maxes over 144hz in recent AAA games at 1080p (280+hz CS:GO), turbo button is easy to enable and helps with hotter thermals, decent I/O for VR headsets or external monitors, good battery life for the performance, definitely a killer laptop for the price point with an incredible 300hz IPS panel that will ruin all other 144hz monitors/panels for you

title: Powerful laptop for gamers and creators, but its graphics aren’t the fastest
text:
On paper, the Predator Triton 500 SE seems like the ideal powerhouse laptop, and it very well could be for advanced content creators. The most demanding gamers, however, will need to decide if the power-constrained graphics chip is a worthwhile trade-off for the laptop’s thin and light design.

The key issue for gaming is the 115W power budget given to the 3080Ti GPU (not mentioned in the specifications but really should be). Acer likely chose that number to reduce heat and improve battery life, but some laptops run the same chip at up to 150W and perform better as a result. This laptop is by no means slow while gaming, but it never unlocks the full potential of its 3080Ti GPU.

Graphics aside, the laptop performs exceptionally. The i9 processor blasts its way through anything I throw at it, and the Gen4 SSD delivers uncompromising storage speeds. Even the SD card reader is faster than what you find on most other laptops, supporting both SD Express cards (up to 985MB/s) and UHS-I (up to 170MB/s). Sadly, inserted SD cards protrude significantly from the laptop, so they aren’t usable as semi-permanent storage expansion.

Physically, the laptop is sleek and understated, and its nearly all-metal construction feels very sturdy (just the screen bezel and rear grille are plastic). The display is noticeably brighter than average, and the extra vertical space provided by its 16:10 aspect ratio definitely helps while juggling many app/document windows. The laptop is relatively lightweight, a little over 5 pounds, but the bulky power brick adds another 1.75 pounds to the total travel weight.

The keyboard feels responsive to type on, but its short-travel keys take some getting used to. For those into RGB, the keyboard has three lighting zones and seven customizable animation modes. The laptop’s downward-facing speakers are just adequate, so you’ll want to plug in headphones or external speakers if you care about sound quality.

Overall, this is an impressive gaming laptop, but it’s not perfect. Mainly, I wish that Acer had found a way to give the GPU a little more power, as I found this laptop’s 3080Ti graphics to be no faster (and even sometimes slightly slower) than my 3080-based laptop that it’s replacing.

title: Gaming laptop for the 40+ crowd that isnt Crazy Looking
text:
So Im a 40+ year old MAN, that likes to game! I also do a lot of traveling so I need a laptop that can game while Im on the road, and use in a professional manner. Sadly this is a difficult thing to find! Not to mention affordable! My last laptop I had was an Asus gaming laptop that had the words "Pit Viper" emblazoned on the front lid of it. And guess what.....Im now known around the office as Pit Viper! Which may seem cool, but when you explain to people why they are calling you that it looses its luster real quick! So farewell to that.

My old pit Viper laptop however was no slouch. It had a 2060 GPU and a Ryzen 4900HS processor. It played games excellently, but looked absolutely silly and more like a childs toy than an actual tool. I figured with this laptop the minor upgrade to a 3060 would be very nominal, but boy was I wrong. It turned out to be a huge improvement for the 2060. The 3060 runs coolers, has much much higher FPS and benches significantly better. Now the CPU on the other hand of this model definelty has its trade offs. It is by no means as fast or as mean as my old 4900hs, but it does use a lot less power than the 4900hs which when you are presenting and dont want to plugin is especially a bonus. However its just no where near as robust as the 4900hs was. Evreything else about this laptop is pretty spot on and pretty run of the mill. The screen is great, with massive refresh and great brightness. It is clear with no lagging or dead pixels. The keyboard has good actuation and not like the short throw macs or other ultrabooks. Battery life is about what you expect out of gaming laptop. For gaming your only going to get about 40 minutes of of this. But for general word processing and work this is really where this Intel processor shines and you get an easy 4+ hours out of single charge, which my old AMD asus would only get about 2.5 at very best. Predictably the laptop is pretty thick as it needs a lot of room to run those fans and vent the hot air, but its still very compact and not terribly heavy. As like everything there are always pros/cons

Pros;
-Incredible value for what you get, hundreds cheaper than its comparable brethren
-Huge improvement leap with 3060 over 2060 and below
-Runs cool with no throttling
-Intel processor sips power and is great for long work sessions
-Looks great and doesnt look like a normal silly looking gaming laptop.

Cons;
-Intel processor while good isnt great, you have to trade off for battery life
-Still made of plastic. However at this price point what do you expect?
-Power brick is massive. Weighs nearly as much as laptop itself. You also cant go without bringing it so you are always trucking it along as well.
-Acer bloatware is clunky. However easily deleted

All in all for a value priced laptop with high end components there is no equal. Its also great for the "adult" crowd who aren't interested in silly lighting or goofy pictures on the unit. It can easily be used in a professional environment just as much as a gaming session. I am incredibly happy that I can get away from my old nick name as well. RIP Pit Viper (you wont be missed)

title: A Fantastic Choice for a Gaming Laptop!
text:
In a nutshell, this laptop is absolutely fantastic, and is the considerable upgrade from my old gaming laptop - an MSI model - that I expected it to be.

Let's start with the display. The screen is a standard, 15.6", 1920 x 1080 screen, with a 144 Hz panel (with a 3 ms response time). My previous MSI laptop had a 120 Hz panel, so I, personally, don't see TOO much of a difference in terms of smoothness and rendering, but I'm sure anyone coming from a more common 60 Hz refresh rate will be blown away. The screen is not overwhelmingly bright (like my MSI laptop was, and I actually had to go into its Dragon Center to lower the overall brightness, in addition to the more accessible brightness just to not be blinded), which is a good thing, but it's definitely more than bright enough for the job - I even feel the need to lower the brightness on occasion. (Like with my old laptop, this can be done using the Fn key and the left/right arrow keys.) The bezel is also very thin, accommodating the screen nicely.

Moving on, the CPU is as advertised: a 10th-gen Intel Core i7-10750H processor, clocked at 2.60 GHz (when idle). I have had no problems with the CPU's performance thus far, and though it bears the same number of cores as my previous i7-8750H (both have six cores), I feel the performance (especially paired with the graphics card) is more than noticeable.

The GPU is an RTX 2060, which features NVIDIA's new Turing architecture, and 6 GB of their next-generation GDDR6 memory (as opposed to the GTX 1060's GDDR5 memory). Though, yes, it runs hot when running heavier games that I enjoy, it has yet to overheat, and while the fans can be noisy when running hot, it's not overly loud, I'd say. Additionally, it comes with a Turbo button, which the manual says it is good for "instant overclocking." To be perfectly honest, I have to use the Turbo button, because I don't overclock my hardware for fear of breaking it, but that's just me; don't let my paranoid butt stop you from overclocking if you'd like.

The Predator also comes with two 8-gig sticks of DDR4 RAM, running at a frequency of 2933 MHz, for a total of 16 gigs of DDR4. My old laptop also had 16 gigs of DDR4, but this RAM is actually a little faster (to my knowledge), so kudos!

The laptop comes with a 512-gig NVMe M.2 drive, which I believe is the fastest type of SSD currently on the market. Unlike other SATA SSDs, NVMe M.2 drives connect directly to the motherboard, rather than through cables. This is where your OS and all of your files and games will be stored. It is lightning-fast, especially compared to my old laptop, whose OS was stored on the SSD; games and such were stored on the terabyte HDD. The only downside to this upgrade (for me personally) was losing that terabyte HDD, but the packaging comes with some equipment for installing a hard drive yourself should you want to another time. The laptop's touchpad area even boasts two slots for SSDs and a slot for an HDD - I have yet to open up my laptop, so I cannot prove nor disprove this.

Speaking of the touchpad, I pretty much completely abandoned using touchpads years ago, and instead use external mice, so I have almost no opinion of it. But I will say this: it's quite soft, yet sturdy, so someone who's inclined to use a touchpad will probably have a pretty good time with it; I'm simply not one of those people.

The Predator also comes with a unique PredatorSense Utility App, which I guess is like Acer's answer to MSI's Dragon Center. I haven't used the PredatorSense a whole lot, but it is useful for system temperature and cooling monitoring, changing the keyboard's RGB coloration, overclocking, and more.

Speaking of the keyboard, I would say it's great, but not perfect. I'm not sure if it's me, but I've noticed a lot more "dropped" characters when I type on this keyboard (even while typing out this review!) than I did with my MSI's keyboard. I am aware I have a very soft touch, so again, it could be me (I also tend to type fast), but I feel like maybe the actuation doesn't respond quite as easily as my old laptop's keyboard did. Overall, though, I like it - it feels good to type with, the keys are nice and big, and BIG kudos to Acer for making the best out of a (relatively) bad situation with the keyboard: while the Pg Up, Pg Dn, and End keys are not dedicated (though the Home key is?), as they share functions, they are the priority when using these keys. What I mean is, the Pg Up key, for example, has a play/pause function, but it's only accessible via the Fn key (like how you can use the arrow keys to adjust the screen's brightness or volume on the fly), so simply pressing Pg Up activates the "Pg Up" function, not the play/pause function. My MSI keyboard, for whatever reason, did not do this, so playing certain games which utilize the Pg Up/Pg Dn/Home/End keys was an absolute pain. The Power Button is also a key, interestingly enough, and I feared accidentally shutting my computer down (or putting it to sleep) while using the numpad, but that has yet to happen.

Finally, the Predator has other common "gaming laptop" features that I would come to expect in the year 2021, such as an HDMI port, three USB ports, an audio jack, an Ethernet port, a mini DisplayPort, and a USB-C port. It does not have a disc drive, which I have no issues with, as I haven't used an actual disc for anything in ages, but it also doesn't have an SD card reader, but that's a minor thing, as I used the SD card reader on my old laptop maybe twice. And frankly, I'd rather have the additional cooling.

All in all, the Acer Predator Helios 300 is a fantastic gaming laptop choice!
