title: Great, but overpriced and with some really crappy issues--dull screen, TINY hard drive, and good luck upgrading
text:
This is a pretty good computer. We have come a long way when it comes to Made in China gaming devices, and gaming laptops in general. I also like the software that Lenovo puts on it (wow, never thought I'd say that). This is cool recovery software and various tools, and there is not a lot of bloat. It is fast, and the specs are more than decent.

Now, on to the issues.

FOR THE SPECS, you could do a lot better with the same amount of money elsewhere. It also can't touch something that a builder could make with the same budget, but that's a given.

But, let's forget about the price for a moment and just discuss it as it is.

The screen is dull and dim. The hard drive and RAM are nice, but they are too small. 175GB useable space is NOTHING for a gaming computer, and 8GB is not much RAM. Fine, you can upgrade later, right? Obviously that will tack on even more money, we know that, but the problem is that this PC is NOT easily upgradeable. You have to remove an enormous amount of screws, and then once you're into the innards, you have to take the battery out. That's right; to even just swap the battery, you have to take the case apart, and to get at the hard drive, you have to take the battery out.

The hard drive and RAM are obviously upgradeable, but getting there is a hassle. I gave up. I'm also unsure if there are two hard drive slots or if the solid state is not a full-size 2.5" hard drive but rather just a small memory bank. Even if that were the case, there should still be room for another hard drive. I would like to upgrade, and still plan to, but it's hard to figure out the configuration, hard to open the thing up, and I have no idea if the recovery software would still be available after swapping hard drives, or if I can just put a hard drive in and keep what is currently in there.

I'd contact Lenovo support, but for some reason I can't even do that with my serial number. The option is greyed out. I can go on the customer forums, but that's it. The user manuals are no help.

The touchpad is also bad. I don't like touchpads anyway, but this one is especially bad.

The keyboard is good!

It is a smooth computer. Everything runs great. It is the best computer I've owned, ever. If not for the poor display, lame touchpad, and huge hassle of upgrade, I'd be really happy, but that, combined with there being better stuff on the market for the same price, and lack of support (maybe because I'm a reviewer?) kind of sours the deal.

title: Best budget gaming laptop I have ever owned
text:
I am very surprised by the quality of this laptop. It is the best sub 2000$ laptop I have ever owned by far. The sound is actually pretty decent. The NVME is a SAMSUNG_MZVL25123 which is a PCIE Gen 4 drive that I was getting about 4.5Gbps read speed (25 percent faster than my Samsung EVO 970). The motherboard (in my model) is a TGL QX60_TLS and the RAM is Kingston DDR 4 PC3200. The Video Card vendor name is Hynix and it does include 6 GBytes of ram with a 192 bit bus. The display is 144 Mhz as described and it gets bright. The IPS back-panel does show some bleed-through but you can only really tell when you shut the laptop down and start it up. It also has a second NVMe slot (on the other side of the laptop) and has the insulator pre-installed on the bottom of the top panel. The keyboard is a little better than "adequate" but not better enough to call it "good". Key travel is short and does not give a very satisfying feed-back.
I could go on all day and provide benchmarks. This laptop has reviews all over the place online and it gets at least really good reviews everywhere I researched it.
The point is that this is the best "budget" gaming laptop I have ever seen.

title: Multitasking and Creative Powerhouse!
text:
This is my first Acer. For someone who viewed Acer as a budget brand, this Predator Triton 500 SE has significantly changed my mind. It’s not perfect, but this is a very nice laptop! It’s expensive, but it’s still inline or even costs less than other brands with similar configurations.

The i9-12900H and 3080TI used in this laptop are currently the fastest processor and graphics card being put into laptops. They are a very powerful combination, but I would argue the 3070TI model is overall the better price/performance option for most users. Regardless, both models are amazing for heavy graphics applications like high detail 3D modeling, gpu rendering, and high-resolution picture or video editing. These models will, of course, be awesome for gaming as well, but there are more gaming centric laptops (cheaper as well) that are better suited for pure gaming use. This laptop is more specifically designed to be a heavy multitasking, creative/creator laptop; and its understated design will fit in anywhere. Nothing but the logo, and the multitude of stickers, would betray this laptop as a gaming capable laptop.

This laptop comes with LPDDR5 ram, and this memory is FAST! It’s getting close to being twice as fast as LPDDR4. Having 32gb will provide all the headroom I will likely ever need for my multitasking workflow. One issue that I do have with this ram is that it is soldered to the motherboard. If it ever goes bad, which is very unlikely, it will require professional or factory replacement. I’ve never had ram go bad on me, but I always prefer for components like ram to be user replaceable/upgradeable.

The storage space will also be an issue for some people. The PT516-52s-99EL model (12900H with 3080TI) comes with a 1TB NVME SSD made by WD, but this won’t be enough storage for many people. Unfortunately, it’s not an easy/user friendly process to add a second SSD to the open M.2 slot on this laptop. Unlike most manufacturers, Acer has created this laptop with an upside-down motherboard. As such, it requires carefully removing many fragile cables, and this is NOT a risk-free process. Frankly, I wouldn’t recommend it. I chose to install a 2TB WD NVME in the open slot, and while I was successful in doing it; I was met with a casualty. The Wi-Fi card is another component that Acer soldered to the motherboard. While removing the white cable (see picture), the receiving motherboard connector completely sheared off the motherboard. I had barely started to apply upward pressure to the wire’s connector, so I believe this component was poorly/inadequately soldered during manufacture. This is unfixable by me, and I also can’t replace the combo WI-FI/Bluetooth card because it’s soldered on. In the end, I lost Bluetooth. I’m disappointed, but I can replace this functionality with a cheap USB Bluetooth Adapter – it could have been much worse. According to Acer’s warranty though, they have stated that opening the laptop and installing a second ssd will not void the warranty – as long as there is no damage caused. In my estimation, the white cable was a factory defect and made the ssd upgrade an unreasonable risk. Knowing that now, I would choose to use an external ssd instead. If you’re considering using an external monitor(s) as well as external ssds, etc; a safer overall option would be using an external USB C Docking Station. Anyway, your mileage may vary if you attempt this upgrade, but I personally wouldn’t do it again. If you do choose to attempt it, I’d recommend going slow, taking pictures, and being as prepared as you can possibly be. Personally, I’ve received A+ certification, I watched a disassembly video for this particular laptop, had the appropriate tools, and I still wasn’t able to avoid the issue I ran into. As a side note, if you aren’t familiar with the different types of cables you will run into, I would recommend watching a video about laptop motherboard connections and how to safely remove/attach them.

Enough of the negative, back to the positive - and personally one of the biggest highlights of this laptop to me - the screen. It uses a BOE BOE0AB5 (NE160QDM-NZ2) panel, and this is a full 10-bit panel that can show 1.06 billion colors. According to a calibration test done by ultrabookreview, gamut coverage for this panel is: 99.8% sRGB, 82.9% Adobe RGB, and 99% DCI P3; and gamut volume for this panel is: 145.5% sRGB, 100.2% Adobe RGB, and 103.0% DCI P3. The Gamut volume is of particular benefit to creative professionals (essentially relates to color accuracy at different brightness levels). For most people, all this essentially means is that the screen is very high quality and looks amazing! It has high contrast, it does not use PVM to adjust the brightness (which can cause eyestrain and headaches in some people), it is an antiglare screen (best for greater versatility in different lighting environments), it has an IPS panel (colors look and stay more accurate when looking at the screen from different angles), it has a 240hz refresh speed (which makes fast action look very smooth and not smeary), and it has a 500 nit peak brightness (many laptop screens only have a 300 nit peak brightness – you need higher nits if you’re planning to use the laptop outside or in very bright environments). To me, the screen is the most important part of a laptop. You spend all your time looking at it, and even the best hardware can’t make up for a bad quality screen. This screen is fantastic and is the best I’ve ever used.

Everything considered, I think this laptop is very impressive but not perfect because of the issues I’ve mentioned. I would like to see Acer fix the motherboard inversion issue – which leads to difficult and dangerous upgradeability issues, and I would like to see none of the main – user replaceable/upgradeable – components be soldered to the motherboard. I can’t, despite these issues, rate this laptop below 5 stars. It’s more of a 4 ½ star laptop to me, but for the sake of this review; I’ll be rounding up to 5.

title: So far, it's doing its job!
text:
My partner and I were looking for an affordable touchscreen laptop we could keep on the coffee table to share. After a fair amount of research, we agreed to give this one a try. I had good luck with an Asus netbook through 2+ years in the Peace Corps in Africa, so I hoped the durability would be comparable.

This is a sharp looking laptop. The screen is very glossy and therefore prone to smudging; I purchased a matte screen protector that I really like, which solved the glossy/smudge problem. The keyboard is a little spread out for my taste, but my partner likes it because he has fat fingers. The keys have a nice tactile feel, and the keyboard is super easy to clean. Doesn't get hung up much, and seems fast enough for what we use it for. Still sorting through some of the Asus features that come built into Windows 8, but I don't really have much of an opinion on them either way. The camera is adequate. The flip function is awesome. We use the computer in traditional laptop mode or exactly the other way around, with the keyboard down and the screen at a 90 degree angle to the table the most; tablet mode is really nice when it's appropriate. We haven't had any issues with any of the various screen angles, or the keyboard automatically turning off when it should. I was pretty easily able to install Xubuntu alongside Windows 8, the other problem I've encountered there is that the touchpad dones't work in Linux (I tried multiple different versions, since not having a touchpad is kind of a bummer.)

2 other things that I find fairly annoying, but aren't total deal breakers:
- The volume control on the keyboard requires 2 hands - 1 for the fn key and the other for the f10, f11, or f12 key. It might be a one-handed deal for folks with big hands, but I can't control the volume one-handed.
- The download speed is, indeed, pretty slow, even sitting right next to the router.

This would probably be a 5-star review if the screen resolution were better than it is. 1366 x 768 is adequate, but makes things look a little funny from time to time.

Update: 9.24.2015
The two-handed volume control is a definite deal breaker for me. I've never gotten used to it, and it irritates me every time I have to put down whatever is in my hands to adjust the volume.

And, 2 of the 3 USB ports have stopped working after only 10 months of use.

Increasingly disappointed. :(

title: A really good laptop that still functions really well after 2 years.
text:
First off, as an undergrad though I use this laptop daily I don't use it that much in general. Probably around 4 hours per day. So some of this may not apply to you if you're a heavy-duty user.
Now I'll go over some pros and cons.

Pros:
1. REALLY fast charging speed and long battery life (about 7.5 hours).
Can easily get through a day without charging.
2. Very short time to restart or to start up.
3. Good feel of keyboard and the keyboard has bright backlights.
Though I do have to say that I like keyboards that provide just a little resistance. So if you like keyboards with minimal resistance, get Macbook.
4. Never lags.
I've never had to restart because the laptop gets stuck. And as long as the conditions are right (discussed in cons), no lags running games either. Even with big games like RD2, Rust and Fortnite.
5. Though I've never done video editing and animation, since they share the same resources as gaming, I'd say this laptop would be a good fit for those as well.

Cons:
1. Fans REALLY loud when gaming.
Even when fully charged.
The fans are also loud if I'm charging and using at the same time on a low battery. So if you're on a tight schedule, make sure not to charge and use on 20%.
2. If charging and gaming at the same time, it lags A LOT.
Always charge before you game. But battery does drain really quickly. So I would say definitely get a cooling fan.
2. Touchpad is difficult to maneuver.
Mouse is recommended.
3. When using night light, sometimes it automatically turns itself off.
Not sure if this is a laptop issue or Windows issue.

On the whole, the pros are way better than the cons. Especially since all of the cons are easily fixable with the purchase of additional tools.
I'm reviewing all of this after 2 years of purchasing the laptop. And I'd say every function is still almost as good as new.
Would definitely recommend.

title: $300 off makes a difference.
text:
I bought the blade 2019 graphics (non 4k) for college and its the the biggest purchase i’ve made in my life. I’ve had it for a couple weeks, so it’s review time!

Disclaimer: I actually got it on sale at a microsoft store which priced matched the discount that amazon was offering at the time at $1390 after tax. But I didn’t buy from amazon thus the “non verified review”

I’m upgrading from a 2012 Macbook pro so the power is off wazoo compared to a measly dual core. I’m overall satisfied with this laptop but for its price, even after the sale, there are some flaws.

First the pros.
-It’s designed beautifully and it’s built well (except for the plastic hinge but it’s still study)
-The port selection is great, as it features thunderbolt on the right side.
-Battery life is exceptional (i’m getting 6-7hrs decent use)
-Display is bright and color accurate.
-Decently powerful considering it’s size.
-windows hello is really convenient

The cons and other annoyances
-I experienced some slight bubbling on my trackpad, like, small air bubbles on the edges of my trackpad which annoy me to death.
-Fingerprint magnet.
-When opening the lid, it doesn’t turn on right away after sleep mode. Other laptops do this but not this one?
-Battery drain when gaming or heavy tasks (Makes sense as tdp of cpu and gpu exceed wattage of the power brick but still annoying)
-I feel like it gets a bit too hot, but looking online says it’s fine?

Overall it’s actually everything I wanted in a laptop. Basically it’s well designed with its black aluminum unibody and thin frame while still packing a powerful whiskey lake quad-core .Furthermore it’s future proof with thunderbolt as I can add in an egpu which i’ll definitely be doing.

However.....

Maybe it’s because I want this laptop to be perfect that i’m finding flaws and being discontent about them but for 1300 bucks I do think that some of these concerns shouldn’t exist.

The blade is really for a specific type of person I would say.
Buy it if you know what your getting into and especially when it’s on sale ($300 off)
but if you aren’t sure or are extremely nervous about the flaws that you read in some of theses reviews look elsewhere.

title: Extremely Pleased
text:
I am extremely pleased with this laptop. It's first boot was into a Linux USB Installer where I proceeded to install Arch Linux. Whindows who? Windows is so....2000.

After installing Arch Linux I ran some tests. Gaming you'll get 2-3 hours of game time provided you're not running it on performance profile. I was able to run The Division 2 (my latest fancy as I revisit it) on ultra settings at about 40fps, so Med/Low settings you'll pull 60 easily, just set an FPS cap at 30 or 60 and happy gaming. Also tested Minecraft and it ran very well, no hiccups of any kind.

It pretty much played everything I threw at it. Divinity Original Sin 2, Ghost Recon Breakpoint, Cyberpunk 2077, Counter Strike Global Offensive (duh), Borderlands 3 and Tiny Tina's Wonderlands; the list goes on. This laptop just nails it.

As for outside of gaming (the real reason I bought it), thanks to the GPU it handles image and video editing very well, as to be expected. Additionally, basic tasks like browsing the web and spread sheet use, note taking ect; I managed to configure the system to pull 11-12 hours of battery life when doing menial and mundane tasks. This is while running steam, beebeep and Teamspeak3 in the background.

I'd buy this laptop again in a heartbeat, without a doubt. Would definitely recommend to anyone who needs a pretty universal workhorse.

The second time just crashed without warning. I had several important document open that are now corrupted. I can't turn back on my computer, because every time I do it tries to diagnose the problem. These are not problems from malware either, I use my old laptop for browsing and surfing, while I use this one for school and programming. I rarely use it for anything else (occasionally I'll use it for YouTube).

title: It’s HOT. Both figuratively and literally.
text:
This thing is a gaming beast. It easily handles MW Warzone. Everything is really smooth. A real powerhouse.
Recording music is also really good. I don’t have to limit my buffer size anymore and that helps a ton. This laptop can also perform well with AutoCAD 3D. No lag when panning across any axis on even the biggest job that I’ve drawn. The WiFi 6 card picks up just about all of the Mbps that I pay for with my service provider. I’m getting about 280-300 Mbps when I run tests on Fast.com. Ping time is better than my PS4. It does support ray tracing but I don’t know why. The laptop can’t handle the extra load well with ray tracing while paired with another monitor. It gets hot quick and I’m afraid that I will cook the CPU.
The battery life lasts about 2-3 1/2 hours depending on what I’m doing so I have to make sure I can plug it in anywhere I go. Would not be good for a long flight or car ride.
NOW ABOUT THE HEAT...
It does get really hot. I downloaded the Intel extreme tuning application and from there I can monitor core temps. It DOES get upwards to 95-98 degrees Celsius under high demand. I bought a 20 dollar laptop fan and it took the temps down by 20 degrees Celsius while under load. When I called Razer support, they said that these core temps are normal for this laptop. It seems a bit extreme seeing as the space between the keys and the screen can get hot enough to sear a raw steak. Literally. I cannot hold my finger there as it starts to burn without the extra laptop fan underneath cooling the chassis while under load. It will literally raise the temperature of the room that the laptop is in. Great heater for winter. That’s the only bad thing though. It gets hot. As I said, the 20 dollar fan helped a great deal. All of the other laptops at this price point had similar cooling issues. I hope that Razer comes up with another solution to cool their laptops because the vapor chamber can’t keep up. Other than that, fantastic laptop. If the CPU doesn’t burn up, I will probably have this laptop for a while. If it does burn up, hopefully it’s still under warranty when it happens.

text:

So a simple task of typing in the area of bottom left of keyboard would cause the laptop to rock back and forth. I tested it on another flat surface. Same situation. Lenovo X1 and Macbook sit perfect on the same desk. Contacted Razer to send me the part. They said they can't and I should return it.

Also I found a ton of info for batteries which "ballooned" from 2019 Razer Blade Base models with videos on youtube. Specifically there was a year old one in which you could clearly see the bulging, So basically I presume you need to change the battery every 2 years to avoid a fire hazard. I noticed that the laptop got hot near bottom right area which is super rare (Macbooks and others I use typically get hotter near vents or near display). I believe the battery just gets hot and the heat just messes up the chemistry even more so only after a year of use the battery starts bulging. The 2019 Razer Blade Base is pretty much the same design as this (this just has updated processor and space for extra storage) so my guess is it will have the same battery challenges that I believe have been part of the Razer Blade experience for years.

Otherwise the components were nice too bad their QC is nowhere near what it should be.

title: After struggling with this problem which gradually got worse I decided to look out a new laptop

I was a little concerned that the computer was being sold by Mobile Advance as I read a coupe of reviews saying that there was problems. When I opened up the box the computer was well packaged and when I saw the black cloth bag that the computer was covered I thought that this was an excellent touch. I did see on the side of the box that the computer was listed as a 2PC. I did notice this on youtube but as I didn't think this was going to be the computer I would get I didn't look at these videos.

The processor in my computer is it-4810MQ 2.8 GHZ and compared to my Toshiba it's much faster. I haven't really timed the boot time of my computer but I would estimate that the boot time is at most 10 seconds and I think I can be on the internet in 20 seconds. There wasn't too much bloatware installed compared to the Toshiba and even the jump from Windows 7 to Windows 8.1 hasn't trouble me too much.

So far I'm delighted with this computer even though I haven't explored many of the features just yet. It is taking me a little time to get used to the keyboard as the numeric keypad is laid out a little differently that what I'm used to as in the beginning I was hitting some wrong keys as my fingers are used to a slightly different layout.

I should add that I was a little concerned about the cooling so I did a little research again and I ended up buying the Cooler Master Notepal U3 Plus. Update 1: Razer will sell their products to Puerto Rico customers. Even on their webise they will ship them to Puerto Rico. Even Best Buy stores in the island sell Razer products. But in case of a warranty claim. If the product needs to be sent for repairs/replacement, it has to be sent first to an address in the USA so it can then be sent to Razer.

This might also apply to any US territory. So, dear purchaser please consider it seriously before purchasing from Razer. Specially if you live in a US territory like Puerto Rico.

Update 2: It turns out that Razer does offer direct warranty support to Puerto Rico. Seems like some CSR were misinformed. In the end I was able to send the faulty laptop to razer and they sent if back repaired. Had to wait about a week which ia not that bad.

title: Heat issues with the HP Gaming Laptop 15-cx0xxx Intel 8th Gen i5 8300H, 1050 Ti 4GB, 8GB RAM,
text:
Hi, I will be reviewing the HP Pavilion Gaming Laptop 15-cx0xxx I bought from Macy’s for Christmas. Intel 8th Gen i5+8300H, NVIDIA GTX 1050 Ti 4GB, 8GB RAM, 16GB Intel Optane Memory, 1TB HDD

I wanted this laptop for two reasons, 1. As a backup work from home laptop and 2. A secondary gaming machine when I didn’t feel like being a basement troll. Let me say up front, HP support was quite amazing in regards to customer service and trying to address the issue.

Despite that, I cannot recommend this laptop. And it is not because it doesn’t perform. This laptop played everything I threw at it smoothly with graphic settings set to medium, medium/high. Heat is a major issue with my laptop. Keep in mind that I don't know if I got a lemon, or if all these models will suffer from a heat issue. However, after three weeks and two stints at the HP repair, the heat issue persisted. It took me disabling the turbo boost on the CPU to get the temperature under control.

Be forewarned, if you decide to buy this laptop, then make sure it does not have a heat issue.

Beyond this, if there was no heat issue? I’d love this laptop.

The nerdy Details:

The biggest problem this laptop has is managing heat. I’ve built multiple gaming machines and out of habit with a new machine I download and install MSI afterburner, primarily to monitor heat levels. And because I did I discovered right away that this Laptop runs dangerously (in terms of the thermal limits of the components) high temps for games I feel it shouldn’t. Like Battlefield 4, Kerbal Space program, and The Long Dark.

Typically, you want low temps at idle, but this laptop temp at idle? Between 55-60c. And once gaming, it went right to mid 80 to 90c. Those kind of temps will shorten the life of most computers, especially during a long gaming session and so I sent it back to HP for repair.

And let me say that HP support did a very good job of handling this, because it was under warranty they didn’t hesitate to have me send it to them. After a couple weeks I got the laptop back and the Wireless wouldn’t work unless I was right next to my router. I suspect (but don’t actually know) when it was in for the heat issue they either damaged the wires or connectors somehow. So I had to send it right back for them to fix. Again no hesitation.

After 3 weeks in the repair shop I was finally able to test. And while the temps were marginally better at idle they were not much better during gaming.

During gaming the temps were now between 80c to 85c though technically it’s not the thermal limit, which by the way is listed at 105c, it’s still not good. Anyhow I gave up on HP and began trying to figure out how to modify the fan profile, which for some reason is locked down. In my opinion, the ability to adjust the fan profile should not be locked at all. I’d be setting the fan profile aggressively, which I’m confident would fix the problem.

If I had to guess? The fans never spin faster than 30 or 40 percent. Anyhow, because I couldn’t set the fan profile, I decided to undervolt the CPU, but even after that, the temps showed little to no improvement.

The fix came once I disabled the Turbo clock on the CPU. Temps at Idle are now in the high 30’s and low 40’s. And during gaming the temps are in the mid 50 to mid 60’s. Which is a significant improvement.

Lastly, I haven’t noticed any difference in gaming performance with BF4, Titanfall 2, both still run very smooth. I will be testing games like Witcher and BFV in the near future.

title: Brutally fast but will need upgraded!
text:
This laptop is a fantastic value for the price and is brutally fast at 1080p. But going into this you must know that unless you're content with just playing a couple of games, and most people are not, then you're going to need to dole out a bit more money, $100-200, in order to add an additional SSD to the laptop, which it does have a space for a secondary SSD. Now you could go with a 1Gb but I'd really recommend you save up and go for a 2Gb as you will find 1Gb runs out fast. Also the memory at 8Gb is likely borderline in need of an upgrade as well.

But, knowing that going on and you will love this laptop. Setup is seriously easy and fast, I was done just by using my voice to command Cortana to setup Windows 10 in about 10 minutes. There is no bloatware that I found (although if memory serves there was some sort of virus protector trial period which I promptly removed, and I'd recommend you do the same, Windows defender will do you just fine without any subscription fees).

The first game I tested I did run into issues and was unable to get it resolved and that was Doom eternal. It indicated that there was not enough memory in the graphics card to run the game. I thought this was due to it using the integrated (ie slow) graphics card rather than the discrete Nvidia 1650 (which is what you want to use) but even after disabling it I was unable to get Doom to run. A cursory glance around the internet appears that this is an issue with several brands of laptops so I moved on to something else: Microsoft Flight Simulator 2020.

Well if you know much about games it is not an easy game to run so if you can run Microsoft Flight Simulator well then you know you've got a keeper. I'm happy to say this game ran it without any issue at all and ran it extremely well. I also was able to run several other modern games without any issue at all and it seems like Doom was just a weird outlying anomaly.

Do be sure when you're running games that you are using your Nvidia card though!

Now, I've been running this laptop for about a week or so and never had it crash once. It boots up super fast into Windows 10, about 11 seconds it seems and is just a joy to use. And I am also driving a 1440p Acer Predator monitor now and games run just great at 1440p I should note. This machine is just a wonderfully light, fast game machine.

All in all this is a fantastic value and appropriately priced. Keep in mind you won't fit a lot of games on the standard 256Gb hard drive and you also should know you don't want to fill up the hard drive completely as Windows 10 will need space in order to install updates and such. Adding an internal hard drive is fairly easy but if that scares you then you can always use an external and this laptop has the ports for it, but know externals do take a slight hit on speed.

I love this machine and plan to use it as my primary machine when I am on the road. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!!

On somewhat older games like Alan Wake, Resident Evil 2 remake and Rise of the Tomb Raider, I've been able to set it to medium-high graphics settings and really fly along. I love the 120hz screen on this laptop although similar to other reviewers, I've noticed that the brightness is not the best. title: Keyboard poorly responsive/GPU and CPU performance are good, as expected
text: I purchased this laptop to be an upgrade from the previous machine I was using. I was encouraged to go forth with the purchase, as cyber Monday included a roughly $200 discount on the total price. Having used the machine now, I wouldn't exactly say I'd be too happy if I did not get it during the holidays, and with that discount. The GPU (RTX 2060) performs well, as expected. I always run system diagnostics as a first priority, when purchasing electronics online, to verify the components come as advertised. Battery life is medium-poor. But that is to be expected with this type of power-drawing performance, and in addition, can get very hot. The Nitro 5 comes with NitroSense pre-installed on the computer. This software lets you monitor the temperature of your CPU and GPU, realtime. As well, you can use it to adjust the speed settings of the internal cooling fans. The cooling fans seem to nearly run full blast (set to automatic) when playing any game. I have tried a few graphic intensive games, as well as Minecraft (which shouldn't be too terribly demanding) and it seems that no matter what, if you're playing a game; expect CPU average temperatures of 89 degrees Fahrenheit. This is, of course, to be expected of a gaming laptop. Of course you could turn down your graphic settings and possibly keep the machine much cooler that way, but that is not exactly something I'd like to do myself, considering the purchase was made specifically to be able to slam those graphic settings to the max whilst still maintaining playable framerates. My biggest bone to pick with this laptop is its keyboard. Its keyboard is quite honestly, very very disappointing. Yes, it has its RED backlighting and nicely sized keycaps to the tune of a full keyboard with numpad; But the keys are very irresponsive. You almost have to mash the keys to have it register a keystroke. As well, you cant just mash the keys, you have to do it almost in the center of the keycap itself. In addition to that, my (A) keycap came from the box a little bit oversized, and I mean by millimeters. But this causes it to catch on the web-bezel in between itself and the (Q) key, and makes a very audible click, as well as make it even harder to register a keystroke.  My solution to the bum (A) key and overall poor responsiveness of all the keys was to purchase a keyboard cover for $6. I got the clear one so I could still have that wicked red glow from the backlight. This seemed to help dramatically. It kept the oversized (or slightly poor positioned) ((A)) key from catching on the bridge between by molding its position. In regards to the poor responsiveness, the keyboard cover provides slightly more resistance to the keys, forcing me to press the keys harder anyway, which seems to result in a registered keystroke. With the keyboard cover, I'm finding myself typing more naturally and making less mistakes than I did without it, it seems to make it possible to not have to press the center of the key as well, as the cover will pushing down on the entirety of each individual keycap by dividing the pressure throughout it. Long story short, buy a keyboard cover with this. It might even save you from crumbs and liquids spills. Thanks for reading, I hope it helped.

title: Much more capable than I was even hoping for!
text:
When I saw the specs included a 50-tier (3050ti) GPU, I was a little worried that it would not have quite enough power for all my games. Obviously, a dedicated GPU would run some of my older games that I wanted to play, but I was worried about some of the more demanding ones. It turns out my worries were for nothing!

This laptop has been great for every game I've thrown at it, from older games to new games that came out this year! Most of the games I've played even run at near-top or top-quality settings! Now, there are a couple of caveats to this claim. First, I'm running these games at 1080p. 4K might be a different story. Also, there are far more demanding titles out there (EX: Cyberpunk) that I have not tried. However, this laptop's 3050ti is far more capable than I originally gave it credit for!

Another nice surprise came when I opened up the back panel. The expandability of this laptop is much better than many other modern laptops on the market. It has 2 m.2 NVMe slots and 2 ram slots, which allows you to expand the original capabilities of this laptop!

A lot of the Legion laptops have LED lighting around the side and on the lid as well and this one does not. It's nice to still have it on the keyboard, but the options are a lot more limited on this model. Speaking of the keyboard, the typing position, although offset, is pretty comfortable and feels good. It doesn't feel cheap and the travel is decent, with a nice satisfying click.

Airflow can be a bit of an issue. When placed on a flat surface, the airflow becomes somewhat restricted and the fans need to ramp up to max to keep up when running games. However, with just a little extra space under the laptop with something like a portable stand (or just one that doesn't have a solid surface supporting the laptop), airflow is significantly increased and the fans usually spin down to a medium speed.

While this laptop isn't the most powerful on the market, I really like the balance of performance and energy/battery efficiency and overall I am very happy with this laptop!

title: The Best Graphic Design/Video Editing Laptop
text:
If you have been looking for a laptop in the last few years, you know that the choices are many. So many in fact that it can be frustrating to make the best choice. There are many manufacturers out there branding their laptops as being made for the content creator. There are equally as many people out there that aren’t aware of laptops that can do content creation just as well as Apple’s products and at a much lower price point for the same or better specifications. I will be honest with you, if you are doing content creation on a laptop that doesn’t have an OLED screen, you may be missing out on a huge benefit to the quality of your work.

Gigabyte often gets over-looked when it comes laptops. You may not have even known that they make laptops. Not only do that make laptops, they do so very well. The detail in design and engineering in performance has been given top priority.

Probably one of the most amazing of these is the Gigabyte AERO OLED 15 SA. I bought this laptop in September 2019. I have not only used it daily since then, I have used it about as hard as one can use a laptop. Aside from normal everyday use, I have used this machine primarily for video editing and gaming. Gigabyte has a separate brand called Aorus that is designed specifically for gaming while their AERO laptops are engineering specifically for content creation and productivity work.

SPECIFICATIONS

The AERO OLED 15 SA comes equipped an Intel i7-9750H processor, a NVIDIA 1660ti GPU, 16GB of Samsung RAM that can be upgraded up to 64GB, and for storage it boasts an extremely fast 512GB Intel 760p M.2 NVMe drive. This Intel storage drive as a Read Speed up to 3230 MB per second and Write speeds up to 1625 MB per second. As a comparison, SATA SSD’s have a Read Speed of around 550 MB per second and Read Speed around 500 MB per second. Your standard laptop HDD, will have Read/Write speeds of 80 to 160 MB per second. As you can see, the drive in the AERO OLED 15 SA is extremely fast. There is also an additional M.2 slot internally to easily add additional storage.

THE DISPLAY

The shining beauty of the AERO OLED 15 SA that will make any photographer drool is its display. It is a 15.6 inch Samsung UHD AMOLED display. Because each one is factory calibrated and X-Rite Pantone certified, the color and clarity gives me the most vivid and true to life image on the screen. This is a photographer’s dream. With the certification and calibration this screen goes through before it arrives on your doorstep, you will no longer have to play the guessing game while editing pictures only to find how off you were when you have the photo’s printed. Putting this laptop side by side with any other laptop will show the night and day difference from what you have been missing.

MY EXPERIENCE

When I got my hands on this laptop, the first thing that I noticed was just how sleek and pretty it is. The design and materials that went into the AERO OLED 15 translate to a laptop that doesn’t feel as if shortcuts were taken. Once the laptop was setup, not only was the standard log in options available, but I am able to log in using facial recognition or using my fingerprint. My usual choice is the fingerprint. The sensor is located on the mousepad and I haven’t once not had it recognize my finger.

Typing on the machine is a breeze. Coming from a work issued Dell laptop, it is so nice to have absolutely every keystroke recognized on the AERO OLED 15 SA. The keystrokes are near silent. For those that like to work in low light conditions, the keyboard is also backlit and you can choose any color you wish, or different lighting options when you type. You can also turn the led option for the keyboard off if you wish.

The laptop is equipped with Microsoft AI. It learns how you use the laptop and allocates resources based on how you as an individual works or plays. I have used this laptop to render 4K video, stream live content, and play Triple A games. Not only has this laptop handled everything that I have thrown at it, it has handled the workload in a way that truly impresses.
If you have never used a laptop that has an independent graphic card and you are used to long battery life then be aware than ANY laptop like this is going to be power hungry. While it is equipped with a 94.24Wh battery, if you are using the laptop on battery power and doing things like gaming or video rendering, the useable time on battery is reduced significantly and I recommend that while doing those tasks, you use the AERO OLED 15 SA while plugged into the power adapter. If you are doing normal tasks, and turn down the brightness of the display, my experience has shown that I can get up to 2 hours of usage while on the battery.

Support

The support behind this laptop is unbelievable. Gigabyte stands 100% fully behind their products. If there is ever an issue with the AERO OLED 15 SA, rest assured that the company will take care of it and do so quickly. It is backed with a 1 year warranty and when you register the laptop, Gigabyte will have a tree planted in your name. As with any company, Gigabyte is a business. Unlike other companies though, my experience has shown that Gigabyte goes beyond the profit margin and truly cares about its consumers, community, and the planet that we live on.

CONCLUSION

In a nutshell, I highly recommend this laptop for video editing and graphic design. Within the first 2 hours of usage, you will realize that this laptop was a very wise investment. At the current price, it’s an unbeatable deal when you consider that other laptops at this level are built with inferior materials and/or components to cut cost and do not have the features or display used for the AERO OLED 15 SA. This laptop in its appearance could be described as elegant, in its power as a workhorse, in its display as pure beauty. If you have been waiting for the perfect laptop for your work in content creation, then wait no more because based on my experience, this laptop will surely impress in every aspect a laptop has to offer.

title: Older model had solid 3 year run, but beware of heat
text:
Not using this exact model, but coming from an Alienware M17 R2 (model obtained around this time 3 years ago), commenting here since people do not tend to go look up previous models, partially from stores making old junk harder to find to prioritize the new, and it takes more effort to find reliability of a line of models, so here we are since I wish more models had these "How good was it after the first impressions wear off" reviews. Take this with a grain of salt, there may be some improvements over time, but pictures of the new models look pretty close to the one, and I doubt they fixed the old issues unless they start doubling the weight by turning it into a giant heat sink. I am typing this on and want to give general impressions and some warnings.

Overall, this has ran pretty solid for the last 3 years, but I am now at a flashing light warning that the battery is unusable and the front of the chassis is swollen to a point I am afraid to open to try even attempt replacement.

First off, getting it out of the box, it was sleek and cool, it features fancy RGB keyboard, and a nice command center to customize colors and brightness to a reasonable degree. It has been able to run a good number of games over its life, but without assistance of a cooling pad it should not be pushed.

Will start with the gaming side of it since that is why you are looking at this model probably. For short bursts, it was able to run the new games at pretty good rates at high settings, but even with it's "fancy cooling" advertised above I would recommend a cooling pad as a minimum to even attempt high end gaming with it, otherwise it runs great for 15-30 minutes, then blacks out after about 3 seconds of notice for the user to take action. Power it on, find the reason to be "overheated", then you proceed to touch the exhaust area near the screen and yell from the mistake of feeling the scorch.
Staying away from higher end gaming and keeping it elevated for some airflow, it has been a champ without heat issues and has been a great contended against the desktop that is a few years older.

A second feature that drew me to this model at the store was the programmable colors. Rainbow seems cool at first, then calm down to some other colors such as green or blue, then as you start to push for sleep you swap it to some offshoot of red probably. All doable, but it has had a reoccurring issue of if you turn any of the lights off (such as the ones on the back), it has a habit of turning them back on until you open the Alienware Control Panel, go the FX area, then without actually changing anything your settings kick back in.

Battery life was never a strong point, but it generally isn't in these laptops. Out of the box, if you treat it as a social media machine, you will get an estimated 3 and a half hours of life out of a full charge, less than an hour if you actually use the GPU for any games. For the decay of the battery, it barely changed after the first year, but by the 2nd year it had lost about 1/3 of its "total capacity" which translated to about half the lifespan. At the 3rd year it claims to have lost another 1/3, but is now flashing at me that it is failed and it immediately shuts down if it gets unplugged from "full power". A pro to the "clunky design" of the location of the power port being middle of the back is that it forces it to be unplugged before going into a bag, which saves it from rushing leading to accidentally wearing down the port far faster, which was what caused my previous laptop to fail.

For general mobility, it has been a bit heavy, which is a given considering the monster hardware within, but it has been a great case. Unlike past laptops I've owned, I have not had any indications of hinges ready to burst, any bending (besides the battery swell), or cracking., It has been very solid, but to save yourself from potential fires please DO NOT use sleep mode unless you are willing to restart it anytime Windows has an update. Windows Update has the wonderful (said with much sarcasm) feature of turning on a computer to let you know updates are ready to install, but then do nothing on its own. Which translates to: it will randomly fire up in your bag despite being closed and from the poor airflow start to overheat. Safety measures should eventually get it to eventually stop or from the battery dying, but since it can't detect the heat tolerance of its carrying case or anything else you care about around it, it starts cooking at a pretty high temperature even if you have nothing running. Thankfully the few times I had this happen, I was pulling it out about half an hour later after driving somewhere. Better alternatives are hibernation mode, or since we are at the age of SSDs, just plain shut it off if you can wait the couple of minutes for any pending shutdown updates.

Which on that note, have not had a slow boot time or even wait period on updates, I am mainly sticking to old paranoia from when computers took over 30 minutes to fully boot and be usable. This has always been ready to go in a minute or so.

For the screen, I have not had any issues. No real comments, the particular variant did not have HDR nor 4k, but considering the issues mentioned with the heat, 4k probably would have been too much for the 2070 in this (reminder, reviewing older model).
I have used this for a lot of daytime and nighttime reading, only time have had issues seeing contents are when sun glare straight on it and it has been in need of cleaning. The picture taken showing screen is distorted both from dim yellow light and an app running to reduce blue light after dark, so its color has been fine, purpose was "See, still in decent condition, and it from same lineup." but doesn't show the power button blinking, and any dark lines may be some cat hair.

Keyboard has been great, but the one I am using features the extended keyboard with the num-pad and additional keys, that took some pain to repurpose into media keys since the stock layout was missing indications for them, which later by accident found they were hidden under FN+Arrow keys. Also despite the heat, unlike some other laptops I've had, when it gets to egg cooking temperatures, it has not spread the heat to the general keyboard, so no burning fingers when trying to rush something through before it shuts itself off.

The touch pad was great for the first month or two, then has barely worked since. After the couple of months, the battery started its swelling from the heat of failed attempts at running new games at high. After the swelling, corners were raised to different levels (attached picture, bottom is sunken in top is sticking out, which isn't much but is enough for bottom right corner to be useless) and right clicking only became possible through two-finger tapping, which if you want a lazy day of no mouse, you cannot do the combo of double tap+hold to aim, then a third finger to click, there has been no "hold right click" making some games impossible to play. Despite the right click issue, it has been very responsive in moving, scrolling, and left mouse clicking via the tap anywhere unlike the Lenovo laptop this replaced.

I cannot speak much to the sound quality since I don't have an ear for it, but for general volume, no issues on it getting loud enough to be heard, usually keep this around 20% for general use and music. Mentioning since a completely different work laptop from Dell at max volume is so quiet it is barely usable for meetings in a quiet room.

As for the new Windows, for anyone on the fence, a couple of comments for it. This one came with Windows 10 and was later upgraded to 11. As for the usability, if you are coming from Mac, you may like the new changes, but as someone having been around since the 90s, the new right click menu and task bar suck, but both are easily fixable with a free tool that handles registry changes for you (avoiding naming since not sure if would be an issue in this review, but should be easy to find searching along lines of "revert Windows 11 taskbar tool", may even be nicer options available now), since the built in options are lacking and hacking the registry is a pain. After getting a familiar look and feel back and getting right click menu back from being useless, it feels like a side-grade to Windows 10. Some differences, explorer is shinier, gaming supposedly better but I gave on trying anything high end already, and new Linux options (WSL). Working about the same as Windows 10, only real complaint left is every couple of weeks it keeps trying to enforce crummy default file grouping in File Explorer, especially in the downloads folder. Another issue has been sometimes when trying to get it to hibernate, it will black out as if it went off correctly, then come back on a second later every time you try, fix has been to restart it then it will properly hibernate for a while. I believe I have locked down cause to being GPU being triggered by the app on Steam called Wallpaper Engine, not sure if an issue from newer versions or from Windows 11, but have only noticed it happening when that is running.
Another issue, but nothing new is if the surrounding temperature is cold, it may not properly come out of hibernation sometimes and will need power button held to fully shut it off before it can properly get back to the login screen, but this has been a re-occurring issue across all manufacturers I have tried over the past 2 decades going back as far at least Windows XP, but a pro to this laptop is that this issue has happened far less than any other prior.

Overall, though it was an expensive model, it did scratch the itch of rare high end gaming, frequent old and lower end games, having a fancy customizable keyboard, and being a solid build, but it was disappointing that I couldn't do "high end gaming" with it as-is considering it had the "fancy latest GPU+high end CPU" of the time and the touchpad has been a mixed bag. Maybe if I got a new cooling pad for it sooner and was more aggressive at installing Windows updates it may have done more.

title: Great Laptop!
text:
Over the years, I have been buying my wife laptops that cost less than $300 every other year or so. Buying another cheap laptop every other year seemed almost to be a necessity because they would ultimately break down, either in terms of slowness, hardware failures, or just physical cracks or button issues.

I finally decided it was time to get her a high quality, well-built laptop. I am a Mac and PC user, while she has only ever been a PC user. I was thinking of getting her a Macbook Air (knowing fully that Apple will be replacing it the near future - hopefully). For her, it would have been enough computer for at least five years. Then I saw this laptop. For the price I paid (on sale), the specs were practically double everything the Macbook Air offered at 2/3 the price. Being a Mac user, I know the intangibles that come with Macs, and also how long they last (I have a 10 year old Mac still going strong). However, I could not pass this deal up.

This is a understated-looking gaming laptop. I'm not a gamer, but I'd say its good enough for causal PC games, while looking almost business grade. You could easily bring this to the office during the day, and play games on it at night.

The keys are backlit in a beautiful white, but can be turned off with the f5 key. The keys are outlined in white too.

It is a fingerprint magnet, but mostly on the keyboard deck and wrist rest. The outer casing seems to resist fingerprints well enough.

It uses an Elan trackpad, not Synaptics.

The screen does not open very wide. This makes standing up and typing on the laptop difficult because you cannot reposition the angle very far. It opens just beyond 90 degrees. Eyeballing it, it might be about 105 degrees.

I Geekbench all of my devices. This laptop scored a 32-bit single core score 3757 and a 64-bit single core score of 3770. It scpred a 32-bit multicore score of 13237, and a 64-bit multicore score of 13603.

It is very fast (with its ssd), has plenty of storage (with its additional hard drive), and doesn't come with a lot of bloatware.

Overall, there is not much bad to say about this laptop. I don't like the limited angle that the screen opens up to. The only complaint my wife has is that she does not like the trackpad. She prefers to have two physical buttons. So, we added a wireless mouse and a lapdesk. Other than that, I think anyone would love this laptop.

PS: I have no issue with the trackpad. I think it is very nice, second only to the glass trackpad on Macs.

title: Beautiful design, but there are some issues
text:
Let me begin by stating that we are a Dell family. I've had several XPS laptops and an Inspiron desktop over the years, and my children all have Alienware desktop computers. So, when I was asked to review the Dell G15 5520 15.6 Inch Gaming Laptop, I went in expecting to fall in love with it. Regrettably, I did not. I waited two months to write this review, hoping that the problems I was having were software-related and that installing all of the updates I could find would solve my problems. There have been two BIOS updates and a slew of other updates since I received this laptop. I installed every required and recommended update, and I kept other software installations to a minimum. I only installed a video conferencing app and a pdf reader from trusted brands. But this laptop keeps crashing. I have had at least 10 blue screens. Furthermore, I had to reinstall Windows because when I started the laptop, it would state that Windows did not load properly, and restarting the PC only helped for a short time.

I've had a number of problems since the beginning. For example, even though the settings are set so that the laptop should sleep when I close the lid, it appears to keep running as the battery drains. I'll go to bed with a fully charged laptop, only to wake up with one that's at 0%. I tried leaving it plugged in, but it gets so hot that I'm afraid it's dangerous. Speaking of how hot it gets, even when doing simple tasks like editing a text document or slides, it appears to work so hard that it is burning up. It's better when it's not plugged in, but I can only get about 2.30 hours out of it on battery power alone, which isn't great. So I've been using this laptop exclusively with a constantly running cooler pad. I can see why this is required for serious gaming, but for light text editing? On top of everything else, my screen began to display multicolored lines last week as well. I thought that was it, but I haven't seen any this week, so fingers crossed.

There are a few features on this laptop that I do enjoy. The design is wonderful. My husband is in the army, and the design is identical to his uniform, so I thought this laptop would make an excellent gift for him. I also like that there is a separate numeric keypad. That was missing from my XPS laptops. It took me a few days to get used to typing more to the left, but once I did, I was hooked. I also like how simple it is to turn the keyboard lights on and off. When I try to work at night, the light definitely helps. Another feature I appreciate is the Dell update app on the laptop. You don't really need to go to their website to get necessary updates anymore. Overall, if it weren't for the technological issues, I think this would be a fantastic laptop. However, based on my recent experiences as well as the weight of this laptop and the power brick, I still prefer my XPS, even if she is a little older.

title: I wanted to love this laptop
text:
Before buying this laptop, I researched all gaming laptops in my price range and after hours of searching, checking specs, reading reviews and watching videos, I decided to go with this MSI GF63 Thin 9RCX. I have now been using it for a little over a year for browsing, doing school work, programming, and gaming in my limited spare time. Overall I've rated it at 3 stars and I'll try to explain why in this review.

First let's start with the cons because let's be honest, that's what everyone wants to know. The first and by far the biggest con with this laptop is that the web cam didn't work right out of the box. Now, this might not bother me that much except we just happened to go into a pandemic and a lockdown and all schooling was done virtually! Zoom was the order of the day there so not having a working web cam was more than annoying. Especially on a laptop that costs this much.

MSI's warranty wasn't much help as I found out that they consider a non working web cam out of warranty as past 90 days when I called them, lesson learned there.

Now to the other gripes I have with this laptop. The bottom ridge under the mouse pad is very uncomfortable to the point that it's even painful after resting my wrist/palm on it for even 5 minutes. The battery life is terrible so I usually just leave it plugged in while I'm using it for anything. The last complaint is that there is a high pitched noise that it makes that I don't know how to explain really except to say that it is very annoying. It might be a noise coming from the SSD or something but I'm not sure.

The good things about this laptop is the price was around $600 after tax and I feel that that is fair for the specs of this laptop. It runs Fallout 4 on ultra at 60 fps and that is the newest game that I play at the moment so I'm definitely happy about that. I like that this laptop is so thin and light, because I plan to use it for traveling. I also like that it came with a 9th Gen Intel CPU and Nvidia graphics; the MSI Dragon Center is also a nice addition, as well as the Nvidia Control panel which allows me to display the FPS while gaming.

There are so many things that I like about this laptop that I really wish that I could give it a higher rating than 3 stars but to me that non working web cam and poor customer service is just unacceptable. I just don't understand how that passes quality control for a BRAND NEW laptop of any price.

title: I really like it
text:
The 3050ti card is far and away the fastest and most capable graphics device I've ever had.

I purchased this laptop for other more important (to me) criteria:

RAM and Cores -- I run Docker and VirtualBox VMs like crazy, and I'm power user for development tools, so I put a machine to some serious load. This laptop stands up almost as well as my Ryzen 7 rack system.

I really appreciate the ports, especially where they are located. I sometimes fold the laptop flat and set it on a tablet stand (actually a photo frame stand). So power, HDMI, and USB ports feed from the top of the unit, behind the screen. This is a really good design. When I use the laptop this way I'm using an external keyboard and mouse. Bluetooth mouse and audio work really well. I've actually ran VSTi synths over Bluetooth with very little latency and this comes as a surprise.

As for gaming, I never even know what games people are talking about, but I tried it with Elder Scrolls Online and it's between 50-100fps. If you need better gaming video than that, you're in a different market, and I doubt you're seriously looking at this laptop. But it gets the job done very well for the only kinds of video games I'm into (Skyrim, ESO).

I could not get it to work with a Lepow USB monitor but it drives a second HDMI monitor just fine.

There's a m.2 nvme slot but getting to it requires more surgery than I've had time to do. Also I wish I could swap the 512GB system drive for a larger NVME, and I'm sure I can do that, but I don't want to break the OEM Windows install. I'll figure out how to deal with this situation sooner or later, and end up with 4TB.

The laptop does get very loud under load. It probably qualifies as "quiet" in terms of dbA but it's a very high pitched pink noise. This machine would not be a good choice for music studio usage. That said, under the low loads of stuff like audio recording, its very quiet, but it ramps up quickly under VSTi synth loads. I would not recommend this device for audio production or any other situation where having a silent PC is important. It's not bad, but this is far from a silent PC, even under moderate loads.

I like the Lenovo keyboard layout a lot. I like the touchpad. I'm very happy with the overall shape, size, weight and performance of the device and will likely purchase another one.

It's priced at the "entry level first computer" kind of price point, but it's a machine capable enough for a developer who needs serious computing power. I don't think it's quite the same as the desktop/server 8core Ryzen, it doesn't have the same kind of overclocking controls or the over-specced VRMs that a desktop boat will have, but without doing formal benchmarks, it "feels" fast and high capacity. I like it a lot.

title: Packs a powerful ultrabook punch with a heavy dose of premium

I had been on the fence for months with my next ultrabook purchase, leaning toward the Surface Laptop 2, considering the stalwart Dell equivalent (XPS) and somehow landing on the Envy. I pored over reviews, technical data, and other analysis but decided on the HP because it was just too much premium and value to disqualify.

This particular version is packed with tech that would cost over $2,000 in a similarly equipped Surface Laptop 2, yet I paid just $1000 on Prime Day. Even at $1299 it's a steal, considering you're getting a full 4k display, 512gb SSD and 16gb RAM. The fingerprint reader and backlit keyboard are bonuses, as is the premium build of the hardware. I came from a Yoga 910 which was a gorgeous laptop with similar specs, but I couldn't stand the keyboard. It was prone to missing my keystrokes, and it was loud, with shallow key travel. The Envy's keyboard proved a far better suitor after testing it out at a retail box store, and the rest is history.

If you are a writer, appreciate fine design, and want a speedy 8th Gen i7 with more storage and RAM than the average user would ever need, here's your ultrabook. Forget the frills of Bang & Olufsen, which is really just a nicely placed license to evoke an extra premium feel rather than a useful sound upgrade, and enjoy the quality build. Don't expect the fingerprint reader to be 100% accurate (it's not), but appreciate the fact that HP put the front-facing webcam where it's supposed to be and deal with the above-average battery life that underdelivers but still excels.

Oh yeah, and grab the two-year accidental damage protection plan which is just $50 through Amazon, rather than paying $200 or more through a retail channel.

It is very easy to scratch and the black color makes the scratches very visible.
I got the Core V2 with it and expected it to work without a glitch but this wasn't the case. Every time I disconnect the core I have to reinstall the driver for the MX150 onboard as Windows doesn't recognize it any more (issue is now resolved after removing all drivers and using GeForce Experience to install the drivers instead).
The location of the right shift key is horrible and takes a lot of time to get used to. I'm a touch typist and this could be the most annoying thing about it. Also, you don't get the context menu key, usually fn+right ctrl without programming it using Synapse 3.
Synapse 3 itself is very buggy and is very annoying having to watch the intro every time my laptop starts.
Windows Hello is beautiful, I never expected to like it that much (Also issues were resolved with the latest updates for Synapse 3, still does not recognize the Core V2 which is a major bummer). Synapse 3.0 also causes all input devices, including the laptop's touchpad and keyboard to stop responding for a few seconds while it starts!
The trackpad is either very sensitive or doesn't do well recognizing palm. Sometimes both the keyboard and the mousepad just act weird. The keyboard on my Surface Go is way better and the touchpad on my XPS 9350, which is way smaller, is also better. On several occasions too some keys double registered, don't know if it's a software or a hardware issue or maybe it's jut that I'm still not used to typing on this keyboard yet.
The documentation, especially with the Core V2, is not sufficient to understand how to properly configure the pair. Is it safe to unplug without disconnecting the GPU first? What if I want to disconnect the GPU only and still use the USB ports and the ethernet port? How will keeping the laptop connected to the core, which means it's always being charged, affect battery life and performance?
Coming out of the Dell experience, I really expected more from this machine and from Razer overall. Dell has this nifty software tool that scans your laptop and tells you exactly which drivers you should get and updates everything automatically. It just works.
Another major let-down was the fact that if you turn on the USB charging feature by adjusting the setting for it in the BIOS, the laptop will actually discharge while turned off. The battery died out on me a couple of times before I took to the internet and found that other people had the same problem too.
Another minor issue but to me is quite annoying, when the power adapter is connected, there is no LED indicator that the laptop is charging which is 1\ very useful when the laptop is actually turned off while charging, and 2\ every other laptop I have ever used does indicate somehow that the laptop is being charged. I understand there's this tiny green LED on the charger itself, but it is just not enough. The LED is actually there right on the front of the laptop! Why are you not using it?
The worst issue I had with it is the rubbish screws used to attach the bottom panel. I have upgraded the original 256 GB SSD to a 512 GB one which was originally installed on my Dell XPS 13. The panel on the Dell can be removed and screwed back on very easily, but on the Razer, it gave me hell, it was as if the screws aren't aligned anymore to the holes in the chassis. All the screws are now scratched with the black paint removed. Very ugly experience really. I guess it is because the screws are painted the same way the unit itself is causing the screw-driver not to gain sufficient grip on them.
It's a lovely little machine, I love how it looks and love its size which is exactly the same as my old Dell XPS 9350 which to me is the perfect size for a laptop. Just make sure you skin it as soon as you get it and carry it in a proper sleeve so it won't get scratched.

As a creator (and not a gamer), I do video and photo editing on this machine, mostly connected to an external monitor and plugged into wall power. In this context, this machine with its specs is probably the best value of 2022 from a major brand name that is broadly available online.

You can find various online reviews of this machine (or its closely-related 2022 G15 relative), so I won't rehash anything really here. But I would just offer these salient points that aren't immediately obvious in some reviews:

The (major) high's for me:
(1) The CPU and GPU are allowed to run high in their power thermal envelopes, so you're getting a lot of performance for this combination of hardware.
(2) The 2022 G16 has a 16:10 screen, which is superior for creation and productivity versus the 2022 G15's 16:9.
(3) The included 2x16GB DDR5 RAM sit in two slots that are user-upgradeable to 2x32GB when I'm ready.

The (minor) low's for me:
(1) The single USB-C Thunderbolt port does not support Power Delivery, so you're stuck using the included brick and barrel power jack for power.
(2) There is no connector on the motherboard for a second M.2 PCIe SDD. They seemingly removed this capability in 2022, though the 2021 G15 did have this.
(3) The trackpad is laughingly small given how big this laptop is. They could have pushed the keyboard higher on the deck to make more room below the keyboard for a bigger trackpad.
(5) When using high performance settings, unsurprisingly, the fans sound like a passenger jet taking off.
(6) The included Dell and Alienware configuration software are unsurprisingly slightly buggy. For example, settings don't always "stick"; the laptop charges up to 100% even when I set it to stop charging, say, 80%; and pressing keyboard backlight button sometimes doesn't do anything until I load up the Alienware config software again.

In my view, the high's far and away outweigh the (minor) low's, especially for how I use the machine.

title: Great specs…. But does it live up to those?
text:
This Alienware m15 R7 Gaming Laptop is definitely a great gaming laptop, with the specs this thing totes I have enjoyed using this over the last few weeks. But there are also some things that I was not a fan of, especially considering the price point of this laptop.

Right out of the box this is definitely a solid laptop. It definitely feels solidly made and has some weight to it as well. I found that the hinge was very smooth and didn’t pickup the bottom when opening, which is a big pet peeve of mine.

The first thing I noticed about this laptop that I was really impressed with was the keypad. As far as a basic keypad goes it’s really nice for both gaming and typing. The keys are smooth and effortless to used, while not being crazy deep. This is probably one of my favorite keypads food date on any laptop.

The trackpad on the other hand is super duper small. Granted it’s fine for most things, but if your planning on using this for work or something other than gaming this may be a major downside. However I will say that the trackpad performs well and I had no issues at all with using it, other than the size of course.

As far as the screen goes it’s ok…I mean it looks good and the color contrast is nice. But I definitely think they could have done much better for the price point. While I do use a 4K monitor for gaming the majority of the time, I would have still preferred a nicer screen. And honestly before the specs were announced I was expecting it to be better.

The camera is absolute crap on this, so if your planning on using it for work or zoom calls then your definitely going to need to buy one. Also on calls the sound quality is not great. It sounds like your in a giant room with an echo no matter where I talked.

Overall it’s definitely a decent laptop, but I think for the price Dell could have done better with things like the screen, camera, and sound quality. Overall I give it 3 1/2 stars.
